Backseat Banton
fact: "Backseat Banton" is the closing track of Bartees Strange's 2025 album Horror, released via 4AD, and it arrived as the record's final pre-release single. Strange performed the song live on Jimmy Kimmel Live! ahead of the album's release.

title: Lie 95
fact: "Lie 95" was the first single from Bartees Strange's third album, Horror (4AD), released in July 2024. It's a love song set along Interstate 95, the highway that runs from Florida to Maine, and the video follows him searching for love up the Northeast corridor.

title: All Your Gold
fact: While recording "All Your Gold" for 2012's The Haunted Man, Natasha Khan and producer Dan Carey got an unusual percussion sound by filling glasses with water and striking them with forks, a session Khan says took forever because the two of them kept cracking up laughing. Khan called this one the "difficult teenager" of the record, since it wouldn't come together for months. She eventually scrapped an early version entirely and rewrote it in a new key with a new chorus before it finally clicked.

title: Daniel
fact: Daniel was the lead single from Bat for Lashes' second album, Two Suns (2009), and became her best-selling single, reaching number 36 in the UK. Her debut, Fur and Gold, had been nominated for the 2007 Mercury Prize.

title: Glass
fact: "Glass" is actually the opening track of Bat for Lashes' second album, Two Suns, released in April 2009, rather than her 2006 debut Fur and Gold. The sweeping opener sets the tone for a record built around Natasha Khan's self-created alter ego, Pearl, a device she used to explore themes of duality throughout the album.

title: Kids In The Dark
fact: "Kids In The Dark" comes from Bat for Lashes' 2019 concept album Lost Girls, on which Natasha Khan created an alter ego named Nikki Pink, heroine of an imagined 1980s girl-gang movie. Khan has said the song grew out of the feeling of driving through Los Angeles at sunset, giving its synth-pop sound an "us-against-the-world" romance.

title: Laura
fact: "Laura" is the only co-written song on Bat for Lashes' 2012 album The Haunted Man, penned with Justin Parker after Natasha Khan's label pushed her to write something with single potential. She worked out the piano chords with Parker, then recorded her vocal take - the one that made the final record - the very first time she sang it.

title: Marilyn
fact: 'Marilyn' is a track from Bat for Lashes' (Natasha Khan) 2012 album The Haunted Man, inspired by Marilyn Monroe as a symbol of old-Hollywood glamour and transformation. Khan sings to the icon almost like an invocation, asking to borrow some of her star power. Beck contributes guitar and synths on the track.

title: Oh Yeah
fact: "Oh Yeah" appears on Bat for Lashes' 2012 album The Haunted Man, written by Natasha Khan and produced by a team including Dan Carey, David Kosten, and Rob Ellis.

title: The Hunger
fact: Bat for Lashes' "The Hunger," from 2019's Lost Girls, started with an old '80s synth organ sound Natasha Khan was playing around with before co-writer/producer Charles Scott IV added bass - the whole album grew out of a screenplay Khan had been writing, inspired by '80s vampire and coming-of-age films.

title: Eden
fact: "Eden" was released as a single in January 2025 ahead of Baths' album Gut (February 2025). Baths is the project of Will Wiesenfeld, who debuted with Cerulean in 2010 on Anticon, and this track builds into a hooky dance-pop song before dissolving into strings.

title: Atlas
fact: "Atlas" is the breakout instrumental from Battles' 2007 debut album Mirrored. Singer-guitarist Tyondai Braxton's vocals were run through pitch-shifting effects to create the track's unmistakable helium-like chant, layered over a shuffling groove based on "schaffel," a rhythm style born in German techno clubs. The song became an unlikely radio and blog hit for the experimental math-rock group.

title: All We Ever Wanted Was Everything
Kick in the Eye
fact: "Kick in the Eye" was released as a single in March 1981 ahead of Bauhaus's second album, Mask, which expanded the band's sound with saxophone, keyboards, and funk-inflected rhythms. The song's title was drawn from a line in Jack Kerouac's novel Satori in Paris. It became one of two singles from Mask to crack the UK Top 60 that year.

title: She's in Parties
fact: "She's in Parties" was Bauhaus's final single, released in 1983 and later included on their album Burning from the Inside; it reached number 26 on the UK Singles Chart. Guitarist Daniel Ash recalled that the lyrics were written as a group exercise on a tour bus, with all three other members shouting out lines and images for singer Peter Murphy to piece together. The band split the following year, with Murphy going solo and the rest forming Love and Rockets.

title: All I Did Was Dream of You (Feat. The Mar�as)
Beaches
fact: beabadoobee's “Beaches” is a song about self-discovery and not waiting around for the right moment - “Don't wait for the tide, just to dip both your feet in” - built on crunchy guitars that recall Weezer's “Island in the Sun.”

title: Memories
fact: "Memories" comes from beabadoobee's 2026 album Pylon, released via Dirty Hit/Interscope. She co-wrote the acoustic-driven track with Shane Moran and Gianluca Buccellati and called it one of the happiest-sounding songs on the record, even though its lyrics dwell on the bittersweet pull of nostalgia.

title: Nothing to Prove (feat. Hayley Williams)
fact: beabadoobee's "Nothing to Prove," featuring Hayley Williams, comes from her 2026 album Pylon - a record whose 14 songs also feature cameos from Turnstile's Brendan Yates and Deftones' Chino Moreno.

title: Sun Has Set
fact: The first single from beabadoobee's 2026 album Pylon is a hard left turn into grunge and '90s alt-rock crunch, a heavier sound than anything she'd released before. She's said the lyrics came straight out of raw diary entries — words she once figured she'd never actually say out loud.

title: Take A Bite
fact: "Take A Bite" is the lead single from beabadoobee's third studio album, This Is How Tomorrow Moves. She's said the song was partly inspired by an Elliott Smith song and partly by a "funky" rhythm she picked up from an Ashlee Simpson track.

title: When I Grow Up (To Be A Man)
Careless
fact: "Careless" was the first single from Beach Fossils' 2013 album Clash the Truth, arriving in December 2012 on Captured Tracks a couple months ahead of the record. It's a hazy, reverb-soaked jangle-pop track that previewed the faster, more urgent direction the Brooklyn band pushed on the rest of the album.

title: Daydream
fact: "Daydream" is a highlight from Beach Fossils' self-titled 2010 debut album, released on Captured Tracks. Frontman Dustin Payseur wrote, recorded, and produced the entire record himself, blending jangly post-punk guitar lines with a hazy, lo-fi sheen that helped define the early-2010s Brooklyn indie scene.

title: Seconds
fact: Seconds is a single from Beach Fossils' 2023 album Bunny, their first full-length in six years. Frontman Dustin Payseur wrote it around the bittersweet feeling of loving someone more than they love you back, pairing the downbeat theme with jangly, upbeat guitar hooks. The contrast between wistful lyrics and sunny instrumentation is a signature of the band's sound.

title: 10 Mile Stereo
fact: "10 Mile Stereo" was recorded in July 2009 at Dreamland Studio in Hurley, New York, for Beach House's breakthrough third album, Teen Dream (2010). The shoegaze-leaning track built a devoted following of its own, selling over 40,000 digital downloads by 2012, the biggest-selling individual track from the album at that point.

Beach House recorded "10:37" during an unusual session that produced two full albums at once, Depression Cherry and Thank Your Lucky Stars, holed up at Studio in the Country in Bogalusa, Louisiana, over the winter of 2014 into 2015. It landed on Depression Cherry as one of the record's heavier, more shoegaze-leaning tracks. Releasing two albums out of one extended session was a first for the duo.

title: Apple Orchard
fact: "Apple Orchard" is the third track on Beach House's self-titled 2006 debut, and its inclusion on Pitchfork's "Infinite Mixtape" series that August helped introduce the duo to a much wider audience. Years later, a stripped-down four-track demo of the song turned up as the B-side to the "Used to Be" single from their later album Teen Dream.

title: April Suzanne (Cover Version)
fact: Beach House's “April Suzanne” is a cover of a 1976 song by Robert Lester Folsom, released as a limited 7″ single (only 1,000 copies worldwide) to celebrate the 50th anniversary of his album Music and Dreams.

title: Become
fact: "Become" is the title track and closer of Beach House's 2023 EP of the same name, a five-song collection pulled from the sessions for their 2022 album Once Twice Melody. The dream-pop duo said the songs didn't feel like they fit into Once Twice Melody's world, so rather than leave them as leftovers, they gave the tracks a home of their own on a standalone release.

title: Dive
fact: 'Dive' comes from Beach House's 2018 album 7, released on Sub Pop. The track slow-builds from hazy synths into a churning, shoegaze-leaning climax with rolling percussion, a bigger sonic swing than the duo's earlier dream-pop work. Lyrically it plays with the tension between wanting to open up and the instinct to hold back, captured in the repeated line 'tell her something, tell her nothing.'

title: Gila
fact: "Gila" is a highlight from Beach House's 2008 sophomore album Devotion, recorded at a space called Lord Baltimore over the summer of 2007. Devotion became the Baltimore duo's first album to chart on the Billboard 200.

title: Heart of Chambers
fact: Beach House wrote "Heart of Chambers," a highlight of their 2008 album Devotion, after noise complaints forced them out of their original practice spot at guitarist Alex Scally's house. They relocated to a new rehearsal space near Baltimore's I-83 highway, where the song came together.

title: Lose Your Smile
fact: "Lose Your Smile" is a standalone Beach House single, paired with the B-side "Alien" and recorded at Palmetto Studio in Los Angeles following the release of their 2018 album 7. It was issued as a 7-inch rather than appearing on a full-length record.

title: Myth
fact: "Myth" is the opening track and lead single from Beach House's 2012 album Bloom, released via Sub Pop. Critics called its organ-and-synth-driven intro a "monumental kick-off" to the record.

title: New Romance
fact: New Romance is from Beach House's eighth album, the double album Once Twice Melody (Sub Pop, February 2022). It was released in four "chapters" starting in November 2021, and the song runs on a swirling, calliope-like synth loop.

title: Pink Funeral
fact: Beach House's "Pink Funeral" comes from 2021's Once Twice Melody, the duo's most expansive record - Alex Scally and Victoria Legrand pair a sweeping, string-driven arrangement with one of their darker electronic backdrops, giving the song an almost film-score quality.

title: Real Love
fact: 'Real Love' is the ninth track on Beach House's 2010 breakthrough album Teen Dream, recorded not in their native Baltimore but at Dreamland, a converted church studio in upstate New York. The album was produced by Chris Coady, who also worked with TV on the Radio, Yeah Yeah Yeahs, and Blonde Redhead, and 'Real Love' is often singled out as one of the record's rare moments of hope amid its wintry, lovelorn tone.

title: Sparks
fact: "Sparks," the opening track on Beach House's 2015 album Depression Cherry, began almost by accident: during a Bristol, England soundcheck, Victoria Legrand's voice looped through the PA, and the duo were so struck by the ethereal sound that they recorded it on their phones. That accidental loop became the vocal hook that runs through the finished song.

title: Used to Be
fact: "Used to Be" began life as Beach House's debut single, released on Carpark Records in October 2008 and written and produced by Victoria Legrand and Alex Scally with Chris Coady. The duo re-recorded the song for their 2010 album Teen Dream, and the original 2008 version later resurfaced on their 2017 compilation B-Sides and Rarities.

title: Walk in the Park
fact: "Walk in the Park" is a dream-pop track from Beach House's breakout 2010 album Teen Dream, written by the Baltimore duo Victoria Legrand and Alex Scally and produced with Chris Coady. It later got a stripped-down rework on the band's iTunes Session EP the same year.

title: Wild
fact: "Wild" was actually the earliest song Beach House wrote for their 2012 album Bloom, coming together while they were still mixing the previous record, Teen Dream. It was tracked during an intensive nine-week session at Sonic Ranch in Tornillo, Texas. The song stands out in their catalog for its dramatic build and climax, capped by a shoegaze-leaning electric guitar bridge that's more amped-up than the duo's usual dream-pop sound.

title: You Came to Me
fact: "You Came to Me" appears on Beach House's debut album "Devotion," recorded at the Lord Baltimore studio in the summer of 2007 and released in 2008 on Carpark Records. AllMusic described it as a "stunner" of dark chamber pop, and the duo made a music video for the track as part of the album's promotion.

title: Zebra
fact: Beach House's Victoria Legrand and Alex Scally met in Baltimore's indie scene and first played together in a band called Daggerhearts before forming Beach House in 2004. Their song "Apple Orchard" being featured on Pitchfork's Infinite Mixtape gave them their first big break.

title: (You Gotta) Fight For Your Right (To Party!)
Egg Man
fact: "Egg Man," from the Beastie Boys' 1989 album Paul's Boutique, opens with the screeching strings of Bernard Herrmann's score for Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho, sampling the famous "Murder" cue from the shower scene. The track later folds in a nod to John Williams' Jaws theme as well. It's one of dozens of samples packed into Paul's Boutique, an album famous for its dense, collage-like production by the Dust Brothers.

title: Intergalactic
fact: "Intergalactic" was the lead single from Beastie Boys' 1998 album Hello Nasty and became the trio's biggest UK hit, reaching No. 5 there and No. 28 on the US Hot 100. Its Adam Yauch-directed video, shot in Tokyo's Shibuya and Shinjuku districts, is an homage to Japanese tokusatsu and kaiju shows, with a giant robot battling a trident-wielding, cephalopod-headed monster. The song went on to win the Grammy for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group.

title: Jimmy James
fact: "Jimmy James," the opening track on Beastie Boys' 1992 album Check Your Head, is named after a stage pseudonym Jimi Hendrix used early in his career while fronting Jimmy James and the Blue Flames. The group originally built the song almost entirely from Hendrix samples, but when the Hendrix estate denied clearance, they re-recorded it keeping only a few approved samples.

title: No Sleep Till Brooklyn
fact: "No Sleep till Brooklyn," a single from Beastie Boys' 1986 debut Licensed to Ill, features a guest guitar solo from Slayer's Kerry King, an unlikely rap-rock pairing that helped make it one of the group's signature tracks. Its title nods to Motorhead's live album No Sleep 'til Hammersmith, reworked into an ode to missing home while on tour.

title: Shake Your Rump
fact: "Shake Your Rump" is one of the most heavily sampled tracks on Paul's Boutique, built from a collage of more than a dozen source records. Its backbone drum groove comes from jazz drummer Alphonse Mouzon's "Funky Snakefoot," layered with pieces of songs by Rose Royce, Afrika Bambaataa, and Funky 4+1, among others. The concluding drum fill before the final rap section is even lifted from Led Zeppelin's "Good Times Bad Times." The Dust Brothers and the Beastie Boys built the whole of Paul's Boutique this way, splicing together an estimated 100 to 300 samples across the album.

title: Bewitched
fact: Beat Happening formed in Olympia, Washington in 1982 among students at Evergreen State College, and became pioneers of the lo-fi, twee-pop sound built on enthusiasm over technical polish. During the recording of "Bewitched," the opening track on their 1988 album Jamboree, guitarist Bret Lunsford's guitar string got caught on a protruding screw — rather than stop, he kept playing and hitting the string harder until it worked itself loose, and the take stayed on the record.

title: Indian Summer
fact: "Indian Summer" is the best-known song from Beat Happening's 1988 album Jamboree, reportedly one of Kurt Cobain's favorite records. Dream-pop band Luna covered it, and Death Cab for Cutie's Ben Gibbard recorded his own version for the soundtrack of the Cobain documentary About a Son.

title: Class Reunion
fact: "Class Reunion" is by Beatrix, the Los Angeles-based chamber-pop project of singer-songwriter Arielle Kasnetz. It's a single from her sophomore album We Swallowed the Sky, and its music video leans into a quirky "Twin Peaks meets The Office" atmosphere set inside a sterile community center.

title: Turn You Down
fact: "Turn You Down" comes from Beatrix's sophomore album We Swallowed the Sky, the project of Los Angeles songwriter Arielle Kasnetz. Kasnetz grew up training in classical piano and vocal scales but didn't start writing her own songs until the pandemic, when she picked up an acoustic guitar she'd been given years earlier. For this album she worked as a trio with co-producers Philip Etherington and Ehren Ebbage.

title: Blue Moon
fact: Beck's 'Blue Moon,' the lead single from 2014's Morning Phase, borrows its title from the classic Rodgers and Hart standard. Beck has said part of the song's inspiration came from reading Peter Guralnick's two-volume Elvis Presley biography, reflecting on who Elvis was starting out versus who he became later in life. The song was actually an old, nearly forgotten demo that Beck rediscovered and added to the album at the last minute.

title: Chemical
fact: "Chemical," from Beck's 2019 album Hyperspace, was co-written and co-produced with Pharrell Williams, who processes and contorts Beck's voice throughout the track. Beck framed the song's central idea — treating love itself as "a chemical" reaction a person can't fully control — with a cold, almost scientific detachment, calling the result "a lullaby delivered from a space shuttle with just one person on it."

title: Cyanide Breath Mint
fact: "Cyanide Breath Mint" appears on Beck's stripped-down, lo-fi 1994 album One Foot in the Grave, recorded at Dub Narcotic Studio. Beck liked the phrase enough that he later named his own music publishing company, Cyanide Breathmint Music, after the song.

title: Dear Life
fact: "Dear Life" opens Beck's 2017 album Colors, produced by Beck alongside Greg Kurstin. The track is built around a jaunty, jazz-tinged piano riff before opening up into rock guitar and vocal harmonies. It was released as an instant-download single when the album was announced, with an accompanying lyric video mixing live-action footage and psychedelic animation.

title: Die Waiting
fact: "Die Waiting" is a duet between Beck and Sky Ferreira from his 2019 album Hyperspace, built around a mystic, slowly building guitar riff layered with electronics. The song is a devotional, patience-themed ballad, with the two trading lines about waiting out hard times for someone they love.

title: Hotwax
fact: "Hotwax" is track two on Beck's 1996 album Odelay, co-produced with the Dust Brothers (credited on the song as E.Z. Mike and King Gizmo alongside Beck). The track layers Beck's own harmonica playing and turntable scratching over a loose breakbeat, a grab-bag collage approach typical of the album's dense, sample-heavy sound.

title: No Distraction
fact: "No Distraction" is a reggae-funk flavored track from Beck's 2017 album Colors, built on a strummy chord progression he's said was partly inspired by the Police. He described writing it about the modern urge to be fully present with someone despite constant phone and screen distractions.

title: Que' Onde Guero
fact: Beck has said 'Que Onda Guero,' from his 2005 album Guero, is 'about growing up' in the Chicano neighborhood of Los Angeles where he spent part of his childhood, built like a 'watercolor, pen-and-ink' sketch of the area. To capture that atmosphere, he recorded ambient street sounds like pushcart vendors, a popsicle cart, and kids playing soccer and wove them into the track. The title itself is slang Beck says he regularly heard shouted at him growing up in the neighborhood.

title: Ride Lonesome
fact: "Ride Lonesome" is the title track and opener of Beck's 15th studio album, released September 2026 — his first new album since 2019's Hyperspace, marking the longest gap of his career. He produced it himself and brought back longtime collaborator Nigel Godrich to mix, landing on the kind of intimate, cinematic sound that made his earlier records so beloved.

title: Run Away
fact: Beck's "Run Away," from 2026's Ride Lonesome, was mixed by longtime collaborator Nigel Godrich - its Tokyo-set music video stars Golden Globe-winning actor Tadanobu Asano, known for roles in Shogun and Thor: Ragnarok.

title: Saw Lightning
fact: Saw Lightning, the lead single from Beck's 2019 album Hyperspace, was co-written and produced with Pharrell Williams, who also plays drums and keyboards and contributes an ad-libbed vocal breakdown on the track. Beck has said he'd wanted to make a record with Pharrell and the Neptunes ever since their sound first broke through around the time of his own Midnite Vultures, making the collaboration two decades in the making. The song later soundtracked a Beats by Dre commercial.

title: Say Goodbye
fact: "Say Goodbye" was the third single from Beck's 2014 album Morning Phase, recorded largely live over just a few days in early 2013 in his hometown of Los Angeles. Beck told The Sun he was "making up the melody as you hear it" on the track, and critics likened its warm, Gram Parsons-style guitar work to Neil Young's Harvest.

title: Seventh Heaven
fact: "Seventh Heaven" comes from Beck's 2017 album Colors, which he recorded over several years with producer Greg Kurstin at Kurstin's Los Angeles studio, with the two of them playing nearly every instrument themselves. Q magazine called it a "lost '80s pop classic," and Rolling Stone described it as "a chiming anthem about falling in love." Introducing it live, Beck has jokingly warned crowds, "This is a very feel-good song, I'm warning you."

title: Teenage Wastebasket
fact: "Teenage Wastebasket" appears on Beck's 1994 album One Foot in the Grave, which was recorded in the basement studio of Calvin Johnson, founder of K Records and the band Beat Happening. Johnson contributed production, co-writing, and backing vocals to the lo-fi, folk-leaning record, which went on to become one of K Records' most successful releases.

title: Thinking About You
fact: Beck released "Thinking About You" as a surprise single in 2024 with no advance warning, marking his first new material since a 2022 Neil Young cover. The mellow, acoustic track was recorded in the same studio where Beck made his 2003 album Sea Change, and he debuted it live on Jimmy Kimmel Live.

title: Uneventful Days
fact: "Uneventful Days" is one of seven tracks Beck co-wrote and co-produced with Pharrell Williams on his 2019 album Hyperspace, a collaboration Beck had wanted to make for years before their schedules finally lined up after his Colors tour. Its music video, directed by Dev Hynes, stars Evan Rachel Wood, Tessa Thompson, and Alia Shawkat, and nods to earlier Beck videos like "Devils Haircut" and "Sexx Laws."

title: Wow
fact: Beck has said 'Wow' came together almost by accident - he stumbled onto a flute-like synth riff while working on a different song, picked up a mic, and freestyled the vocals on the spot. He nearly left it off 2017's Colors entirely, doubting anyone would like it, until his label pushed to release it as a single.

title: Adored
fact: Adored was the second single of 2025 from New York five-piece Been Stellar, following Breakaway, ahead of their debut album Scream From New York, NY. The band is Sam Slocum, Skyler Knapp, Laila Wayans, Nico Brunstein and Nando Dale.

title: Passing Judgement
fact: 'Passing Judgement' is the lead single and second track off Been Stellar's 2024 debut album Scream From New York, NY, produced by Dan Carey. The band was still finishing the song's lyrics during their first-ever UK tour in the summer of 2022, which gives the final recording its loose, slightly chaotic live energy. Singer Sam Slocum has said the song is really about how judging others often comes from feeling unsure of yourself.

title: Godzilla Rises
fact: "Godzilla Rises" comes from Austin art-punk trio Being Dead's 2024 album EELS, produced by John Congleton. Despite the title, it's actually a tender love song addressed to the giant movie monster himself. The band's members -- Falcon Bitch, Shmoofy, and Nicole Roman-Johnston -- are known for swapping instruments and trading lead vocals throughout their live sets.

title: Nightvision
fact: "Nightvision" was the third single from Being Dead's 2024 album EELS, produced by John Congleton. It's a quieter turn for the Texas trio, opening with a subdued, almost pop-leaning hook before an acoustic rhythm pulls it into folkier, nocturnal territory. The track runs under three minutes and sits as one of the album's moodiest detours.

title: A Candle's Fire
fact: 'A Candle's Fire' opens Beirut's 2011 album The Rip Tide with a single accordion that blooms into a full horn section, the signature sound bandleader Zach Condon built his career on. The track features Jon Natchez on baritone saxophone and background vocals from fellow singer-songwriter Sharon Van Etten. It's one of the brassiest, most orchestral moments on a record that otherwise leans into quieter, more intimate songwriting.

title: Caspian Tiger
fact: "Caspian Tiger" by Beirut (the project of Zach Condon) was originally composed for the soundtrack of A Study of Losses, a production by the Swedish circus company Kompani Giraff. Named for an extinct tiger subspecies once found around the Caspian Sea, the track opens with solo piano before harp and brass enter, echoing the Renaissance and choral influences found throughout Condon's earlier work.

title: Cliquot
fact: Cliquot appears on Beirut's 2007 album The Flying Club Cup. While making the record, bandleader Zach Condon immersed himself in Jacques Brel and French chanson music, picking up new instruments like French horns and euphoniums to build out the album's brass-heavy sound, while violinist and composer Owen Pallett contributed orchestral string arrangements.

title: East Harlem
fact: Zach Condon wrote the melody for "East Harlem" when he was just 17, years before Beirut existed, and rediscovered it while combing through old home recordings while making 2011's The Rip Tide. The song was released as the album's lead single and was named Pitchfork's "Best New Track" upon release.

title: Elephant Gun
fact: "Elephant Gun" got its start tucked onto the "Lon Gisland" EP before becoming the title track of Beirut's 2007 "Elephant Gun" EP — and it gave the band their first-ever music video, directed by Alma Har'el.

title: Fisher Island Sound
fact: Fisher Island Sound was released in October 2021 to announce Beirut's album Artifacts. Zach Condon wrote it while staying at bandmate Ben Lanz's old family cottage on the Connecticut coast, which sits on the body of water named in the title.

title: Gallipoli
fact: Beirut's title track "Gallipoli" came from a chance encounter - Zach Condon stumbled into a brass band procession carrying a saint's statue through the Italian town of Gallipoli, with church bells ringing and the band's sound bouncing off the narrow streets. He wrote the entire song the next day in one sitting, pausing only to eat.

title: Guericke's Unicorn
fact: "Guericke's Unicorn" is from Beirut's album A Study of Losses, written for a stage show commissioned by the Swedish circus Kompani Giraff and inspired by Judith Schalansky's novel An Inventory of Losses. The title refers to a supposed fossil unicorn that was really reconstructed from the bones of animals like a mammoth and a narwhal.

title: Nantes
fact: "Nantes," from Beirut's 2006 debut Gulag Orkestar, was partly inspired by Jamaican dub producer King Tubby's reggae records; Zach Condon has joked about the connection, and the band reportedly plays the song as a straight reggae tune at soundchecks, just never during an actual show. Condon recorded the whole album as a teenager in his bedroom in Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: No No No
fact: Beirut recorded 'No No No' and the rest of the album together in just two weeks, tracking live in the studio with bassist Paul Collins and drummer Nick Petree in fall 2014. It was frontman Zach Condon's first new material after taking time off from touring, and the album came out on 4AD on September 11, 2015.

title: Perth
fact: Beirut is essentially one person, Zach Condon, who dropped out of high school in Santa Fe at 17, moved to Paris, and fell in with a group of musicians playing Balkan brass-band music - a sound that became the foundation of his project.

title: Postcards From Italy
fact: Beirut's "Postcards from Italy" comes from 2006's Gulag Orkestar, recorded mostly alone in his childhood bedroom by a teenage Zach Condon before he finished the album in New Mexico with Jeremy Barnes of Neutral Milk Hotel and A Hawk and a Hacksaw.

title: Santa Fe
fact: Beirut frontman Zach Condon grew up in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and told Mojo the 2011 song is a "positive song about the hometown I once felt such a distance from," written after visiting as an adult with a more established career. The song's distinctive electric organ part actually came from an old instrument Condon was recording at his parents' house over a Christmas visit, originally meant for a documentary soundtrack before he repurposed it here.

title: So Many Plans
fact: 'So Many Plans' is the lead single from Beirut's 2023 album Hadsel, named for the Norwegian island where frontman Zach Condon spent time in 2020. There, a local organ enthusiast introduced him to the pipe organ at the Hadselkirke church, whose sound became the foundation for the record; Condon called the song's lyric a 'covid-times lament' that turned into a gentle lullaby balancing acceptance, hope, and giving up.

title: Vagabond
fact: "Vagabond" appears on Beirut's third studio album, The Rip Tide (2011). Critics singled it out as the record's turn toward orchestrated, '70s-style AM pop, a notable stylistic shift from the Balkan-brass sound bandleader Zach Condon had built his earlier releases around.

title: Expectations
fact: 'Expectations' appears on Belle and Sebastian's 1996 debut Tigermilk, which began as a class project - Stuart Murdoch's demos were picked for a recording session run by students in a music-business course at Glasgow's Stow College. That college assignment ended up launching both the album and the band itself.

title: Get Me Away From Here, I'm Dying
I Don't Know What You See In Me
fact: Belle and Sebastian's "I Don't Know What You See In Me" marked a first for the band - their first-ever co-write with an outside songwriter, Scottish producer Wuh Oh (Peter Ferguson), on the lead single from 2023's Late Developers.

I'll Be Your Pilot
album: How To Solve Our Human Problems
fact: 'I'll Be Your Pilot' is Stuart Murdoch's tender ode to his young son Denny, written for Belle and Sebastian's How to Solve Our Human Problems EP trilogy. Murdoch said becoming a father made him feel like the pilot character from Antoine de Saint-Exupery's The Little Prince, which inspired the song's desert and flying imagery.

title: Is It Wicked Not to Care?
album: The Boy with the Arab Strap
fact: "Is It Wicked Not to Care?" appears on Belle and Sebastian's 1998 album The Boy with the Arab Strap and marks the first time multi-instrumentalist Isobel Campbell sang lead vocals for the band. Frontman Stuart Murdoch wrote the song the morning after Scotland's win over Denmark in World Cup qualifying.

title: Safety Valve
fact: "Safety Valve" is actually older than Belle and Sebastian itself — Stuart Murdoch wrote it before the band had formed. It sat unreleased for decades until it finally surfaced on the soundtrack to the 2019 film Days of the Bagnold Summer, giving fans a glimpse of Murdoch's songwriting style in its earliest, twee-pop form.

title: Same Star
album: How To Solve Our Human Problems

title: Sleep the Clock Around
album: The Boy with the Arab Strap
fact: This nearly five-minute epic off 1998's The Boy with the Arab Strap features Isobel Campbell trading verses with Stuart Murdoch in one of the band's most richly arranged early duets. It's become a fan-favorite deep cut precisely because of that interplay — two voices circling each other over a patient, slow-build arrangement.

title: The Blues Are Still Blue
fact: "The Blues Are Still Blue" was the second single from Belle and Sebastian's 2006 album The Life Pursuit, produced by Tony Hoffer. It's an unusually straightforward, rollicking rock song for the famously twee Scottish band, and despite its energy the lyrics are, as critics have noted, nominally about something as mundane as doing laundry.

title: Unnecessary Drama
fact: "Unnecessary Drama" was the lead single from Belle and Sebastian's 2022 album A Bit of Previous, the Scottish band's first full studio album since 2015. It was recorded in their hometown of Glasgow after the pandemic derailed original plans to record in Los Angeles, and its video shows the band comically working out their tensions with a therapist and team-building exercises.

album: Fold Your Hands Child You Walk Like A Peasant

title: What Happened to You Son?
fact: This song was actually written for Belle and Sebastian's 2023 album Late Developers but got cut at the last minute because the record ran one track too long. Frontman Stuart Murdoch wrote it looking back at his own late teens, a rough stretch when he was struggling at university while living and breathing the music of that era. Despite its wistful, questioning title, the song ends on a hopeful note about finding a way forward.

title: Young And Stupid
fact: Belle and Sebastian released "Young and Stupid" in 2022 as a single from their album A Bit of Previous. Frontman Stuart Murdoch sings it from the perspective of his whole generation looking back fondly on youthful recklessness, and the lyric video was built entirely from childhood and teenage photos of the band members themselves.

title: Legal Man
Feed the Tree
fact: "Feed the Tree," from Belly's 1993 debut album Star, hit No. 1 on the Billboard Modern Rock Tracks chart. Songwriter Tanya Donelly originally wrote it as a possible contribution to a second Breeders album, but when bandmate Kim Deal committed to a long Pixies tour, Donelly started Belly instead rather than wait around. Paul McCartney reportedly sent Donelly a personal note congratulating her on the song.

title: Floating On A Moment
fact: 'Floating On A Moment' was the first taste of Lives Outgrown, Portishead singer Beth Gibbons' solo debut album, which took about a decade to finish. She made the record with Simian Mobile Disco's James Ford and former Talk Talk drummer Lee Harris producing. The album marked a real departure from Portishead's trip-hop sound and went on to earn a Mercury Prize nomination.

title: Reaching Out
fact: "Reaching Out" is a single from Beth Gibbons' debut solo album, Lives Outgrown, released in 2024 via Domino Recording Company — her first-ever solo full-length after decades fronting Portishead. The album, produced by Gibbons, James Ford, and Lee Harris, took roughly ten years to record, and the song's video was an interactive piece made with visual artist Weirdcore.

Crazy In Love feat. Jay Z
Hymnostic
fact: "Hymnostic" is the gospel-flavored highlight of Big Red Machine's 2018 self-titled debut, the collaborative project between Bon Iver's Justin Vernon and The National's Aaron Dessner. Dessner has said the song was designed as a communal singalong meant to invite as many voices as possible to join in, and Vernon noted it could work just as well arranged with fiddles and banjos.

title: Thirteen
fact: "Thirteen," written primarily by Alex Chilton with a credit to Chris Bell, was recorded in late 1971 at Ardent Studios in Memphis for Big Star's debut album #1 Record. Rolling Stone later ranked it among the 500 greatest songs of all time, calling it one of rock's most beautiful depictions of early adolescence. It's Big Star's most-covered song, with versions by Elliott Smith, Garbage, and Wilco among dozens of others, and Chilton himself singled out Garbage's cover as a favorite.

title: Century
fact: Big Thief's 'Century' comes from 2022's sprawling double album Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You, which the band pieced together across four completely different recording sessions. They tracked in a barn in upstate New York, a canyon house in Topanga, a cabin in the Colorado Rockies, and a studio in Tucson, Arizona, over about five months. All told, they wrote and recorded 45 songs before narrowing things down to the final tracklist.

title: Forgotten Eyes
fact: "Forgotten Eyes" appears on Big Thief's 2019 album Two Hands, which the band tracked live at Sonic Ranch studio in the desert outside El Paso, Texas, with almost no overdubs. Nearly every vocal on the record was a single live take, and the song opens with drummer James Krivchenia's kit mic'd so closely it sounds like he's playing in the room with the listener. The album arrived just months after its companion release, U.F.O.F., giving Big Thief two studio albums in a single year.

title: Happy With You
fact: "Happy with You" appears on Big Thief's 2025 album Double Infinity. It was co-written by all three band members - Adrianne Lenker, Buck Meek, and James Krivchenia - the first time songs on a Big Thief album carried all three names, and its lyrics are structured in the form of a haiku.

title: Heavy Bend
album: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You
fact: "Heavy Bend" appears on Big Thief's 2019 album U.F.O.F., recorded with longtime producer Andrew Sarlo at Bear Creek Studios, a converted barn on a farm outside Woodinville, Washington. The rural, intimate setting fed into the hushed, atmospheric sound that defines the record. U.F.O.F. was the first of two Big Thief albums released that year, paired later with the louder Two Hands.

title: Incomprehensible
fact: Incomprehensible opens Big Thief's sixth album, Double Infinity (4AD, 2025), their first as a trio. The band recorded it live over about three weeks at the Power Station studio in New York City, with producer Dom Monks.

title: Little Things
album: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You

title: Masterpiece
fact: "Masterpiece" is the title track of Big Thief's debut studio album, released May 27, 2016 on Saddle Creek Records. NPR's Bob Boilen singled it out as one of the best songs he'd heard that year.

title: Mythological Beauty
fact: Big Thief's Adrianne Lenker and Buck Meek met at a show in Boston, then reconnected in Brooklyn as undergrads at Berklee College of Music. They toured as a duo for two years before forming a full band with fellow Berklee grads Max Oleartchik and James Krivchenia in 2015.

title: No Fear
fact: 'No Fear' appears on Big Thief's 2025 album Double Infinity. It's a hypnotic, mantra-like piece built from looping bass and guitar, with Adrianne Lenker repeating spare, meditative lines like 'there is no fear, mind so clear, mind so free.'

title: No Reason
album: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You
fact: Big Thief's "No Reason," from 2022's Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You, came together after the band heard someone playing flute from a nearby lookout tower while recording in the Colorado Rockies. That musician turned out to be Richard Hardy, a veteran session player who had worked with Carole King, and the band invited him to sit in, adding his flute to the finished track.

title: Not
fact: "Not" was the lead single from Big Thief's fourth album, Two Hands (2019). The band first recorded it live at Sonic Ranch studio in Tornillo, Texas, during the album's main sessions, but felt the take needed more room to breathe, so they scrapped it and re-recorded the song months later at Sound City Studios. Producer Andrew Sarlo, who has worked on every Big Thief album, oversaw both versions.

title: Orange
fact: "Orange" is the sixth track on Big Thief's third album, U.F.O.F. (2019), produced by longtime collaborator Andrew Sarlo. Its gentle, softly strummed arrangement has drawn comparisons to folk singer-songwriter Joan Shelley, giving the song a melody that feels centuries old within the album's more atmospheric material.

title: Paul
fact: Big Thief's "Paul," from their 2016 debut album Masterpiece, reads like a song about an ex-lover, but Adrianne Lenker has said it's really about reconciling two sides of her own personality - she described the lyrics as arriving almost like a future version of herself narrating "the whole story."

title: Real Love
fact: "Real Love" appears on Big Thief's debut album, Masterpiece, released May 27, 2016 on Saddle Creek Records (not on the later Capacity, as is sometimes assumed). It was released as a single on March 17, 2016, making it one of the first songs the band ever put out.

title: Red Moon
album: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You
fact: 'Red Moon' comes from Big Thief's sprawling 2022 double album Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe In You, recorded across four different sessions from upstate New York to Topanga Canyon and Tucson. The song leans into an Appalachian folk sound, powered by a wailing fiddle from guest musician Mat Davidson, who records solo as Twain.

title: Shark Smile
fact: Big Thief's "Shark Smile," from 2017's Capacity, was recorded in a farmhouse the band was house-sitting at the time - Adrianne Lenker has said she turned her guitar amp all the way up to 10 for the first time while cutting it, inspired by a tour-van diet of Springsteen's Nebraska.

title: Simulation Swarm
album: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You

title: Spud Infinity
album: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe In You
fact: "Spud Infinity," from Big Thief's 2022 album Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You, gets its distinctive twang from a jaw harp played by Noah Lenker, the younger brother of singer Adrianne Lenker. The playful, folk-flavored track quickly became a fan favorite for its loose, celebratory energy.

title: Strange
fact: "Strange," from Big Thief's 2019 album U.F.O.F., was described by Stereogum as "a jaunty funhouse of a song that unwinds like a twisted nursery rhyme." The track leans into surreal, dreamlike nature imagery — at one point picturing a luna moth crying "lime green tears" — as the arrangement gradually dissolves into a hazy, psychedelic mist of reverb and bubbling bass.

title: Terminal Paradise
fact: "Terminal Paradise" first appeared as the opening track of Big Thief singer Adrianne Lenker's 2018 solo album abysskiss. Big Thief later released their own version of the song too, including a live recording made at The Bunker Studio.

title: The Only Place
album: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You

title: Time Escaping
album: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You
fact: "Time Escaping" was tracked at a home studio in California's Topanga Canyon with engineer Shawn Everett, just one stop on a well-traveled recording trail. Big Thief cut the 20 songs on Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You across four separate sessions in four very different locations, from upstate New York to the Colorado Rockies.

title: Two Hands
fact: "Two Hands" is the title track of Big Thief's fourth album, released in October 2019 just five months after its companion record U.F.O.F. — the band called Two Hands the "earth twin" to that more ethereal album. It was recorded live off the floor at Sonic Ranch studio in Tornillo, Texas, with producer Andrew Sarlo, giving it a rawer, more stripped-down sound than its predecessor.

title: UFOF
fact: "UFOF," the title track of Big Thief's 2019 album U.F.O.F., gets its name from the phrase "UFO friend." The song opens with Adrianne Lenker bidding goodbye to a mysterious, otherworldly "UFO friend" who is "taking up root in the sky," making it one of the band's most ethereal, dreamlike tracks.

title: Vampire Empire
fact: Vampire Empire was released as a single on September 13, 2023, backed with Born for Loving You. It was recorded and produced by Dom Monks at Teatre de Cal Eril studio in Guissona, Spain, during a tour, and became a live favorite after a performance on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert.

fact: Billy London was created in 1978 when American-born musician Billy Barth moved to Britain to embrace its pop and punk scene. "Woman" was a 1981 single for RSO/Polydor produced by Nigel Gray, and it was rediscovered on the 2025 compilation All The Young Droids: Junkshop Synth Pop 1978-1985.

Army of Me
fact: "Army of Me" was written and produced by Bjork with Graham Massey of 808 State, and served as the lead single for both her 1995 album Post and the soundtrack to the film Tank Girl. Its stomping industrial groove is built around a slowed-down sample of the drum break from Led Zeppelin's "When the Levee Breaks."

title: Big Time Sensuality
fact: Bjork's "Big Time Sensuality," from 1993's Debut, was her breakthrough US hit - she's said the song, despite its title, isn't really about romance: "A lot of my songs...are about my friends, not my lovers. It's not erotic or sensual even if it may sound like that." Its music video has her dancing on the back of a truck driving through New York City.

title: I Miss You
fact: "I Miss You" was the sixth and final single from Björk's second album, Post (1995), released in February 1997 on One Little Indian. Björk wrote and produced it with Howie B.

title: At the Party
album: At the Party With My Brown Friends
fact: "At the Party" is the opening track and lead single from Black Belt Eagle Scout's 2019 album At the Party With My Brown Friends on Saddle Creek Records. Written by Katherine Paul in her bedroom, the song reflects on finding the inner strength to support the people close to you, built around the comfort of a tight-knit friend group.

album: The Land, The Water, The Sky

title: I Said I Wouldn't Write This Song
album: At the Party with My Brown Friends
fact: "I Said I Wouldn't Write This Song" comes from Black Belt Eagle Scout's 2019 album At the Party with My Brown Friends, the project of Pacific Northwest musician Katherine Paul. Paul has said the song is about a feeling she didn't expect to write about but that ultimately had to come out, and its animated video draws on Northern imagery like cloudberry picking and Arctic landscapes.

title: Indians Never Die
fact: "Indians Never Die" is a track from Mother of My Children, the debut album by Black Belt Eagle Scout, the project of musician Katherine Paul, who grew up on the Swinomish Reservation in Washington state and is Swinomish and Inupiaq. The album was first self-released in August 2017 through Good Cheer Records before being reissued by Saddle Creek Records in September 2018, introducing Paul's music to a much wider national audience.

title: Loss & Relax
fact: Katherine Paul, who records as Black Belt Eagle Scout, wrote 'Loss & Relax' while thinking about the ferries that carry people across the Salish Sea near her home in the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community. She's said she was reflecting on how canoes -- a traditional form of transportation for her people -- have given way to ferries over time, and how that links past and present. The song closes on a note of resilience, picturing her community continuing to thrive on its ancestral waters.

title: My Blood Runs Through This Land
album: The Land, The Water, The Sky
fact: My Blood Runs Through This Land is from The Land, The Water, The Sky (Saddle Creek, 2023). Katherine Paul, a member of the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community, made the album about her move from Portland back to her homelands, and Evan Benally Atwood directed the video.

album: At the Party With My Brown Friends

title: Scorpio Moon
album: At the Party With My Brown Friends
fact: 'Scorpio Moon' appears on Black Belt Eagle Scout's 2019 album At the Party With My Brown Friends, by Swinomish/Inupiaq musician Katherine Paul. Paul has said the 'party' in the title symbolizes the world, and her 'friends' represent fellow Indigenous people and people of color. Much of the album's sound traces back to music she grew up with on the reservation, including her family's drum group, the Skagit Valley Singers.

title: Soft Stud
fact: Black Belt Eagle Scout is the project of Katherine Paul, a Swinomish and Inupiaq musician who has released three albums on Saddle Creek Records. The name came from a conversation with a friend about never having met a black belt who was also an Eagle Scout.

title: Besties
fact: "Besties" marked Georgia Ellery's (also of Jockstrap) debut turn as lead vocalist for Black Country, New Road, serving as the lead single from their 2025 album Forever Howlong. Opening on a distinctive harpsichord line, the light-hearted, tongue-in-cheek track plays with the blurry space between close friendship and unrequited romantic feeling.

title: Happy Birthday
fact: "Happy Birthday" is a baroque-pop single from Black Country, New Road's 2025 album Forever Howlong, the band's first studio release since 2022's Ants from Up There and since three members stepped up to share lead vocals. Critics compared its ornate arrangement to Joanna Newsom and The Beatles, and the band paired it with a stop-motion music video directed by Lesley-Anne Rose. Lyrically, it's a wry reminder that privilege doesn't guarantee happiness.

title: Strangers
fact: "Strangers" is a quieter, searching song about feeling slightly out of step with the world around you, where everyday objects and small signals start to feel like verdicts on whether you belong. Black Country, New Road released the track in March 2026 through War Child Records.

title: The Big Spin
fact: The Big Spin appears on Live at Bush Hall, recorded over two nights in December 2022 at Bush Hall in London. The band debuted a whole set of brand-new songs live there before any of them had studio versions.

fact: Black Flag started out as Panic in 1976 before renaming due to a conflict with another band using the name. Founder Greg Ginn ran the label SST Records to release their music - a name he'd originally used as a kid selling electronics kits.

title: Rise Above
fact: "Rise Above" opens Black Flag's 1981 debut album Damaged and became one of hardcore punk's defining anthems about refusing to be controlled by outside pressure. It's also tied to the band's lineup history: singer Henry Rollins joined Black Flag after being pulled onstage to sing at an impromptu New York show, impressing the band enough that they asked him to become their permanent vocalist.

title: TV Party
fact: Written by guitarist Greg Ginn, "TV Party" first appeared on Black Flag's 1981 album Damaged. The band re-recorded it twice more: once for a 1982 promotional EP with new drummer Emil Johnson (slower tempo, added hand claps), and again in 1984 for director Alex Cox's cult film Repo Man and its soundtrack. Each version namechecks different TV shows that were popular when it was recorded.

title: It Always Comes to Me
fact: Black Marble's “It Always Comes to Me” sketches a character who always seems to get away with things, charm or deceit - a modern cousin of The Kinks' “Dedicated Follower of Fashion.”

title: Chondromalacia Patella
fact: black midi named this Cavalcade single after a real medical condition, chondromalacia patella, a type of knee pain from worn cartilage that one of the band members developed from running. Frontman Geordie Greep built the song's lyrics around that experience of pushing through pain on a run and then recovering from it. It's one of the more unusual song titles to come out of the UK's experimental rock scene.

title: Hogwash and Balderdash
fact: black midi's “Hogwash and Balderdash” tells the story of two runaway convicts on the run from the law - who happen to be chickens named Hogwash and Balderdash.

title: Speedway
fact: "Speedway" was first released in January 2019 as a tour-only 12-inch before landing as track two on black midi's debut album Schlagenheim later that year. It marked one of bassist Cameron Picton's first lead-vocal turns for the band, giving the song a quieter, more subdued feel next to the record's noisier tracks.

title: Sugar/Tzu
fact: "Sugar/Tzu" is a single from black midi's second album, Hellfire (2022), telling a speculative story of two 600-pound boxers fighting in a fictional "Leadweight" division in the year 2163. Its music video, directed by Noel Paul, won Best Cinematography in a Video at the 2022 UK Music Video Awards.

fact: "23," the title track of Blonde Redhead's seventh album (2007), centers on the numerological pull of its titular number as a stand-in for fate and the passage of time. The band deliberately aimed for a more spontaneous, less overanalyzed songwriting approach on this record, trading the melancholy of their earlier album Misery for a more energetic, streamlined sound.

title: Spring and by Summer Fall
fact: "Spring and by Summer Fall," also from 2007's 23, pairs a dense, guitar-heavy, propulsive sound with lyrics that use the changing seasons as a metaphor for shifting relationships and self-identity. Its opening line — "I look in your eyes and can only see my own complexion" — sets up the song's theme of searching for yourself in how others reflect you back.

title: Somewhere in Between
fact: Somewhere in Between was released July 17, 2025 as a double single with Mind Loaded, ahead of Blood Orange's fifth album, Essex Honey (August 29, 2025). Dev Hynes' album features collaborators including Lorde, Caroline Polachek, Daniel Caesar and Mustafa.

title: Vivid Light
fact: "Vivid Light" is a highlight from Blood Orange mastermind Dev Hynes' 2025 album Essex Honey, and it features an unexpected guest vocalist: acclaimed novelist Zadie Smith, a longtime friend of Hynes who had never sung on a record before. The two later performed the song together live on BBC Radio 6 Music.

fact: "Dangerous Game" comes from bassist Blu DeTiger, who started playing bass at just seven years old. She wrote, produced, and played nearly every instrument on the track herself ahead of her 2024 debut studio album, All I Ever Want Is Everything.

fact: The title "Tarkovski" is BODEGA's pun on Russian filmmaker Andrei Tarkovsky, inspired by his book Sculpting in Time; the band was amused that Tarkovsky often broke his own stated rules of filmmaking. It's the lead single from their 2024 album Our Brand Could Be Yr Life, itself a riff on Michael Azerrad's famous book about the American underground rock scene, Our Band Could Be Your Life. The song's video even restages a famous candle-carrying scene from Tarkovsky's film Nostalghia before swerving into straight-up pop choreography.

title: Completely Half
fact: 'Completely Half' is the lead single from Bolis Pupul's debut album Letter To Yu, co-produced by Soulwax and released on their Deewee label. Pupul, who's of both Belgian and Chinese heritage, built the song around the line 'completely half on my behalf,' playing with the math of a mixed identity. The video, shot on the streets of Hong Kong, was directed by acclaimed Magnum photographer Bieke Depoorter.

title: 00000 Million
fact: "00000 Million" closes Bon Iver's 2016 album, 22, A Million, a piano-driven track that ties together the record's roughly thirty minutes of experimental production. Every song title on the album begins with a number holding personal significance to bandleader Justin Vernon, who described the "22" as representing himself and the closing "million" as something vast and elusive.

title: 22 (OVER S88N)
fact: On Bon Iver's album 22, A Million, Justin Vernon said the number 22 represents himself, something tangible, while "a million" stands for something abstract and infinite - each song's odd, symbol-filled title works the same way.

title: 29 #Strafford APTS
fact: '29 #Strafford APTS' appears on Bon Iver's 2016 album 22, A Million. The quirky title is meant to be read aloud exactly as written - '29 hashtag Strafford apartments' - a nod to a real address. Musically it's one of the more conventional folk-guitar moments on an otherwise glitchy, heavily processed record.

title: 8 (circle)
fact: "8 (circle)" is the fourth single from Bon Iver's 2016 album 22, A Million. Its lyric video features black-and-white artwork by Eric Timothy Carlson, who worked closely with the band throughout the recording sessions to create the visual identity for the whole album, where every track title includes a number.

title: Calgary
fact: "Calgary" was the first single from Bon Iver's self-titled second album (2011). Like much of the record, the song is named after a real place chosen mostly for its emotional resonance rather than literal geography — Justin Vernon has said he wrote about the Canadian city despite never having been there.

title: Heavenly Father
fact: Justin Vernon wrote Heavenly Father for the soundtrack of Zach Braff's film Wish I Was Here. After watching a rough cut, he started humming and the song's title phrase came out. It returned to streaming in 2026 as part of Bon Iver's VOLUMES archive series.

title: HEAVENLY FATHER - Mediolanum, Milan, IT. Nov 05 2022
album: VOLUMES: ONE SELECTIONS FROM MUSIC CONCERTS 2019-2023 BON IVER 6
fact: Bon Iver's Justin Vernon wrote “Heavenly Father” for Zach Braff's film Wish I Was Here after talking with his own brother about the film's story of two brothers - it became a song about searching for peace.

title: Holocene
fact: Bon Iver's Holocene takes its title from both the current geological epoch and a bar in Portland, Oregon. Its three verses trace three different moments from Justin Vernon's life in his hometown of Eau Claire, Wisconsin, and the music video was filmed among Iceland's glaciers.

title: If Only I Could Wait (feat. Danielle Haim)
iMi
fact: "iMi" began as an idea Justin Vernon worked on with engineer Josh Berg at his April Base studio in Wisconsin. Minnesota musician Bobby Raps and producer Wheezy (known for his work with Young Thug and Future) contributed drum programming before Vernon finished the track at Sonic Ranch studio in Texas. It appears on Bon Iver's 2019 album i,i.

title: Jelmore
fact: "Jelmore" is from Bon Iver's fourth album, i,i (August 2019), and was released as a single in the weeks before the album alongside "Faith." At about two and a half minutes, it's one of the album's shorter tracks.

title: Naeem
fact: This i,i (2019) track was originally titled "I Can Hear Crying," but Justin Vernon renamed it in honor of his friend and collaborator Naeem Juwan, the rapper/producer known as Spank Rock, who also co-wrote another song on the album. Vernon has called him "one of the most inspirational artists I know."

title: RABi
fact: "RABi" closes Bon Iver's 2019 album i,i, built from an interplay of horns, synths, and layered group vocals. The album itself was rolled out unusually, with tracks released one by one, hour by hour, the day before its official August 9, 2019 release, and features guest contributions from James Blake, Aaron Dessner, Bruce Hornsby, Moses Sumney, and Channy Leaneagh.

title: S P E Y S I D E
Towers
fact: "Towers" appears on Bon Iver's self-titled 2011 album, whose ten songs are all named after real or invented places meaningful to frontman Justin Vernon. The record was made at April Base Studios, a former veterinary clinic in Fall Creek, Wisconsin that Vernon and his brother bought and converted into a recording studio.

title: Woods
fact: 'Woods,' from Justin Vernon's heavily Auto-Tuned 2009 Blood Bank EP, caught Kanye West's ear, who sampled it for 'Lost in the World' on 2010's My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy. West's call about the sample led to an invitation for Vernon to fly out and work directly in West's Hawaii studio sessions.

fact: Bonnie "Prince" Billy's "A Minor Place" opens 1999's I See a Darkness, Will Oldham's first album under that stage name - critics have described its nursery-rhyme-like opening melody as a kind of statement of purpose for the record. The title track later caught Johnny Cash's attention, who recorded his own version of it.

title: Squid Eye
fact: "Squid Eye," from Bonnie "Prince" Billy's 2019 album I Made a Place, tackles the real-world subject of rising sea levels, but with a playful touch — the lyrics joke about diving in like "Aquaman's kid" and having the eyes of a squid. Rather than despair, the song frames adapting to a changing world as an act of resilience, wonder, and even childlike fun.

title: The World's Greatest
fact: Will Oldham, recording as Bonnie 'Prince' Billy, took R. Kelly's 2001 arena-sized anthem "The World's Greatest" and turned it into a hushed, mournful acoustic ballad for his 2007 covers EP Ask Forgiveness on Domino. It's a genre-hopping party trick he's pulled off more than once, finding the sad, quiet song hiding inside a big pop hit.

fact: $20 was one of three singles boygenius released together in January 2023 to announce their debut album, The Record (Interscope, March 2023). Julien Baker wrote it and sings lead, with Phoebe Bridgers and Lucy Dacus adding harmonies. The album gave all three members their first number-one albums in the UK.

title: Bite The Hand
fact: boygenius wrote “Bite the Hand” about the strange etiquette of fame - not feeling obligated to give fans a piece of yourself just because they bought a ticket, while still making music that's honest.

title: Emily I'm Sorry
fact: 'Emily I'm Sorry' is one of three boygenius songs featured in 'the film,' a 14-minute short directed by Kristen Stewart and released alongside their debut album the record. In its segment, Phoebe Bridgers sings lead while monster trucks circle around her, with bandmates Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus joining her for a fiery finale.

title: Me & My Dog
fact: 'Me & My Dog' first appeared on boygenius' self-titled 2018 debut EP, one of several nearly finished songs each member brought into the studio for that project. The band loved the song's live ending so much — the house lights coming up at a sold-out Brooklyn Steel show that year — that they sampled the crowd's cheers from that exact moment and wove them into 'Letter to an Old Poet,' the closing track of their 2023 album the record. It's a rare case of a band sampling their own earlier concert to tie two albums together.

title: Not Strong Enough
fact: On "Not Strong Enough," from boygenius' 2023 debut album The Record, Phoebe Bridgers revealed that the key lyric "not strong enough to be your man" was a direct nod to Sheryl Crow's 1994 hit "Strong Enough." The song became the first single by any of the three members' projects to top Billboard's Adult Alternative Airplay chart.

title: Salt in the Wound
fact: "Salt in the Wound" comes from boygenius's self-titled 2018 EP, which Julien Baker, Phoebe Bridgers, and Lucy Dacus wrote and recorded together in just five days at Sound City Studios. Each member arrived with one finished song and one half-formed idea, and the trio fleshed out all six tracks collaboratively. The track layers Dacus's lead vocal with Bridgers's higher harmonies and a towering guitar solo from Baker.

title: Souvenir
fact: "Souvenir" closes out boygenius's self-titled 2018 EP on Matador Records, the trio's first release together. Julien Baker, Phoebe Bridgers, and Lucy Dacus each take their own verse on the hushed, acoustic track, and a lyric from the song — "twenty dollars and a souvenir" — resurfaces years later in "$20," a track on the group's 2023 full-length, the record.

title: Stay Down
fact: "Stay Down" comes from boygenius's self-titled 2018 debut EP. Julien Baker, Phoebe Bridgers, and Lucy Dacus formed the group after bonding on a shared tour, then holed up at Sound City Studios in Los Angeles for just four days in June 2018, with each member bringing one nearly-finished song for the others to help build out. Baker's contribution became "Stay Down."

title: Learning to Lie
fact: Brad Sucks is the one-man project of Ottawa musician Brad Turcotte, an early champion of giving music away for free online — his 2003 album I Don't Know What I'm Doing became a cult favorite of the Creative Commons era. "Learning to Lie," a 2025 single, arrived with an official music video built around a sci-fi pickleball match.

title: cbd
fact: brakence (Randy Findell) was a self-taught teenage producer from Columbus, Ohio who wrote, recorded, and mixed basically all of "cbd" and the rest of his debut album "Hypochondriac" himself. NPR named the track one of its favorite songs of 2022.

fact: Prove It to You, from Brittany Howard's 2024 album What Now, is a 1990s house-inspired dance track. Howard said she wanted to write a fun four-on-the-floor song, and critics have compared its feel to Underworld.

title: What Now
fact: "What Now" is the title track and lead single from Brittany Howard's second solo album, released in 2023 as her label debut on Island Records following 2019's Jaime. Howard wrote and produced the song with longtime Alabama Shakes collaborator Shawn Everett, recording at two storied Nashville studios, Sound Emporium and historic RCA Studio B.

title: Follow The Light
fact: Follow the Light was the first single from Spell Blanket (2024), a collection of demos that Broadcast singer Trish Keenan recorded between 2006 and 2009. It keeps the band's habit of building songs from short, repeating lyrics.

title: The Games You Play
fact: "The Games You Play" surfaced on Broadcast's 2024 rarities collection Spell Blanket, released via Warp Records. It's actually a vocal version of an earlier instrumental called "DDL," which had previously appeared on the All Tomorrow's Parties 1.0 compilation and the band's 2006 odds-and-ends album The Future Crayon, with the newly unearthed recordings dating from 2006-2009.

title: Valerie
fact: Broadcast's “Valerie” takes its name and melody from the 1970 Czech film Valerie and Her Week of Wonders, a major inspiration for the band's dreamy, psychedelic sound.

title: 7/4 (Shoreline)
fact: True to its title, this standout from Broken Social Scene's 2005 self-titled album is built on an unusual 7/4 time signature. Despite the odd meter, the Toronto collective's arrangement feels effortlessly propulsive, making it one of the band's most accessible songs. It's often cited by musicians as a go-to example of a danceable, listener-friendly odd-time track.

title: Anthems for a Seventeen Year-Old Girl
fact: "Anthems for a Seventeen Year-Old Girl" is a standout from Broken Social Scene's landmark 2002 album You Forgot It in People, built from a simple opening banjo line that gradually layers in strings, horns, and percussion. Twenty years later, the band marked the album's anniversary with a tribute record featuring a cover of the song by Maggie Rogers and Sylvan Esso.

title: Can't Find My Heart
fact: Broken Social Scene is a Toronto musical collective founded by Kevin Drew and Brendan Canning in 1999 that has included anywhere from 6 to 19 members - alumni include Feist and Metric's Emily Haines.

title: Halfway Home
fact: 'Halfway Home' was Broken Social Scene's first new song in seven years when it arrived in 2017 as the lead single from Hug of Thunder. The band debuted it live on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert around the same time.

title: Not Around Anymore
fact: "Not Around Anymore" is the lead single from Broken Social Scene's 2026 album Remember the Humans, their first record in nearly a decade. The Toronto collective reunited with producer David Newfeld, who also produced their breakthrough You Forgot It in People (2002) and their 2005 self-titled album.

title: Only The Good I Keep
fact: "Only the Good I Keep" is the second track on Broken Social Scene's 2026 album Remember the Humans, the Canadian collective's first new record in nearly a decade. For this song the band handed the mic to singer Hannah Georgas, who steps forward to lead it with striking clarity.

title: Stars and Sons
fact: "Stars and Sons" comes from Broken Social Scene's breakthrough "You Forgot It in People" (2002), the album that expanded the Toronto collective from a core quartet to eleven members, including Feist, and won a Juno Award for Best Alternative Album. More than two decades later, Toro y Moi covered the song for a 2025 tribute album celebrating the record.

title: Superconnected
fact: 'Superconnected' comes from Broken Social Scene's self-titled 2005 album, the sprawling Canadian collective's third full-length. Core members Kevin Drew and Brendan Canning were joined by contributors including Leslie Feist, Amy Millan, and k-os, and longtime producer David Newfeld was credited as an official band member for the first time. The record is considered a high point of the band's dense, layered, orchestral-meets-indie-rock sound.

title: The Call
fact: "The Call" is co-written and lead-sung by guitarist Andrew Whiteman, from Broken Social Scene's 2026 album Remember the Humans — the band's first new album in roughly nine years. For it, the Toronto collective reunited with producer David Newfeld, who had helmed their beloved early-2000s records You Forgot It in People and Broken Social Scene.

fact: Buck Meek's "Can I Mend It?," from 2026's The Mirror, was produced by his Big Thief bandmate James Krivchenia - the album also features Adrianne Lenker on vocals, plus contributions from harpist Mary Lattimore and composer Alex Somers on synths.

title: Gasoline
fact: Gasoline is from The Mirror (2026), the fourth solo album from Big Thief guitarist Buck Meek. Big Thief drummer James Krivchenia produced it, and Adrianne Lenker sings backup vocals on the song.

title: I Would Hurt a Fly
fact: "I Would Hurt a Fly" comes from Built to Spill's 1997 album Perfect From Now On, which the band had to record three separate times to get right. At one point producer Phil Ek was driving session tapes from Seattle to Boise for additional overdubs when the master reels were accidentally destroyed by heat, sending the band back into the studio once more before the album was finished.

title: In The Morning
fact: "In the Morning" appears on Built to Spill's 1994 album There's Nothing Wrong With Love, recorded at John & Stu's studio in Seattle and produced by Phil Ek. The album became a touchstone of 1990s indie rock, loosely centered on songwriter Doug Martsch's reflections on growing up, and it later received a 30th-anniversary vinyl reissue from Sub Pop.

title: Liar
fact: Liar appears on Built to Spill's 2006 album You in Reverse, their first new album in four years. The band aimed for a looser, more live-sounding record this time, recording at Steve Lobdell's Audible Alchemy studio to capture the feel of their in-person jams rather than layering parts track by track. Doug Martsch's extended, winding guitar lines became a hallmark of the album's more improvisational approach.

title: Strange
fact: "Strange" opens Built to Spill's 2001 album Ancient Melodies of the Future and features Sam Coomes of the band Quasi guesting on Roxichord organ. Frontman Doug Martsch has said the songs on this album were some of the simplest he'd written in years, marking a deliberate shift toward more concise songwriting.

title: Traces
fact: Traces is the second track on Built to Spill's 2006 album You in Reverse. It was the first Built to Spill album recorded as a four-piece, with guitarist Jim Roth joining the lineup, and the first record since their 1993 debut not produced by longtime collaborator Phil Ek.

title: Untrustable/Part 2 (About Someone Else)
fact: The closing track on Built to Spill's 1997 album Perfect From Now On, "Untrustable/Part 2 (About Someone Else)," came out of a famously grueling recording process. Doug Martsch first tried overdubbing nearly every instrument himself, scrapped that, then re-recorded the album with bassist Brett Nelson and drummer Scott Plouf — only for those tapes to be ruined by heat in producer Phil Ek's car on the drive from Seattle to Boise, forcing the band to record the whole album a third time.

title: All I Do
fact: 'All I Do' opens Bully's 2023 album Lucky for You, building from a shimmering, reverb-laden guitar line into the record's trademark huge riffs. Frontwoman Alicia Bognanno made the album with producer JT Daly at his Nashville studio, and it took roughly seven months to finish - the longest gestation period of any Bully record up to that point.

title: Days Move Slow
fact: Bully's "Days Move Slow" was the second single from 2023's Lucky for You, produced by J.T. Daly - it followed "Lose You," a collaboration with fellow Nashville rockers Soccer Mommy, and took about seven months to come together, the longest gestation of any Bully record to that point.

title: I Remember
fact: "I Remember" was the first single from Bully's 2015 debut album Feels Like. The sub-two-minute punk track was written and sung by frontwoman Alicia Bognanno, who also produced and mixed the recording herself.

title: Let You
fact: "Let You" is track six on Bully's third album, "SUGAREGG" (2020), recorded with producer Graham Walsh at Palace Studios in Toronto. The bass-driven track marked a new, more collaborative studio approach for frontwoman Alicia Bognanno after two self-produced records.

title: Stuck In Your Head
fact: "Stuck in Your Head" is a track from Bully's 2020 album SUGAREGG, the first Bully record made as a true solo vehicle for frontwoman Alicia Bognanno. Bognanno, who studied audio engineering before starting the band, co-produced the album with John Congleton and Graham Walsh and released it through Sub Pop.

title: Trying
fact: "Trying" is a standout single from Bully's 2023 album Lucky for You, the project of Nashville singer-songwriter Alicia Bognanno, released via Sub Pop. The song's howling chorus and driving rhythm section examine Bognanno's tendency toward self-criticism.

title: Where to Start
fact: Bully frontwoman Alicia Bognanno has said "Where to Start" was partly inspired by Chumbawamba's 1997 hit "Tubthumping" -- she was picking apart its melodic structure and trying to mimic it when the song came together. It appears on 2020's SUGAREGG, the first Bully album written and recorded as Bognanno's solo project. The track was originally tracked at Pachyderm Studios before being re-recorded at Palace Studios in Toronto with engineer Graham Walsh.

title: Black Light
fact: "Black Light" comes from the 2020 EP pop songs 2020 by Bumper, a collaborative project between Ryan Galloway of the band Crying and Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast. It's one of several tracks the pair wrote together, blending synth-pop production with their indie-rock backgrounds.

title: Too Many Creeps
fact: Guitarist Pat Place wrote the lyrics to "Too Many Creeps" in minutes while working the box office at a cinema on New York's Bleecker Street, annoyed by passersby's unsolicited comments. Released as a single in 1980 on 99 Records, it became a downtown dance-punk anthem for the band, a No Wave-adjacent group formed in New York in 1979. The single reached #57 on Billboard's club play chart.

title: Boredom
fact: Boredom is on the Buzzcocks' Spiral Scratch EP, recorded December 28, 1976 at Indigo Sound Studios in Manchester with producer Martin Hannett and released in January 1977 on the band's own New Hormones label. According to the back cover, Boredom was recorded on the first take. Singer Howard Devoto left soon after to form Magazine.

title: Ever Fallen In Love (With Some You Shouldn't've?)
fact: Pete Shelley wrote "Ever Fallen in Love (With Someone You Shouldn't've?)" in 1978 at just 23, inspired by a line of dialogue from the film Guys and Dolls that he half-caught on TV while the band stayed overnight at an Edinburgh guesthouse. He finished the lyrics the next day sitting in the band's tour van outside the city's main post office. The song reached number 12 on the UK singles chart and was named NME's Track of the Year for 1978.

title: Everybody's Happy Nowadays
fact: "Everybody's Happy Nowadays" was a 1979 Buzzcocks single, backed with "Why Can't I Touch It?", released a few months before their third album, A Different Kind of Tension (September 1979, United Artists). The song was meant ironically, though some fans thought the band had sold out when Pete Shelley played it on Top of the Pops.

title: I Don't Mind
album: Another Music In A Different Kitchen

title: What Do I Get?
fact: Buzzcocks' "What Do I Get?" gave the band their UK chart debut in 1978, peaking at #37 - it followed "Orgasm Addict," their first single, which the BBC refused to play on air. Pete Shelley wrote it and producer Martin Rushent helmed the session.

title: Perspective
fact: "Perspective" was released in March 2023 as the first new music from the New York duo Cafuné (Sedona Schat and Noah Yoo) since they signed to Elektra Records and their viral hit "Tek It." It was co-produced by Imad Royal, who has also worked with Doja Cat and Carly Rae Jepsen.

title: The Moment
fact: 'The Moment' opens Cafune's 2025 album Bite Reality, released September 12, 2025. Sedona Schat sings lead with Noah Yoo on guitar and Connor Parks on drums, self-produced by the duo and mixed by Noah Glassman.

title: Ain't No Rest for the Wicked
Comfort Eagle
fact: CAKE's title track "Comfort Eagle" is more widely known by its repeated hook, "Building a Religion" - frontman John McCrea wrote it as a metaphor for the marketing and propaganda that disguises what a product actually is. Fans voted it in as the album's second single, but its release was canceled after the September 11 attacks.

title: Friend Is a Four Letter Word
Race Car Ya-Yas
fact: "Race Car Ya-Yas" is a brisk, 81-second deep cut from CAKE's 1996 album Fashion Nugget, built around Vincent Difiore's signature trumpet alongside John McCrea's vocals. It's tucked among the album's bigger hits, "The Distance" and the band's cover of "I Will Survive," as one of the record's shortest, punchiest tracks.

title: Short Skirt/Long Jacket
fact: CAKE frontman John McCrea wrote "Short Skirt/Long Jacket" after noticing someone wearing two visually opposite fashion choices at once, and built the song around that kind of contradiction. It was the lead single from 2001's Comfort Eagle, but its radio momentum stalled when it came out right around the September 11 attacks, leaving it with a modest chart peak. It's remained one of CAKE's most popular songs anyway, and an instrumental version became the theme song for the NBC series Chuck.

title: The Distance
fact: Released in 1996 as the first single off Fashion Nugget, 'The Distance' was actually written by CAKE's guitarist at the time, Greg Brown, who was surprised the band even picked it as a single. Frontman John McCrea has described it as a song about a race car driver straining toward a finish line he'll never reach — 'a song about success and failure, and failure of success.' It became CAKE's most enduring hit, climbing to No. 4 on the Alternative Airplay chart.
