fact: This is actually Talking Heads' 1983 single "Burning Down the House" from Speaking in Tongues. The song became Talking Heads' only US top-ten hit, peaking at No. 9.

The six-and-a-half-minute fuzz-pop track features guest vocals from Seoul singer Della Zyr, a string arrangement by Rei Miyamoto of the Osaka band Vampillia, and trumpet from Fin Fior.

fact: All five members of Parcels grew up together in Byron Bay, Australia, and formed the band in their final year of high school. After moving to Berlin, they played a 2016 Paris show that happened to have Daft Punk in the crowd - leading to a co-writing credit on the duo's single "Overnight."

title: Give Up the Funk (Tear the Roof Off the Sucker)
P. Funk (Wants to Get Funked Up)
Almost Had To Start A FightIn And Out of Patience
fact: This title is actually two separate Parquet Courts songs run together: "Almost Had to Start a Fight" and "In and Out of Patience," both from the band's 2018 album "Wide Awake!" Producer Danger Mouse, who helmed the record, insisted the two tracks be spliced into one two-part song, which is why they're often logged and listed as a single combined title.

title: Before the Water Gets Too High
Dust
fact: "Dust" opens Parquet Courts' 2016 album Human Performance with a Talking Heads-inspired groove and a chorus that simply repeats "dust is everywhere, sweep." Frontman Andrew Savage said the album grew out of him "questioning my humanity" and feeling "like a machine programmed to be human showing signs of defect."

title: Homosapien
fact: Parquet Courts' "Homosapien" was the final single from 2021's Sympathy for Life - while most of that album grew out of extensive studio jams that got edited and spliced together, "Homosapien" found the band heading back to a more straightforward, guitar-driven garage-rock sound.

title: Tenderness
fact: "Tenderness" closes out Parquet Courts' 2018 album Wide Awake!, the band's first collaboration with producer Brian Burton, better known as Danger Mouse. It was recorded at Sonic Ranch in Tornillo, Texas, and Electric Lady Studios in New York City. The sunny, piano-driven closer is a deliberate change of pace from the album's punkier tracks, with frontman Andrew Savage singing about slowing down in a world that feels sped up.

title: Total Football
fact: "Total Football" opens Parquet Courts' 2018 album Wide Awake! and takes its title from a tactical system popularized by the Dutch national soccer team at the 1974 World Cup, in which any player could fill any position on the field. Singer Andrew Savage said the soccer concept gave him a starting point for lyrics about the balance between collectivity and individuality.

title: Uncast Shadow of A Southern Myth

fact: Grounded is on Pavement's 1995 album Wowee Zowee, recorded in November 1994 at Easley Recording in Memphis, Tennessee, with more sessions in New York the following February. The song dates back to the Crooked Rain, Crooked Rain era.

title: Harness Your Hopes
fact: Pavement recorded "Harness Your Hopes" during sessions for 1997's Brighten the Corners, but it was left off the album and tucked away as a B-side on the 1999 Spit on a Stranger EP. Decades later, streaming-algorithm discovery turned the once-overlooked B-side into Pavement's most-streamed song, and it became the only Pavement track ever certified gold.

title: Spit on a Stranger
fact: Pavement's "Spit on a Stranger" opens 1999's Terror Twilight, the band's Nigel Godrich-produced final album - its single also included the deep cut "Harness Your Hopes," which years later, thanks to Spotify's algorithm, unexpectedly became the band's most-streamed song.

title: Stereo
fact: Pavement's 1997 single "Stereo," from the album Brighten the Corners, opens with Stephen Malkmus wondering aloud about Rush singer Geddy Lee's famously high voice: "How did it get so high? I wonder if he speaks like an ordinary guy?" A bandmate chimes back, "I know him, and he does" — one of indie rock's more memorable random celebrity shout-outs.

title: The Hexx
fact: Pavement first played a faster, louder version of 'The Hexx' live on their Brighten the Corners tour; that recording was later edited and retitled '...And Then' for release as a vinyl B-side to 'Spit on a Stranger.' For Terror Twilight, the band re-recorded it with producer Nigel Godrich into the slow-building, atmospheric closer that many critics called the closest Pavement ever got to sounding like a Radiohead record.

title: Unseen Power of the Picket Fence
fact: Pavement wrote “The Unseen Power of the Picket Fence” as a loving, joke-filled tribute to R.E.M. for a 1994 charity compilation - Stephen Malkmus jokingly name-drops their songs and admits “Time After Time” was his least favorite, which reportedly needled Michael Stipe a little.

title: Zurich Is Stained
fact: "Zurich Is Stained" comes from Pavement's 1992 debut album Slanted and Enchanted, recorded on a shoestring budget at drummer Gary Young's home studio over about ten days. It remains the only Pavement album to feature Young behind the kit.

title: If Ever You're In My Arms Again
Alrighty Aphrodite
fact: "Alrighty Aphrodite" was an early single from Vancouver band Peach Pit's 2018 debut album, Being So Normal. Its lyrics borrow imagery from classical art, opening with a nod to Botticelli's The Birth of Venus, where the goddess stands in a giant clamshell, and later referencing the sculpture known as the Crouching Venus.

title: Fool
fact: "Fool" appears on Perfume Genius's 2014 album Too Bright and leans into an almost 1950s doo-wop sound, built around finger snaps and warm backing vocals. It was the third single and music video released from the album.

title: It's a Mirror
fact: "It's a Mirror" premiered in January 2025 as the lead single from Perfume Genius's seventh studio album, Glory, produced by Blake Mills. The song was described as a "ferocious rocker" built on dueling guitars, backed by a music video directed by Cody Critcheloe.

title: Natural High
fact: 'Natural High' is Perfume Genius' first new song since his 2025 album Glory, co-produced with Pascal Stevenson of the band Fashion Club. The six-minute track was written for The Lesson, a music-and-dance stage collaboration with choreographer Kate Wallich, and gradually builds from moody keyboard figures into a full house-music rave-up by its end. It's a good showcase of how far Perfume Genius has pushed beyond traditional song structure in recent years.

title: Normal Song
fact: 'Normal Song' first appeared on Perfume Genius's 2012 album Put Your Back N 2 It. Years later, its use in film and television earned it a nomination for 'Best Sync Usage' at the 2017 Libera Awards, which honor independent labels and artists.

album: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
fact: Perfume Genius' "On The Floor," from 2020's Set My Heart on Fire Immediately, evokes Eighties R&B by way of Tina Turner and Erasure - the album was produced by Blake Mills with contributions from veteran session players Jim Keltner and Pino Palladino. Mike Hadreas directed the song's music video himself.

title: Slip Away
fact: The video for "Slip Away," the first single from Perfume Genius's 2017 album No Shape, was directed by Andrew Thomas Huang and features Mike Hadreas and dancer Teresa "Toogie" Barcelo moving through a lush, dreamlike landscape in towering high-heeled boots. Choreographer Sara Silkin built the routine around the challenge of dancing in those heels, giving the clip its theatrical, otherworldly feel.

title: Without You
album: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
fact: "Without You" appears on Perfume Genius's 2020 album Set My Heart on Fire Immediately. The strummy, major-key track finds Mike Hadreas singing about the ache of distance from someone important to him, part of a record he described as being about the strange, meaningful connections people share. Musically it's one of the album's warmest, most straightforwardly uplifting songs.

title: All A Mystery
fact: "All A Mystery" marked Phantogram's 2024 signing to Neon Gold Records and takes its title from a line Josh Carter and Sarah Barthel used to sing together back when they first started writing songs in a barn-turned-recording-studio. Produced by John Hill, the single later appeared on their fifth studio album, Memory of a Day.

title: Attaway
fact: "Attaway" appears on Phantogram's 2024 album Memory of a Day, released via Neon Gold Records. The title is actually a made-up word the duo coined as a playful twist on the phrase "atta boy" or "there ya go." The track was produced with John Hill, part of a batch of collaborators the band brought in for the record.

fact: Phoebe Bridgers' “Bobby” is her most straightforward love song yet, widely believed to be about her partner Bo Burnham - a warm departure from the melancholic tone of her earlier album Punisher.

title: Garden Song
fact: Alongside her solo work, Phoebe Bridgers has recorded as one-third of boygenius with Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus, and as half of Better Oblivion Community Center with Conor Oberst of Bright Eyes. She's won four Grammy Awards from eleven nominations.

title: I Can't Wait
fact: "I Can't Wait" is from Phoebe Bridgers' 2026 album "Lost Weekend," co-produced by Bridgers with Tony Berg, Ethan Gruska, and Jack Antonoff. Its music video, directed by Chris Maggio and Pablo Rochat, follows a single housefly buzzing through Los Angeles, landing on faces, chasing light sources, and darting inside a guitar.

title: I Know The End
fact: Phoebe Bridgers' "I Know the End" closes out 2020's Punisher with a three-part build that ends in a cathartic scream - when she performed it on Saturday Night Live in February 2021, she capped the segment by smashing her guitar against a studio monitor.

title: Liberty Tree
fact: Liberty Tree, the tenth track on Phoebe Bridgers' third album, Lost Weekend (August 2026), is named for the Liberty Tree Mall in Danvers, Massachusetts. Bridgers turned the mall into the setting of a song about finding love in an unlikely place.

title: Lost Boys
fact: 'Lost Boys' is the lead single from Phoebe Bridgers' 2026 album Lost Weekend, co-written with Christian Lee Hutson, Marshall Vore, Bo Burnham, and Alex G. Its music video reunites Bridgers with her boygenius bandmates Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus, alongside Alex G, for a medieval-themed visual. It's a nice reminder of how tightly connected this whole circle of indie songwriters really is.

title: On Video
fact: "On Video" was written by Phoebe Bridgers for the end credits of the 2026 A24 thriller Primetime, starring Robert Pattinson. She co-wrote it with Jack Antonoff and Christian Lee Hutson, with production handled by Antonoff, Ethan Gruska, and Marshall Vore, and has since added it to her live setlist on tour.

title: That Funny Feeling
fact: Phoebe Bridgers released her studio cover of Bo Burnham's "That Funny Feeling" in October 2021. She and Burnham had already debuted it live together as a surprise duet at Largo at the Coronet in Los Angeles that August - the song's first-ever live performance - before she put out her own version.

title: If I Ever Feel Better
fact: "If I Ever Feel Better" samples Japanese jazz musician Toshiyuki Honda's 1979 track "Lament." Released in 2000 from Phoenix's debut album United, it became the French band's highest-charting single internationally, reaching the top 10 in Belgium, Italy, and Spain.

Impossible House
fact: "Impossible House" comes from Phosphorescent's 2024 album Revelator, which songwriter Matthew Houck produced and recorded in his own Nashville studio over about six months. The lyrics include a playful pop-culture reference, likening a character to "that McCallister kid" left home alone, a nod to the Home Alone movies.

title: Revelator
fact: "Revelator" is the title track and lead single from Phosphorescent's 2024 album Revelator, singer-songwriter Matthew Houck's eighth studio album and his first for Verve Records. Houck has said finishing this song was what made him realize he was writing an entirely new record, one built around themes of coming home, partnership, and family.

fact: Caribou is on Come On Pilgrim, the Pixies' 1987 debut mini-album. The band's next record, Surfer Rosa, was recorded that winter with producer Steve Albini.

title: Debaser
fact: Frank Black wrote "Debaser" after watching the 1929 surrealist short film Un Chien Andalou in a college film studies class, and coined the song's title himself — a "debaser," he explained, is "one who debases," and he wanted to introduce the word into the language. The chorus deliberately mixes languages, with Black singing the intentionally garbled phrase "un chien andalusia" simply because, in his words, "it sounds good."

title: Dig for Fire
fact: "Dig for Fire" appeared on Pixies' 1990 album Bossanova and marked the first time the band used a drum machine, with Dave Lovering playing live drums on top of it. Frontman Black Francis has described the song as a deliberate homage to Talking Heads, joking he was "not even trying to hide" the David Byrne influence. An earlier, very different version of the song had actually been recorded with Steve Albini back in 1987 during the Surfer Rosa sessions.

title: Here Comes Your Man
fact: Black Francis wrote 'Here Comes Your Man' as a teenager, inspired by the small earthquakes he experienced growing up in California, and called it 'hobo film noir' about train-hopping drifters. The band was initially reluctant to release it, feeling it was 'too pop' for their sound, so it sat unused for years. It finally appeared, produced by Gil Norton, as a single from 1989's Doolittle and became one of the Pixies' biggest songs.

title: Monkey Gone To Heaven
fact: Monkey Gone to Heaven, from 1989's Doolittle, was the first Pixies song to feature outside musicians, bringing in two cellists and two violinists for its string arrangement. The lyrics mix environmental imagery with a bit of biblical numerology ("if man is five, then the devil is six, then God is seven"). It was released as the album's lead single ahead of Doolittle.

title: Wave of Mutilation
fact: Beyond the familiar version on 1989's Doolittle, the Pixies recorded an entirely different, slower arrangement of "Wave of Mutilation" known as the "UK Surf" version, originally released as a B-side to the "Here Comes Your Man" single. The song's title was later reused for Wave of Mutilation: Best of Pixies, a 2004 career-spanning compilation.

fact: "Missed" is the second track on PJ Harvey's 1993 album Rid of Me, produced by Steve Albini, with Rob Ellis on drums and Stephen Vaughan on bass. A demo version of the song later surfaced on her 2022 compilation B-Sides, Demos & Rarities.

title: The Letter
fact: "The Letter" was the lead single from PJ Harvey's 2004 album Uh Huh Her, reaching No. 28 on the UK Singles Chart. For the first time since her 1993 demos collection, Harvey self-produced the record and played nearly every instrument herself, recording much of it alone on a four- and eight-track home setup before longtime collaborator Rob Ellis added drums.

fact: "You Said Something" appears on PJ Harvey's 2000 album Stories from the City, Stories from the Sea, which won the Mercury Prize in 2001. The song is set on a rooftop in Brooklyn at one in the morning, and it was later paired with "This Is Love" for a 2001 single release.

title: Dreams Go
fact: Dreams Go is the title track of PoliÃ§a's sixth album (October 17, 2025), eight songs recorded at Pachyderm Studio in Minnesota. It was produced by Ryan Olson with guest production from Peder Mannerfelt.

title: Cheater
fact: "Cheater" is the title track of Norwegian art-punk band Pom Poko's 2021 second album, released on the UK label Bella Union. The band formed in Trondheim after three music-conservatory students recruited singer Ragnhild Fangel Jamtveit for a one-off literary festival gig and just kept going. Musically, the track swings from whisper-quiet verses into a loud, stuttering punk instrumental breakdown by its end.

title: Doll Song
fact: "Doll Song" is the ninth track on Pom Pom Squad's second album, Mirror Starts Moving Without Me, released October 25, 2024. Its music video leans into the song's doll imagery, with frontwoman Mia Berrin appearing as a porcelain-style figurine.

title: Head Cheerleader
fact: Pom Pom Squad's "Head Cheerleader," from 2021's Death of a Cheerleader, was co-produced by frontwoman Mia Berrin and Sarah Tudzin of illuminati hotties - the album blends riot-grrrl and Kerplunk-era Green Day influences with Motown and old Hollywood glamour.

title: Spinning
fact: "Spinning" is the lead single from Pom Pom Squad's sophomore album Mirror Starts Moving Without Me, the project led by New York songwriter Mia Berrin. Built on crystalline piano and a slow-shuffling beat, the song's video, co-directed by Berrin and Benjamin Lieber, is staged inside a surveillance-room set.

Margolin has said it's about being heartbroken and reclaiming your own joy rather than depending on someone else for it; its video, directed by Margolin's sister Ella, was filmed at Paris's Centre Pompidou.

title: All Mine
fact: "All Mine" was the lead single from Portishead's self-titled second album, released in 1997. Written by Geoff Barrow, Beth Gibbons, and Adrian Utley, and produced by the band with Dave McDonald, it became the Bristol trip-hop group's only song to crack the UK Top 10, peaking at number 8.

title: Roads
fact: "Roads" is the eighth track on Portishead's 1994 debut album Dummy and is notable for containing no samples, unlike most of the record, instead built around Beth Gibbons' vocals and a Fender Rhodes-style keyboard theme. Despite becoming one of the album's most beloved songs, it was never released as a single, though it later turned up on the soundtracks for the films Nadja and Tank Girl.

title: The Rip
fact: The Rip, from Portishead's 2008 album Third, opens as a sparse acoustic-guitar folk ballad before shifting halfway through into a pulsing electronic arpeggio passage. The band has noted that their vintage Siel Orchestra synthesizer's built-in sequencer wasn't advanced enough to play the arpeggio pattern they wanted, so they had to find workarounds in the studio. The song was released as the album's second single.

title: Wandering Star
fact: "Wandering Star," from Portishead's landmark 1994 debut Dummy, was written by Beth Gibbons and Geoff Barrow and produced by Adrian Utley alongside the band. Its eerie atmosphere is built partly around a sample of Eric Burdon and War's "Magic Mountain," woven into the trip-hop sound that helped define the genre.

title: Perfect Hand (Power Snatch version)
album: Box For Buddy, Box For Star
fact: "Perfect Hand" was written and released by Nate Amos as This Is Lorelei for the deluxe edition of "Box for Buddy, Box for Star." Paramore's Hayley Williams and producer Daniel James loved it so much that covering the song together is literally what got their new side project, Power Snatch, started — their glitchy, hazier version became the band's debut release.

title: Focus
fact: "Focus" is the lead single from Preoccupations' fifth album, Ill at Ease, out on Born Losers Records. The Calgary post-punk band's Matt Flegel co-produced the track with bandmate Scott "Monty" Munro, giving their usually shadowy sound an unexpected shimmer, with guitar work inspired by INXS. It's one of the shinier moments yet from a band built on darker post-punk.

Memories
fact: The version of "Memories" on PiL's 1979 album Metal Box is actually two different studio takes edited together, noticeable in how bassist Jah Wobble's playing shifts in volume partway through the track. The single version released that October used only one of those takes and has never been officially reissued on CD.

title: Flowers of Romance
fact: After bassist Jah Wobble left the band, John Lydon and Keith Levene leaned into a nearly bass-less, percussion-heavy sound for this 1981 title track, built from tribal-style drumming, gamelan-inspired percussion, and oddball instruments like bowed bass and banjo run through heavy effects. Producer Nick Launay brought his love of big, gated drum sounds to the sessions.

title: This Is Not A Love Song
album: This Is What You Want... This Is What You Get
fact: John Lydon wrote 'This Is Not a Love Song' as a sly joke on himself — after his record label suggested he pen a nice, marketable love song, he responded with a tune where he plays an arrogant corporate sellout, tongue firmly in cheek. The gamble worked: it became PiL's biggest UK hit, climbing to No. 5 on the singles chart.

title: I'll Be Missing You feat. Faith Evans & 112
Begging For Change
fact: Pulp cut this one at the legendary Abbey Road Studios for War Child's HELP(2) charity album, with Damon Albarn, Grian Chatten, Kae Tempest and Carl Barat all pitching in on backing vocals alongside a children's choir. It's a full-circle moment for Jarvis Cocker: back in 1996, Pulp's Different Class lost the Mercury Prize to the original Help compilation, and Cocker still donated his band's own prize money to War Child.

title: Spike Island
fact: "Spike Island," released in 2025 as Pulp's first new song in over a decade, is named after The Stone Roses' legendary 1990 outdoor concert in Widnes, Cheshire, that drew nearly 30,000 fans. Jarvis Cocker said he wasn't actually there, but wrote about the event's lasting cultural ripple through British music — and about a DJ who kept shouting "Spike Island, come alive!" over the PA.

title: Pretty
fact: "Pretty" was the lead single from Puma Blue's 2023 album Holy Waters, his first record made with a full live band rather than alone in his bedroom. It was recorded over two sessions at Echo Zoo Studios in Eastbourne, England, with a roster of co-producers including Andrew Sarlo (Bon Iver), Gabe Wax (Soccer Mommy), and Luke Smith (Foals, Depeche Mode).

title: Pile of Clothes
fact: Pile of Clothes is from I Am Obsessed, a five-track release from PUNCHBAG in April 2026. The South London brother-sister duo mixes the raw energy of punk with the exuberance of pop.

title: Olive Garden
album: Who Will Look After The Dogs?
fact: 'Olive Garden' started life as a quiet acoustic guitar demo written by PUP singer Stefan Babcock, until drummer Zack Mykula heard it and pushed the band to make it as heavy as possible instead. The finished version, recorded with producer John Congleton in Los Angeles in 2024, buries that sweet vocal melody under a wall of detuned, grinding guitars on the band's 2025 album Who Will Look After the Dogs?. It's a good snapshot of PUP's habit of turning soft ideas into some of their loudest songs.

title: Pray For Rain
fact: Pure Bathing Culture's Sarah Versprille and Daniel Hindman met in college in New Jersey and started writing songs together while living in Brooklyn, before relocating to Portland, Oregon in 2011, where the band came together.

title: Abracabruti
fact: "Abracabruti" comes from Pure Carriere's 2025 album Visions de l'enfer. The Quebec City act is a duo formed in 2017 by Jean-Michel Letendre-Veilleux and Laurence Gauthier-Brown, who also play in other local projects like Beat Sexu and Victime.

title: Place Of My Own
fact: Place of My Own is from Purity Ring's 2025 self-titled fourth album, a concept record that works as the soundtrack to an imagined role-playing video game. The duo cited games like Nier Automata and Final Fantasy X as inspiration.

The two artists met online in 2023, and the track layers Abstract's vocals over a looping, showtune-style piano line with string arrangements from producers Johan Lenox and Oleka. It's known among fans for its emotional, country-tinged take on emo rap.

fact: Quarters of Change formed in New York City in 2017 when Ben Acker and Jasper Harris, who met in elementary school, joined with Ben Roter and Attila Anrather. "Heaven Bound" is a single from the band's sophomore album Portraits, blending late-2000s rock and dream-pop influences.

Easy Street
fact: "Easy Street" is a 2026 single from Queens of the Stone Age featuring outlaw-country singer Nikki Lane, marking the band's first-ever official collaborative single. Josh Homme produced it with bandmate Michael Shuman, and they intentionally kept the recording loose and demo-like, leaving in tempo shifts and imperfect handclaps rather than polishing them out.

title: Insignificant Other
fact: Queens of the Stone Age's Josh Homme has described 'Insignificant Other' as being about how someone can feel like your whole world and then simply vanish from it, and the strange vertigo of being on the receiving end of that disappearance. Musically, the track leans toward a warmer, bluesier, more classic-rock sound compared to the band's usual riff-heavy attack. It's from Perfecth, the band's follow-up to 2023's In Times New Roman...

title: The Lost Art of Keeping a Secret
album: The Lost Art of Keeping a Secret

title: Feel
album: The Long and Short of It

title: Apparition
fact: Quivers are an alt-rock quartet from Melbourne, Australia, made up of Sam Nicholson, Bella Quinlan, Michael Panton, and Holly Thomas. "Apparition" arrived in 2024 when the band signed to Merge Records, and it appears on their album Oyster Cuts, with a sound the band has said borrows a bit from the Rolling Stones and Pavement.

title: Aftermath
fact: "Aftermath" was released as the second single from R.E.M.'s 13th studio album, Around the Sun, in November 2004. Written by Peter Buck, Mike Mills, and Michael Stipe and produced by Pat McCarthy with the band, the song reached number 41 on the UK Singles Chart.

title: All the Way to Reno (You're Gonna Be a Star)
fact: R.E.M.'s "All the Way to Reno (You're Gonna Be a Star)," from 2001's Reveal, was originally titled "Jimmy Webb on Mars" as what guitarist Peter Buck called a tribute to the songwriter the band admired. The title is intentionally ironic, since Reno, Nevada, is more of a modest Las Vegas stand-in than a place anyone actually becomes a star.

title: Bad Day
album: In Time: The Best of R.E.M. 1988 - 2003

title: Daysleeper
fact: R.E.M.'s "Daysleeper" was the first single from 1998's Up - Michael Stipe wrote the lyrics after noticing the word "Daysleeper" on an apartment door and wondering about the life of the person living behind it. The music itself had actually been written years earlier, during the New Adventures in Hi-Fi sessions, but sat unused until Stipe found words for it.

title: Driver 8
fact: Driver 8 is about the Southern Crescent, a passenger train that ran on Southern Railway lines until 1979. It is from R.E.M.'s 1985 album Fables of the Reconstruction, which was recorded at Livingston Studios in London with producer Joe Boyd.

title: E-Bow the Letter
fact: "E-Bow the Letter" was the first single from R.E.M.'s 1996 album New Adventures in Hi-Fi, written by all four band members and produced by Scott Litt with R.E.M. Its title comes from the E-Bow, an electronic device Peter Buck used to bow his guitar strings into sustained, droning notes. The track is a duet featuring punk-poet Patti Smith on vocals, which guitarist Peter Buck later called a career highlight.

title: Fall On Me
fact: Fall on Me, from Lifes Rich Pageant (1986), started as a song about acid rain and became one of R.E.M.'s early environmental songs. It was the album's first single and reached number 94 on the Billboard Hot 100.

title: Imitation of Life
fact: "Imitation of Life" was the lead single from R.E.M.'s 2001 album Reveal, written by Peter Buck, Mike Mills, and Michael Stipe and produced by the band with Pat McCarthy. Its title is borrowed from Douglas Sirk's 1959 film of the same name, used as a metaphor for the push and pull between adolescence and adulthood, and the song topped charts across the UK and mainland Europe while reaching the US Top 10 on rock radio.

title: It's The End Of The World As We Know It (And I Feel Fine)
Life and How to Live It
Man On The Moon
fact: R.E.M.'s "Man on the Moon" started life as an instrumental called "C to D Slide" that almost got scrapped - Michael Stipe couldn't find lyrics for it until Andy Kaufman's oddball legacy, including his pro-wrestling stunts and Elvis impersonation, gave him something to write about. The song later lent its title to the 1999 Jim Carrey biopic about Kaufman.

title: Orange Crush
fact: R.E.M.'s Orange Crush is a quietly anti-war song - the title nods to Agent Orange, the defoliant used in the Vietnam War, drawing on singer Michael Stipe's memories of growing up on Army bases where his father served. The subtlety worked almost too well: a British TV host once introduced it on air as "great on a summer's day."

title: Radio Free Europe
fact: R.E.M. recorded their debut single in April 1981 in producer Mitch Easter's converted-garage studio in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. It came out that July on the tiny independent label Hib-Tone, making it the band's first-ever release, before they re-recorded it for 1983's Murmur. In 2009 the Library of Congress added the song to the National Recording Registry for helping set the template for college-radio indie rock.

title: We Walk
fact: On "We Walk," from R.E.M.'s 1983 debut Murmur, the odd dull thud heard throughout the track is actually a slowed-down recording of drummer Bill Berry playing pool. It's one of several unconventional recording tricks producers Mitch Easter and Don Dixon used to give the album its distinctive, hazy atmosphere.

title: What's the Frequency, Kenneth?
fact: The title comes from a bizarre real-life incident in October 1986, when a stranger confronted CBS news anchor Dan Rather on a New York City street while repeatedly demanding, "Kenneth, what is the frequency?" The attacker's identity and motive stayed a mystery for years, which fascinated Michael Stipe enough to build a song around the odd phrase for R.E.M.'s 1994 album Monster. Rather later took the strange tribute in stride, even joining the band onstage to sing along to it.

title: (Nice Dream)
fact: Radiohead wrote "(Nice Dream)" back in 1992, and producer John Leckie shaped its atmosphere on The Bends to echo George Harrison's "My Sweet Lord," aiming for the feel of a guardian angel and a calm, garden-like setting. It was one of four songs, alongside "Sulk," "The Bends," and "Killer Cars," recorded first as possible singles when album sessions began at RAK Studios in March 1994.

title: Black Star
fact: Radiohead's "Black Star" came out of an unplanned session during the making of The Bends - producer John Leckie stepped out one day, and engineer Nigel Godrich stayed behind with the band to record it, in what became his first work with Radiohead. Godrich has produced every Radiohead album since.

title: Bloom
fact: "Bloom" opens Radiohead's 2011 album The King of Limbs. Thom Yorke has said the song was inspired by the original BBC Blue Planet documentary series, calling the idea of discovering unknown forms of life one of the most profound concepts he'd encountered. Years later the band reworked the track with composer Hans Zimmer as "(ocean) Bloom" for a Blue Planet II trailer.

title: Bodysnatchers
fact: "Bodysnatchers," from 2007's In Rainbows, was recorded live with the full band playing together in one take — the only track on the album done that way. It was tracked at Tottenham House, a crumbling country mansion in Wiltshire where the band lived in caravans during sessions with producer Nigel Godrich.

title: Burn the Witch
fact: Radiohead first attempted "Burn the Witch" during the Kid A sessions around 2000, finally releasing it 16 years later in 2016 with a striking stop-motion video. Director Chris Hopewell's claymation clip, built in just 14 days, deliberately apes the visual style of the classic British children's show Trumptonshire, giving the song a distinctive vintage-kids'-TV look.

title: Daydreaming
fact: Daydreaming, the second single from Radiohead's A Moon Shaped Pool (2016), has a video directed by filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson, who has used Jonny Greenwood's music in several of his films. Anderson and the band sent 35mm prints of the video to select theaters to screen.

title: Decks Dark
fact: "Decks Dark" is the third track on Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool. Its string and choir arrangements were written by Jonny Greenwood and performed by the London Contemporary Orchestra under conductor Hugh Brunt, giving the track its distinctive female-chorus backdrop.

title: Desert Island Disk
fact: "Desert Island Disk," from Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool, takes its title from the BBC's long-running radio program Desert Island Discs. For this record, longtime producer Nigel Godrich changed his approach, capturing the band on tape as they worked through Thom Yorke's acoustic demos together for the first time, blending the group's early folk-leaning sound with its later electronic experimentation.

title: Everything in its Right Place
fact: Radiohead's "Everything in Its Right Place" started as a piano song, but early full-band arrangements kept falling flat - the breakthrough came when Thom Yorke and producer Nigel Godrich took it apart and rebuilt the piano chords as synth tones instead.

title: Fake Plastic Trees
fact: Thom Yorke wrote "Fake Plastic Trees" after being struck by the artificial plants and manufactured feel of London's then-newly redeveloped Canary Wharf docklands. During recording for The Bends, producer John Leckie sent the rest of the band out of the room so Yorke could cut a quiet guide vocal alone, and Jonny Greenwood recalled Yorke nailing it in three takes.

title: Feral
fact: "Feral" is one of the most abstract, largely instrumental tracks on Radiohead's 2011 album The King of Limbs, produced by longtime collaborator Nigel Godrich. Thom Yorke's voice is chopped into yelps and stutters that function more like another percussion part than a lead vocal, set against itchy, tribal drum patterns influenced by the dubstep and electronic scene surrounding artists like Burial and Four Tet. Fans and critics have often singled it out as the most compelling, fully-formed moment on an album that was initially underrated.

title: Ful Stop
fact: Ful Stop, from Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool, features extra drums from Clive Deamer, who had played with the band on The King of Limbs tour. The strings and choir on the album were arranged by guitarist Jonny Greenwood and performed by the London Contemporary Orchestra.

title: Go To Sleep
fact: "Go to Sleep" is a track from Radiohead's 2003 album Hail to the Thief, produced with longtime collaborator Nigel Godrich. The band recorded most of the album in just two weeks at Ocean Way Recording in Hollywood, then finished additional recording and mixing at their own studio in Oxfordshire, England.

title: Go to Sleep. (Little Man Being Erased.)
I Might Be Wrong
fact: The version of "I Might Be Wrong" many fans know best is actually a live recording, released on Radiohead's 2001 live album I Might Be Wrong: Live Recordings. Captured during the band's Kid A and Amnesiac-era tour, the live arrangement leans harder into the rhythm section than the more atmospheric studio version from Amnesiac, giving it a rawer, more rock-driven feel.

title: I Want None Of This
fact: "I Want None of This" is a previously unreleased Radiohead track the band contributed to Help: A Day in the Life, a 2005 charity compilation for War Child. Alongside contributions from artists like Coldplay and Gorillaz, the album was written, recorded, and released within about a day, going on to become one of the fastest-selling download albums of its time.

title: Identikit
fact: Radiohead debuted "Identikit" live at the American Airlines Arena in Miami on February 27, 2012, years before it had an official studio release. The band later tracked a version at Jack White's Third Man Records studio during a tour stop, though those recordings were ultimately scrapped; the song finally surfaced in finished form on 2016's A Moon Shaped Pool.

title: If You Say the Word
fact: Radiohead's members met as students at Abingdon School in Oxfordshire, England, and originally called themselves On a Friday - a nod to the day of the week they rehearsed in the school music room.

title: Ill Wind
fact: 'Ill Wind' was a bonus track tucked into the deluxe box set of Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool, released alongside the band's unused James Bond theme 'Spectre.' Built on a bossa nova rhythm with Thom Yorke singing in falsetto over icy layered synths, it stayed a rarity until the band finally put it on streaming services in 2019. Once released, it quietly climbed to No. 8 on Billboard's Alternative Digital Songs chart.

title: Jigsaw Falling Into Place
fact: Radiohead released In Rainbows in 2007 letting fans pay whatever they wanted for it, with no minimum price. The average payment ended up around .26 - and the album still went on to debut at No. 1 once it got a physical release.

title: Like Spinning Plates
fact: 'Like Spinning Plates,' from Radiohead's 2001 album Amnesiac, is built on the reversed backing track of an early electronic version of the then-unreleased song 'I Will.' Thom Yorke said that after hearing the tape played backward he thought the melody sounded better that way, so he learned to sing the lyrics backwards and then reversed that vocal take again to get the song's eerie, warped sound.

title: Lotus Flower
fact: The video for Lotus Flower, from The King of Limbs, was directed by Garth Jennings and choreographed by Wayne McGregor. Thom Yorke's dancing in it turned into the "Dancing Thom Yorke" internet meme in 2011.

title: Lucky
fact: Radiohead recorded "Lucky" in just five hours on September 4, 1995, at producer Brian Eno's invitation, for The Help Album, a charity compilation benefiting War Child's work with children affected by the Bosnian war. The band considered it some of their best work at the time, and it was later included on their 1997 album OK Computer.

title: Morning Mr Magpie
fact: The title of this In Rainbows (2007) track nods to an old British superstition about magpies: spotting a lone magpie is considered bad luck, so tradition holds that you should greet it ("Good morning, Mr. Magpie, how's your wife?") to ward off misfortune. The custom is tied to the children's rhyme "One for Sorrow," which assigns a fortune to the number of magpies spotted. It's a bit of British folklore tucked into one of the album's more skeletal, guitar-driven arrangements.

title: Packt Like Sardines in a Crushd Tin Box
Paranoid Android
fact: "Paranoid Android" was stitched together from three separate song fragments, each originally written by a different band member, in a process inspired by the multi-part structure of the Beatles' "Happiness Is a Warm Gun." Recorded at St Catherine's Court, a 15th-century mansion near Bath, the first edit ran over 14 minutes — including a long Jonny Greenwood organ interlude — before being trimmed to six and a half minutes for OK Computer.

title: Present Tense
fact: "Present Tense" was written around 2008, and Thom Yorke first played it, then titled "The Present Tense," in a solo set at the UK's Latitude Festival in 2009. It was also performed with Atoms for Peace before Radiohead finally released it on A Moon Shaped Pool in 2016.

title: Reckoner
fact: 'Reckoner' grew out of sessions for an unfinished Radiohead track called 'Feeling Pulled Apart by Horses' and was reworked for years before landing on In Rainbows. All five band members played percussion together to record its cathartic rhythm track at an English country house, and the album's title itself comes from a lyric in the song.

title: Sail to the Moon. (Brush the Cobwebs Out of the Sky.)
Street Spirit
fact: Street Spirit (Fade Out) closes Radiohead's 1995 album The Bends and was released as a single in January 1996, reaching number five on the UK charts, the band's highest position at that point. Thom Yorke cited the music of R.E.M. and Ben Okri's novel The Famished Road as inspirations, and the black-and-white music video was directed by Jonathan Glazer, who later directed Radiohead's "Karma Police" video.

title: Subterranean Homesick Alien
fact: This OK Computer (1997) deep cut borrows its title from Bob Dylan's "Subterranean Homesick Blues," but the song itself traces back to a college essay Thom Yorke wrote imagining himself as an alien observing the people of Oxford. Radiohead layered in woozy electric piano chasing the vibe of Miles Davis' Bitches Brew.

title: The Gloaming. (Softly Open Our Mouths in the Cold.)
fact: Every song on Radiohead's 2003 album Hail to the Thief carries a two-part title, and "The Gloaming. (Softly Open Our Mouths in the Cold.)" is the eighth track, written by all five band members and produced with longtime collaborator Nigel Godrich. The title word "gloaming" is an old term for twilight or dusk.

title: The Numbers
fact: "The Numbers" is from Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool. That October the band released an official video of Thom Yorke and Jonny Greenwood performing a stripped-down version of the song outdoors using a vintage Roland CR-78 drum machine, directed by filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson.

title: There There. (The Boney King of Nowhere.)
Tinker Tailor Soldier Sailor Rich Man Poor Man Beggar Man Thief
fact: This track from Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool borrows its title from a traditional English counting rhyme once used in children's fortune-telling games, such as counting cherry stones or buttons to predict a future profession. Director Richard Ayoade, known for the films Submarine and The Double, made a short companion video for the song.

title: We Suck Young Blood. (Your Time Is Up.)
Where I End and You Begin. (The Sky Is Falling In.)
Beat on the Brat
fact: Ramones' "Beat on the Brat" grew out of Joey Ramone watching a spoiled kid's meltdown in his Forest Hills, Queens apartment lobby - the band played it live for over a year before recording it, and its opening chord change was lifted straight from bubblegum-pop songs like "Yummy Yummy Yummy." U2 later covered it for a 2003 Ramones tribute album.

title: Gimme Gimme Shock Treatment
fact: Ramones' "Gimme Gimme Shock Treatment," from 1977's Leave Home, was written by Dee Dee and Johnny Ramone at artist Arturo Vega's loft - the title nods to electroconvulsive therapy, filtered through the band's usual dark, satirical humor rather than anything to be taken literally.

title: Havana Affair
fact: 'Havana Affair' appears on the Ramones' self-titled 1976 debut album, playing a Cold War-era spy storyline for laughs, with the narrator boasting about becoming 'a guide for the CIA' in pre-revolution Havana. Johnny Ramone was such a fan of the Red Hot Chili Peppers' cover version that he chose to open the 2003 Ramones tribute album We're a Happy Family with it.

title: I Wanna Be Sedated
fact: Ramones' "I Wanna Be Sedated," from 1978's Road to Ruin, is Joey Ramone's ode to sheer boredom - inspired partly by a miserable London Christmas stuck in a hotel room with Dee Dee Ramone, and partly by getting burned by hot water and needing hospital treatment. It was also the first song Marky Ramone ever recorded with the band, nailed in just two takes.

title: I Wanna Be Your Boyfriend
fact: Drummer Tommy Ramone wrote this track partly as a counterpoint to the band's run of 'I Don't Wanna' songs, like 'I Don't Wanna Walk Around with You.' It's the slowest song on the Ramones' 1976 debut album and the most unusually arranged, featuring a twelve-string guitar, glockenspiel, and tubular bells played by outside studio musicians, with engineer Rob Freeman even joining in on the closing backing vocals.

title: Pinhead
fact: The Ramones' "Pinhead," from 1977's Leave Home, ends with the band's famous rallying cry "Gabba gabba hey." That chant traces back to the 1932 Tod Browning film Freaks, which the band caught at an art-house cinema after an outdoor gig got rained out, and a line from the movie became the inspiration for the song's "we accept you, one of us" refrain.

title: Rock 'n' Roll High School
fact: The Ramones wrote this for the 1979 Roger Corman film Rock 'n' Roll High School, in which they starred. They first recorded it with producer Ed Stasium, then Phil Spector remixed it for the movie, and they later re-recorded it with Spector for 1980's End of the Century; it reached number 67 in the UK.

title: Ruby Soho
fact: Written by Tim Armstrong, Lars Frederiksen, and Matt Freeman, "Ruby Soho" was the third single from Rancid's 1995 album ...And Out Come the Wolves. The song is about the strain touring puts on relationships, with the narrator heading off to another "destination unknown" and a girl he leaves behind. It became one of Rancid's biggest hits, reaching #13 on the Billboard Modern Rock Tracks chart.

Penny in the Lake
fact: Penny in the Lake is from Singin' to an Empty Chair, the 2026 album from the Chicago band Ratboys. The song was released with a video and an announcement of a Chicago benefit show.

title: What's Right?
fact: What's Right? is a single from Ratboys' album Singin' to an Empty Chair (February 6, 2026, New West Records). Julia Steiner said they treated the song like a studio experiment, stitching together three drum performances recorded in three different-sounding rooms.

Tell All the World About You
Crime
fact: Real Estate's "Crime" comes from their self-titled 2009 debut, which Pitchfork gave an 8.5 and its Best New Music tag - an early sign of the acclaim the Ridgewood, New Jersey band would keep earning.

title: Darling
fact: 'Darling' is the opening track on Real Estate's 2017 album In Mind, the follow-up to 2014's Atlas. It was the band's first album recorded with new guitarist Julian Lynch, who joined after founding guitarist Matt Mondanile departed. True to the New Jersey band's laid-back style, the song opens with nearly a full minute of guitar jamming before any vocals come in.

title: Easy
fact: 'Easy' is the lead track on Real Estate's 2011 album Days, which the New Jersey band recorded over five months in a barn in New Paltz, New York with producer Kevin McMahon. Its music video was released through Funny or Die and directed by comedian Tom Scharpling.

title: Green Aisles
fact: "Green Aisles," written by frontman Martin Courtney, is the second track on Real Estate's 2011 album Days, recorded over five months in a converted barn in New Paltz, New York, with producer Kevin McMahon. Lyrically, it's a wistful look back at aimless summer drives from the band's suburban New Jersey adolescence.

title: Had To Hear
fact: Had to Hear opens Real Estate's third album, Atlas (March 2014), and was released as a single that August. It shows off the band's signature chiming guitar chords and Martin Courtney's gentle vocals, and critics compared the album's opening pair to Galaxie 500.

title: It's Real
fact: "It's Real" is the sunny, surf-tinged highlight from Real Estate's 2011 album Days, the New Jersey band's first release for Domino Records. It was written by guitarists Martin Courtney and Matt Mondanile and produced by Kevin McMahon. With its easy, singalong "whoa-oh-oh" chorus, it's one of the clearest examples of the band's breezy jangle-pop sound.

title: Paper Cup
fact: "Paper Cup," a single from Real Estate's 2020 album The Main Thing, features guest vocals from Amelia Meath of Sylvan Esso over lush strings and backing harmonies. Frontman Martin Courtney has described the song as reflecting on getting older while still working as a touring musician.

title: Ribbon
fact: Real Estate's founding members were childhood friends from Ridgewood, New Jersey who played music together in high school, kept trading songs while away at different colleges, and reunited to form the band after graduating.

title: Stained Glass
fact: "Stained Glass" is a track from Real Estate's 2017 album In Mind, written collectively by band members Alex Bleeker, Jackson Pollis, Julian Lynch, Martin Courtney, and Matt Kallman and produced by Cole M.G.N. When it was released, the band paired it with a tutorial video teaching fans how to play the song's guitar tabs and keyboard parts themselves.

title: Talking Backwards
fact: Real Estate's "Talking Backwards," the lead single from 2014's Atlas, was recorded at New York's Magic Shop studio with producer Tom Schick - Pitchfork named it a Best New Track, and NPR and Rolling Stone both later called it one of the best songs of that year.

title: The Main Thing
fact: "The Main Thing" is the title track of Real Estate's 2020 album and was the last song written for the record. Frontman Martin Courtney wanted to write something like an inspirational anthem while weighing whether touring as a musician was compatible with being a parent of young kids, and the brief track builds to an energetic, psychedelic guitar solo.

title: Water Underground
fact: "Water Underground" is the lead single from Real Estate's 2024 album Daniel, co-written with Sammi Niss and produced by Daniel Tashian. Its music video pays tribute to the 1990s Nickelodeon sitcom The Adventures of Pete & Pete.

title: Downtown People
fact: "Downtown People" is the title track and first single from the debut album by Rebounder, an NYC band made up of brothers Dylan and Noah Chenfeld. They made the record together, trading instruments and ideas in their windowless Greenpoint, Brooklyn studio, with small contributions from Jesse Rutherford and Gianluca Buccellati; it's out on Nettwerk.

title: Brother
fact: Red PK is the project of Andy "Red" PK, a Chicago-based pedal steel and guitar player who spent years as a sideman for bands like Ratboys, Squirrel Flower, and Free Range before stepping out as a solo artist. "Brother" appears on Horse Like Me, his 2026 debut LP and the first time he'd recorded his own songs in a proper studio, working alongside friends Seth Engel and Nick Levine. Andy only picked up pedal steel a few years earlier, before quitting a day job in marketing in 2025 to pursue music full time.

title: Get Down
fact: 'Get Down' comes from Red PK's 2026 debut album Horse Like Me, recorded and mixed at Ohmstead studio in Chicago. The project is led by Andy 'Red' PK, a longtime touring guitarist and pedal steel player for Chicago bands like Squirrel Flower and Ratboys, who co-produced the record with drummer Seth Engel and close friend Nick Levine. It's his first time stepping out from behind other artists to front his own record.

title: Don't Leave Me (Ne me quitte pas)
Ghost
fact: Remember Sports started out simply as Sports, based in Gambier, Ohio, before renaming in 2017 to avoid confusion with another band called Sports - around the same time they relocated to Philadelphia.

title: Thumb
fact: "Thumb" is track three on Remember Sports' 2026 album The Refrigerator. Singer Carmen Perry wrote it from the perspective of her 15-year-old self, and the song strays from a standard pop structure with bursts of raucous distortion.

title: Never Be Anyone Else But You
Last Frontier
fact: Last Frontier, from Ride's 2024 album Interplay, started as a rough demo out of guitarist Mark Gardener's home studio that almost didn't make the record until producer Richie Kennedy heard potential in it and reworked the arrangement with a driving, Joy Division-inspired backbone. Singer Andy Bell wrote the vocal melody by improvising live at the microphone rather than working it out in advance, a first for him.

title: Monaco
fact: "Monaco" comes from Ride's 2024 album Interplay, the shoegaze band's third studio release since reuniting in 2014. It was produced by the band with Richie Kennedy and mixed by Claudius Mittendorfer. Ride actually debuted the then-unreleased song live back in February 2023, sneaking the new track into a tour where they were otherwise performing their classic 1990 debut album, Nowhere, start to finish.

title: Peace Sign
fact: "Peace Sign" began as a jam at guitarist Andy Bell's OX4 studio in 2021 and was originally titled "Berlin." It became a single from Ride's 2024 album Interplay, with Bell saying the lyrics were inspired by the documentary The Alpinist, about free climber Marc-Andre Leclerc.

title: Talk That Talk feat. Jay Z
We Found Love feat. Calvin Harris
Science Vs. Romance
fact: Rilo Kiley's "Science Vs. Romance," from 2001's Take Offs and Landings, was written by Jenny Lewis and Blake Sennett - Stereogum later ranked it among the band's ten best songs.

title: Silver Lining
fact: 'Silver Lining' comes off Rilo Kiley's fourth and final album, Under the Blacklight (2007), where the band deliberately chased a glossier, more radio-ready sound, dabbling in everything from yacht-rock grooves to disco sheen from track to track. The gamble paid off commercially, with the album becoming their highest-charting release, debuting at No. 22 on the Billboard 200.

title: The Execution of All Things
fact: The Execution of All Things is the title track of Rilo Kiley's second album (2002). The Los Angeles band, led by Jenny Lewis and Blake Sennett, went to Nebraska to record it with Bright Eyes' Mike Mogis and new drummer Jason Boesel.

title: The Frug
fact: "The Frug" appeared on Rilo Kiley's self-titled 1999 EP and namechecks a string of 1960s dance crazes, including the Frug, the Freddie, the Robocop, and the Smurf. It's a fitting subject for singer Jenny Lewis, who as a child actor danced both the Frug and the Freddie on-screen in the 1989 film Troop Beverly Hills.

title: With Arms Outstretched
fact: "With Arms Outstretched," from Rilo Kiley's 2002 album The Execution of All Things, features a makeshift boy choir made up of friends and bandmates, including singer-songwriter Conor Oberst. The song has had a long cultural afterlife, soundtracking the final scene of Showtime's Weeds (mirroring its use in the show's pilot) and later appearing in the Looking for Alaska miniseries.

Kicking The Heart Out

fact: Do You Love Your Company? is track 5 on Ron Gallo's Stardust Birthday Party (October 5, 2018, New West Records). In the video, Gallo confronts many versions of himself.

title: Back Of A Truck
fact: On "Back of a Truck," from his 2026 album American Stories, Rostam swaps in a different classic song lyric each time the chorus repeats, including lines borrowed from Bob Dylan's "Don't Think Twice, It's Alright" and the Supremes' "You Keep Me Hangin' On." Musically it blends twangy pedal steel with Middle Eastern microtonal electric saz, aiming for the feeling of driving across America with the windows down.

fact: "Hardy" reunites Rostam with Clairo, whose 2019 debut album "Immunity" he produced. The track's lush orchestral backbone actually began as an instrumental Rostam put together back in 2012, built around a sample of Georges Delerue's score for Truffaut's 1973 film "Day for Night."

The song was named BBC Radio 1's 'Hottest Record' on release, and its road-trip theme later inspired the duo's 'Meet Me in the Car' tour name.

Coinstar
fact: "Coinstar," released by Runnner (Noah Weinman) in January 2025, was the first song since starting the project that Weinman wanted to record with a full, big studio sound, complete with soaring pedal steel. He's described it as being about the tug-of-war between wanting a stable, settled life and wanting to keep touring, using a coin flip as a running metaphor for that indecision.

title: Halfway Up The Lawn
fact: "Halfway Up The Lawn" is a single from runo plum's debut album patching, released in November 2025. The Minneapolis songwriter grew up in a small town in rural Minnesota, discovered music through Perpich Arts High School, and taught herself production after leaving college in 2019, ultimately recording patching with co-producer Lutalo Jones in a rented cabin in Vermont.

title: Sickness
fact: "Sickness" was the lead single Minneapolis musician Runo Plum used to announce their debut album Patching. The track, built around soft percussion and melancholic guitar, was co-produced with Lutalo and features contributions from instrumentalist Noa Francis.

title: Darling
fact: S. Raekwon is Steven Raekwon Reynolds, a producer and multi-instrumentalist from Buffalo, New York, now based in New York City, who writes, produces, and plays nearly every instrument on his own records himself.

title: Glad
fact: Glad was co-written and co-produced by Tom Rowlands of The Chemical Brothers, with Jez Williams of Doves on guitar. It came from International (September 2025), which Saint Etienne have said is their final studio album.

title: Only Love Can Break Your Heart
Take Me To The Pilot
fact: Despite sharing its title with a classic 1970 Elton John song, Saint Etienne's "Take Me To The Pilot" is a completely original 2025 track, co-written and co-produced with Paul Hartnoll of the electronic duo Orbital. Frontman Bob Stanley describes it as a swirling, futuristic tune about escape and reinvention.

title: May Day
fact: 'May Day' comes from Saintseneca's 2025 album Highwalllow & Supermoon Songs, the Columbus, Ohio band's first release in seven years. It's actually a 21-track project split into three sections -- a core album called Highwalllow orbited by two shorter 'moons' -- and 'May Day' lands on the Viridian Moon half. Songwriter Zac Little built the sprawling record with longtime collaborator Glenn Davis, with Bright Eyes' Mike Mogis handling the mix.

title: Sleeper Hold
fact: "Sleeper Hold" was the first single from Saintseneca's third album, "Such Things" (2015), and remains one of the Ohio band's most straightforwardly hooky songs. Co-founder Zac Little has said the track grew out of questions about "the physics of consciousness," while musically it leans into maximalist, harmony-laden pop choruses, with Little and bandmate Maryn Jones trading vocals.

title: Bring It On Home to Me
Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen
People Watching
fact: The title track from Sam Fender's album People Watching gave the Geordie singer his third straight UK Number One album, with the biggest opening week for a British act since Harry Styles' Harry's House. The album also broke the 21st-century record for fastest-selling vinyl release by a UK artist, moving 43,000 vinyl copies in its first week. The single itself reached the UK top five and went Platinum.

title: Seventeen Going Under
fact: 'Seventeen Going Under' turned into a real trophy case for Sam Fender — it won the Ivor Novello Award for Best Song Musically and Lyrically in 2022, beating out heavyweight nominees like Adele, and helped him pick up Best British Alternative/Rock Act at the Brit Awards that same year. Not bad for the title track off just his second album.

fact: "Lizard" appears on Samia's 2025 album Bloodless, which was recorded at Sylvan Esso's Betty's studio in Durham, North Carolina, and at collaborator Jake Luppen's Minneapolis studio. The album was produced by longtime Samia collaborator Caleb Wright alongside Luppen.

title: The Game Of Love Feat. Michelle Branch
I'll Be Gone
fact: "I'll Be Gone" is a track from SASAMI's 2025 album Blood on the Silver Screen, written and composed by Sasami Ashworth. When the album got a deluxe "Director's Cut" reissue, the song came back in a whole new form: a remix by comedian and actress Patti Harrison.

"9" appears on SAULT's 2021 album Nine, a release the anonymous UK collective made available to buy or stream for only 99 days before pulling it. The song was co-written by singer Cleo Sol along with Dean "Inflo" Josiah and other members of the collective, and its buoyant guitar line offers an uplifting counterpoint to the album's heavier tracks.

title: Bitter Streets
fact: "Bitter Streets" appears on Nine, one of several albums from SAULT, the deliberately mysterious UK collective led by producer Inflo and singer Cleo Sol. The group has built its reputation on surprise releases, dropping five full albums at once with almost no warning in 2022 alone. For years the band kept its lineup so secretive that fans and critics could only slowly piece together who was actually behind the music.

title: Don't Waste My Time
fact: SAULT's "Don't Waste My Time" comes from 5, the anonymous British collective's 2019 debut album - the opening chapter in a remarkably prolific run of celebrated releases the group has kept up without ever doing press or revealing its full lineup.

title: Fearless
fact: "Fearless" is the second track on Untitled (Rise), a 2020 album by the mysterious and largely anonymous UK collective SAULT, made available for only a limited run before being pulled from streaming. Riding '80s synths and a driving bassline, it pairs a laid-back R&B groove with an insistently upbeat refrain: "Be yourself at all times... be fearless."

title: Free
fact: SAULT is a British collective that has kept its members almost entirely anonymous since 2019 - the only name that reliably shows up in the liner notes is producer Inflo, also known for his work with Michael Kiwanuka and Little Simz.

title: Let Me Go
fact: SAULT is an anonymous British music collective that avoids media interviews entirely - even their exact lineup is unconfirmed, though producer Dean “Inflo” Josiah Cover (who's worked with Michael Kiwanuka and Little Simz) is rumored to be a member.

title: Smile and Go
fact: Smile and Go is the fifth track on 7, the second album by British group SAULT, released in September 2019. Producer Inflo worked with vocalist Cleo Sol on it.

title: Why Why Why Why Why
fact: "Why Why Why Why Why" is track four on 5, the 2019 album by the anonymous UK collective SAULT, released through Forever Living Originals. SAULT built its reputation by releasing music with almost no promotional interviews or photos, letting records like 5 speak for themselves.

title: Husbands
fact: "Husbands," from Savages' 2013 debut album Silence Yourself, borrows its title from a 1970 John Cassavetes film about three friends navigating a midlife crisis. Frontwoman Jehnny Beth said the song grew from a feeling that people today have become disconnected, "like smoke."

title: T.I.W.Y.G.
fact: 'T.I.W.Y.G.' (short for 'This Is What You Get') is a track from Savages' 2016 album Adore Life, the follow-up to their debut Silence Yourself. Singer Jehnny Beth opens the song with the line 'This is what you get when you mess with love,' and the band has said the whole record is ultimately about love's power to transform and change people. Drummer Fay Milton drives the track, building from tense hi-hat taps into a full post-punk release.

title: Disco Life
fact: Say She She is a disco-funk trio - Piya Malik, Sabrina Cunningham, and Nya Gazelle Brown - who met and built their sound across New York City, cutting their teeth with a residency at Brooklyn's Union Pool and playing their first show as a band at the venue Barbes. Drawing on '70s heroes like Chic and Nile Rodgers, the group records with analog gear and tape to keep their sound retro.

title: DAYS GO BY (feat. Toro y Moi)
The Old Man's Back Again (Dedicated to the Neo-Stalinist Regime)
Reconcile
fact: "Reconcile" comes from Scott McMicken's 2023 solo debut album Shabang, his first release after stepping away from his longtime band Dr. Dog. Rather than recording with old friends, McMicken worked with a cast of musicians hand-picked by producer Nick Kinsey, deliberately encouraging improvisation in the studio to capture a loose, free-spirited energy. McMicken has described the song as a way of staying close to "the open spirit of letting go."

title: Flame
fact: "Flame" was written by Lou Barlow and released as a single in January 1999 off Sebadoh's self-titled album The Sebadoh. Produced by Eric Masunaga and Rich Costey, it became the band's highest-charting UK single, reaching number 30 on the UK Singles Chart.

title: Skull
fact: "Skull" is from Sebadoh's 1994 album Bakesale, written by Lou Barlow and produced by Tim O'Heir, recorded partly at Fort Apache Studios and partly at home. It was the first Sebadoh album made after founding member Eric Gaffney left the band, though he still played drums on four of its tracks. Sub Pop released "Skull" as a single with a black-and-white video, and it reached number 84 on the UK singles chart.

Its brooding electronic textures came from guitarist Sean Coyle-Smith's at-home experimentation, with singer Charlie Steen noting that Coyle-Smith and drummer Charlie Forbes brought a Depeche Mode-influenced electronic sound to the track.

title: Cutthroat

title: The Boy
fact: Shannon and the Clams' "The Boy," the lead single from 2018's Onion, was recorded in just ten days at Dan Auerbach's Easy Eye Sound studio in Nashville - the song blends 1950s girl-group melodies with 1960s surf-rock guitar.

title: Comeback Kid
fact: "Comeback Kid" was the lead single from Sharon Van Etten's fifth album, Remind Me Tomorrow (January 2019, Jagjaguwar), produced by John Congleton. The album marked a big shift in her sound, moving from guitar and piano toward synthesizers, organs, and harmoniums.

title: Consolation Prize
fact: "Consolation Prize" is the second track on Sharon Van Etten's 2009 debut album, Because I Was in Love, making it one of the earliest songs she ever released. The record was later remixed and reissued in 2017 as "(it was) because i was in love," with two additional bonus tracks.

fact: The title track of Sharon Van Etten's 2015 EP I Don't Want to Let You Down came from leftover sessions for her album Are We There, produced by Van Etten alongside Stewart Lerman. Rather than shelve the extra songs, she gathered five of them into this standalone EP release.

title: I'll Try
album: We've Been Going About This All Wrong
fact: 'I'll Try' is a track from Sharon Van Etten's 2022 album We've Been Going About This All Wrong, repeating its simple title phrase over icy synths and big drums. The song finds Van Etten pushing back against public judgment and sticking to what she believes, set to an upbeat arrangement of distorted guitars and layered instrumentation that contrasts with the album's more somber moments.

title: Let Go
fact: Sharon Van Etten wrote 'Let Go' in 2020 with producer Giorgio Angelini and composer Mike Semple. When she released it as a single, she paired it on the B-side with a cover of 'Some Things Last a Long Time' by Texas singer-songwriter Daniel Johnston.

title: Mistakes
album: We've Been Going About This All Wrong

title: One Day
fact: "One Day" is the lead single from Sharon Van Etten's 2010 album Epic. The record's hazy, warm guitar sound carries an obvious Fleetwood Mac Rumours influence, and Van Etten even dedicated the album sleeve to the band, writing: "Dedicated to Fleetwood Mac. You changed my world."

title: Our Love
fact: "Our Love" comes from Sharon Van Etten's 2014 album Are We There, which she co-produced herself with Stewart Lerman. Part of it was tracked at Electric Lady Studios in New York, the storied room originally built for Jimi Hendrix.

title: Seventeen
fact: Sharon Van Etten's "Seventeen," from 2019's Remind Me Tomorrow, is an ode to New York City that started out as a slow, Lucinda Williams-style dirge before turning into a Springsteen-esque anthem. Its music video pairs Van Etten with an actress playing a teenage version of her, retracing her old haunts around the city.

fact: Sharp Pins is the lo-fi pop project of Chicago musician Kai Slater (also of the band Lifeguard) - “It's a Mod Mod World” is deliberately recorded to sound like catching a British Invasion hit on a handheld AM radio in the 1960s.

title: Live Without Her Love
fact: "Live Without Her Love" is Sharp Pins' cover of a song by the English mod-revival band Squire, cut for the 2026 tribute album Mod Mayday 23, a loving homage to the classic 1979 mod compilation Mods Mayday '79. Sharp Pins is the lo-fi power-pop solo project of Chicago musician Kai Slater, who also plays in Lifeguard and Dwaal Troupe.

title: Popafangout
fact: "Popafangout" is from Sharp Pins' 2025 album Balloon Balloon Balloon. Bandleader Kai Slater wrote and mixed the track himself, and its companion music video was shot on 16mm film.

title: It Was Mine
fact: Seattle songwriter and producer Shelby Natasha wrote "It Was Mine" for a project run by the Bushwick Bookclub, where musicians create songs inspired by whatever book the group is reading. At the time it was Isabel Allende's novel Violeta, narrated by an elderly woman looking back on her life, and Shelby has said the character reminded her of her own grandmother. The song, which blends Chinese folk influences with lo-fi R&B, appears on her debut EP released in 2026.

We Came to Play
fact: This ripper is the lead single off Show Me the Body's 2022 album Trouble the Water. True to the NYC band's signature, frontman Julian Cashwan Pratt still plays his trademark banjo on it — just run through a wall of effects and distortion, giving one of their most straightforwardly punky tracks an odd, twangy backbone.

title: Blooberg
fact: "Blodberg" (Icelandic for thyme) marked Sigur Ros's first new music in seven years when it was released in 2023. The roughly seven-minute track features orchestral contributions from the London Contemporary Orchestra, conducted by Robert Ames, with Jonsi singing partly in Icelandic and partly in the band's invented language, Hopelandic.

title: Hljomalind
fact: "Hljomalind," from Sigur Ros's 2007 release Hvarf/Heim, is named after a Reykjavik record store once run by Kristinn "Kiddi Kanina" Saemundsson, the band's manager at the time. The song had actually been performed live since 1999 under earlier working titles, including "Rokklagid" ("The Rock Song") and "The Rabbit and the Prince."

fact: Sigur Ros' Icelandic song title “Inní mér syngur vitleysingur” translates to “Within me a lunatic sings.” It's the second track on their 2008 album Með suð í eyrum við spilum endalaust.

title: Starálfur
fact: "Starálfur," meaning "staring elf," appears on Sigur Rós's 1999 album Ágætis byrjun. Sung in Icelandic by Jónsi, the lyrics describe going to bed after a long day in blue pajamas and suddenly noticing the mythical staring elf gazing back from the room.

title: Ísjaki
fact: Sigur Ros formed in Reykjavik in 1994 and is named after singer Jonsi Birgisson's baby sister, Sigurros Elin. Jonsi is known for playing his guitar with a cello bow, a technique that helped define the band's ethereal sound.

title: People
fact: "People" appears on Silver Jews' 1998 album American Water, the record that reunited David Berman with Pavement's Stephen Malkmus, who trades vocal lines with Berman throughout the song. The track rides 1970s-style wah-wah guitar and is often cited by fans as a prime example of Berman's witty, detail-packed songwriting.

If You Don't Know Me By Now

fact: Sincere Engineer is Chicago's Deanna Belos, who once aspired to be a dentist before punk rock (and Chicago band Alkaline Trio) took over. She borrowed the band's name from a phrase she heard The Lawrence Arms' Brendan Kelly use in an interview.

title: Cities in Dust
fact: "Cities in Dust" was the lead single from Siouxsie and the Banshees' 1986 album Tinderbox, released in October 1985. It reached number 21 in the UK, and its lyrics describe the ancient Roman city of Pompeii and its later excavation.

title: Kiss Them for Me
fact: "Kiss Them for Me" became Siouxsie and the Banshees' biggest American hit, reaching number 23 on the Billboard Hot 100 after its 1991 release from the album Superstition. Its title borrows from the 1957 film Kiss Them for Me, which starred Jayne Mansfield and Cary Grant, and the lyrics work in Mansfield's real-life catchphrase "divoon."

title: Monitor
fact: "Monitor" appears on Siouxsie and the Banshees' 1981 album Juju, featuring guitarist John McGeoch's hypnotic, distorted playing and production by Nigel Gray. The lyrics imagine a world watched over by surveillance screens, giving the song an Orwellian, CCTV-style atmosphere years before such themes became common in pop music.

title: Peek-a-boo
fact: 'Peek-a-Boo' was built by taking a reversed loop of a brass-and-drum part the Banshees had originally arranged a year earlier for a cover of John Cale's 'Gun,' then layering in a new melody, a one-note bass line, and a distinctive accordion part. The unusual combination, which NME once called 'Oriental marching band hip hop,' gave Siouxsie and the Banshees their first-ever entry on the US Billboard Hot 100 in 1988.

title: She's a Carnival
fact: "She's a Carnival" is track four on Siouxsie and the Banshees' 1982 album A Kiss in the Dreamhouse, with Steven Severin on bass, John McGeoch on guitar, and Budgie on drums. Critics have described it as a gutsy, organ-driven rocker that lives up to its title.

title: Spellbound
fact: "Spellbound" was the first single from Siouxsie and the Banshees' 1981 album Juju, co-produced by the band with Nigel Gray. It was the first single to feature guitarist John McGeoch, who had joined after the band toured the UK in February 1981 to debut the new material, and the song reached No. 22 on the UK Singles Chart.

title: Forgiving
fact: "Forgiving" was produced by Steph Marziano, who Sir Chloe first worked with on a trial basis before deciding to record their entire sophomore album together. The pair ended up making the whole record over two months at Marziano's studio in London. The song appears on Sir Chloe's 2025 album Swallow the Knife.

title: Up Above My Head I Hear Music In The Air
Dragon
album: And Your Song is Like a Circle
fact: "Dragon" appears on Skullcrusher's (Helen Ballentine's) 2025 sophomore album And Your Song Is Like a Circle. The track is built from a looping piano arpeggio mirrored by a programmed, washed-out drum loop, giving it a murky, echoing quality. Its music video plays with scale, showing a miniature version of Ballentine surrounded by trinkets and toys on a desk while a human-sized version of her sits beside it and sings.

title: Song for Nick Drake
fact: Skullcrusher's "Song for Nick Drake" is Helen Ballentine's homage to the late folk singer's music - the song traces specific memories, like train rides and long walks, tied to listening to his songs. It followed her debut EP and a b-side cover of Radiohead's "Lift."

title: All Hands On The Bad One
album: All Hands On The Bad One
fact: "All Hands on the Bad One" is the title track (and third song) from Sleater-Kinney's fifth album, released May 2, 2000 on Kill Rock Stars. The record was produced by John Goodmanson at Jackpot! Studio and later earned a GLAAD Media Award nomination for Outstanding Music Album.

title: Anonymous
fact: "Anonymous" appears on Sleater-Kinney's 1996 album Call the Doctor, which the trio wrote in just three weeks and recorded in four days with producer John Goodmanson. The record is also notable for having no bass guitar at all — guitarists Corin Tucker and Carrie Brownstein built its entire sound from two interlocking guitar parts.

title: Dig Me Out
fact: Sleater-Kinney's "Dig Me Out," the title track from their 1997 album, marked the debut of drummer Janet Weiss, who went on to become the band's longest-serving member - guitarist Carrie Brownstein has said the song's riff started life as a nod to Iggy Pop and David Bowie's "China Girl."

title: Get Up
fact: "Get Up" was released as a single from Sleater-Kinney's 1999 album The Hot Rock and marked a deliberate shift toward a more melodic, danceable sound compared to the band's earlier, rawer records. Its music video was directed by filmmaker Miranda July.

title: Hell
fact: "Hell" was the lead single from Sleater-Kinney's 2024 album Little Rope, produced by John Congleton and recorded at Flora Recording & Playback in Portland, Oregon. Its striking music video was directed by Ashley Connor and stars filmmaker and actress Miranda July in a theatrical, abstract performance piece.

title: I Wanna Be Your Joey Ramone
Modern Girl
fact: Released on 2005's The Woods, 'Modern Girl' is structured in three distinct musical sections mapping onto the emotions 'happy,' 'hungry,' and 'angry,' as Carrie Brownstein sings in character as someone whose comfortable, consumer-driven life unravels. The song's key lyric later gave Brownstein the title for her 2015 memoir, Hunger Makes Me a Modern Girl.

title: Say It Like You Mean It
The Day I Went Away
fact: "The Day I Went Away" appears on Sleater-Kinney's self-titled 1995 debut album, one of only two songs on the record to run past the three-minute mark at a time when the band's songs were typically short and fast. The album was recorded on a tight budget in the earliest days of the Olympia, Washington trio, before Janet Weiss joined on drums. It's a touchstone for fans tracing the band's evolution toward more expansive songwriting.

title: You're No Rock n' Roll Fun
album: All Hands On The Bad One

title: Locust Laced
fact: Sleigh Bells' "Locust Laced" comes from 2021's Texis, the duo's fifth album and first in five years - its music video imagines the band performing on an old-timey country TV program that spirals into complete chaos.

title: Breadcrumb Trail
fact: The opening track on Slint's landmark "Spiderland" (1991), "Breadcrumb Trail" quietly shifts through unusual time signatures — 7/4, 12/8, 15/8 — while Brian McMahan half-sings, half-narrates a story about meeting a carnival fortune teller and riding a roller coaster. The math is nearly invisible under the song's hushed soft-loud-soft dynamics.

title: So Far Down
fact: "So Far Down," written by guitarist Patrick Pentland, appears on Sloan's 2025 album Based on the Best Seller, the band's 14th studio record. The Halifax, Nova Scotia band is unusual in that all four members — Chris Murphy, Jay Ferguson, Patrick Pentland, and Andrew Scott — write songs and sing lead vocals, and the lineup has remained unchanged since forming in 1991.

title: Like a Child Hiding Behind Your Tombstone
turning down flowers
fact: turning down flowers is the six-minute closer of dollhouse, the debut album from New York band Slow Fiction (Tight Knit Records, 2026). The band produced it themselves, with Sonny DiPerri mixing.

title: Better Man
fact: "Better Man" is the lead single from Slow Pulp's 2026 album "Melodie," the Chicago band's first record made with producer Elliot Kozel. Singer Emily Massey's understated vocal anchors the hooky indie-rock track, which arrived with a Ben Turok-directed video full of strobes and sparklers.

title: Red Car
fact: On Slow Pulp's “Red Car,” a 1996 Mazda becomes a stand-in for the possibility of starting over - part of their album Melodie, about feeling stuck and finding a way to move on.

title: Spill
fact: Slow Pulp's "Spill" was actually the first song written for 2023's Yard - but it didn't click until producer Elliot Kozel got involved years later, and it ended up finding its home instead on 2026's Melodie.

title: Alison
fact: "Alison" opens Slowdive's 1993 album Souvlaki. Early versions of the Souvlaki material were initially rejected by Creation Records boss Alan McGee, who then gave the band full creative control; around the same time Slowdive reached out to Brian Eno, who admired their music and ended up contributing to two other tracks on the record.

title: Machine Gun
fact: 'Machine Gun' is the second track on Slowdive's 1993 album Souvlaki, built from the same hazy, reverb-soaked guitar layers that define the record's shoegaze sound. Songwriter Neil Halstead wrote much of Souvlaki while processing the end of his real-life relationship with bandmate Rachel Goswell, who still shares co-lead vocals with him on the track.
