Dry the Rain
fact: "Dry the Rain" opened The Beta Band's 1997 debut EP Champion Versions and later appeared on the compilation The Three EPs. Bassist Richard Greentree said the song was written to bridge folk music and hip-hop, and it builds from a simple acoustic opening into a brass-heavy, gospel-tinged finale featuring trumpet from Jonathan Levien. The track became the band's best-known song after a memorable cameo in the 2000 film High Fidelity.

title: Do You Want Me Now
fact: "Do You Want Me Now" appears on The Beths' 2020 album Jump Rope Gazers. The New Zealand band built the mid-tempo track around Beach Boys-style backing harmonies and country-leaning guitars, a notable departure from their usual power-pop sound, to match frontwoman Elizabeth Stokes's reflection on the strange, stilted limbo of a long-distance relationship.

title: Great No One
fact: 'Great No One' is the opening track and lead single (released October 2017) from The Beths' 2018 debut album Future Me Hates Me. Frontwoman Elizabeth Stokes has described the record's songs broadly as being about infatuation and self-directed telling-offs, delivered through the band's signature hyper-melodic power-pop.

title: Jump Rope Gazers
fact: "Jump Rope Gazers" is the title track of The Beths' 2020 sophomore album. Singer Liz Stokes has described the title as an image of two people holding either end of a jump rope — connected, yet kept apart by the distance between them, which mirrors the song's theme of the push and pull in a relationship. The band performed it, complete with a clarinet solo, for NPR's Tiny Desk concert series.

title: Knees Deep
fact: "Knees Deep" was a last-minute addition to The Beths' 2022 album Expert in a Dying Field, built around one of guitarist Jonathan Pearce's standout guitar lines. Singer Elizabeth Stokes has said the song is a metaphor for her own habit of cautiously wading into things rather than diving in headfirst, an idea the music video plays with by showing the band bungee jumping.

title: Metal
fact: "Metal" is a single from The Beths' fourth album, Straight Line Was a Lie, released in 2025 on Anti- Records. The New Zealand band built the whole record around the idea that life doesn't improve in a straight line, but moves in cycles instead -- a theme "Metal" helped introduce before the album was even announced.

title: Out of Sight
fact: "Out of Sight" is the third single from The Beths' 2020 album Jump Rope Gazers, with a music video that shows the band going bird watching, shot on Super 8 film and mixed with archival bird footage. Singer Elizabeth Stokes said the band deliberately played the song "more fragile" than they usually allow themselves to be, highlighting bassist Benjamin Sinclair's melodic playing.

title: Silence Is Golden
fact: "Silence Is Golden" was the first single from The Beths' 2022 album Expert in a Dying Field. Frontwoman Liz Stokes has said the song is about stress and anxiety manifesting as an intolerance to noise, with the guitars growing more fuzzed-out and chaotic as it builds; recording was interrupted by a four-month COVID lockdown, and the band finished the album during a three-day session in Los Angeles.

title: Straight Line Was a Lie
fact: Straight Line Was a Lie is the title track of The Beths' fourth album, released August 29, 2025 on Anti-. Reviewers called it a headphones album for its layers of instrumentation, and frontwoman Elizabeth Stokes said linear progression is an illusion.

title: Take
fact: "Take" is track seven on the Beths' 2025 album Straight Line Was a Lie, produced by the band's guitarist Jonathan Pearce. Singer Liz Stokes has said the song grew out of a distinctive 16th-note drum pattern their drummer came up with, which ended up dictating the whole track's tempo, and she considers it a musical sister song to "Not Running" from earlier in their catalog.

title: Watching The Credits
fact: Beths frontwoman Elizabeth Stokes has admitted she doesn't love actually watching movies, she just loves reading about them, often skipping straight to the Wikipedia plot synopsis. That habit of absorbing movies without watching them became the inspiration for "Watching the Credits," which was recorded during the Expert in a Dying Field sessions but held back to be its own standalone single, complete with violins and a key change.

title: Whatever
fact: "Whatever" was the lead single from The Beths' debut EP Warm Blood, which the Auckland band independently released in March 2016 before they'd signed to a label. Produced by guitarist Jonathan Pearce, the song became an early breakout track that helped earn the four-piece glowing reviews from the New Zealand music press.

title: Your Side
fact: "Your Side" is a bonus track on the 2023 deluxe reissue of The Beths' album Expert in a Dying Field. The New Zealand band wraps the warm, sincere love song in a breezy touch of '70s-style sway, full of devotion and promises to travel through the night just to be there for someone.

title: No Angels
fact: "No Angels" marked The Big Pink's return in 2022 after a decade away, and frontman Robbie Furze built the track around a sample of "Light On" by the little-known band Bad Cop, which he'd stumbled on by chance while listening to the radio during a drive to visit a friend in Los Angeles. The shoegaze-leaning single was produced by Tony Hoffer, known for his work with Beck, Air, and Phoenix.

title: All Hands Against His Own
fact: "All Hands Against His Own" appears on The Black Keys' 2004 album Rubber Factory, which was recorded in an abandoned General Tire factory in the band's hometown of Akron, Ohio. The duo tracked the album on a reel-to-reel recorder using tape recycled from old fried-chicken radio commercials that never aired.

title: Everlasting Light
fact: The Black Keys' Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney grew up a few houses apart in Akron, Ohio, and first met around age nine - though it was their older brothers who eventually pushed the two to start jamming together in Carney's basement.

title: I Forgot To Be Your Lover
fact: The Black Keys' version is a cover of William Bell's 1968 soul single, co-written by Bell and Booker T. Jones, which reached No. 45 on the charts. The song later became the foundation for Billy Idol's 1986 hit "To Be a Lover," though The Black Keys' rendition -- from their 2024 album Ohio Players -- stays closer to Bell's original, dressing it in orchestral strings and organ.

title: Just Got to Be
fact: "Just Got to Be," released in 2007 from The Black Keys' album Magic Potion, was recorded by Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney in Akron, Ohio. The song later turned up on the soundtrack of the video game NHL 08 and in an AT&T commercial, and its music video shows the duo performing on stage at Akron's Italian Center with no audience present.

title: Doe
fact: "Doe" opens the Breeders' 1990 debut album Pod, recorded in just two weeks in Edinburgh, Scotland, with producer Steve Albini, fresh off producing the Pixies' Surfer Rosa. Kim Deal started the Breeders as a side project with Throwing Muses guitarist Tanya Donnelly, rounding out the lineup with bassist Josephine Wiggs and Slint drummer Britt Walford. Pod became a favorite of Kurt Cobain's, who named it one of his all-time favorite albums.

title: Anenome
fact: "Anenome" dates back to 1996 and was later included on The Brian Jonestown Massacre's 2004 compilation Tepid Peppermint Wonderland: A Retrospective, which introduced newer fans to deep cuts from the band's famously prolific catalog. Frontman Anton Newcombe was known for releasing multiple full albums in a single year during the band's 1990s heyday.

title: Jealous Boy
fact: Jealous Boy appears on Welsh band The Bug Club's 2025 Sub Pop album Very Human Features. Core members Sam Willmett and Tilly Harris met in school at age 14 and have traded vocals ever since; on this track the two go back-and-forth on lead lines. The band's quirky name comes from a childhood bug-collecting club started by Willmett's brother.

title: Watching the Omnibus
fact: Watching the Omnibus, the lead single from The Bug Club's seventh album Every Single Muscle (2026), runs just 79 seconds. The Welsh band recorded the 18-track album with Tom Rees at Rat Trap Studios in Cardiff, and Mikey Young mastered it.

title: I'll Feel a Whole Lot Better
So You Want to Be a Rock 'n' Roll Star
(They Long To Be) Close To You
Let Forever Be
fact: "Let Forever Be" was co-written with, and features vocals from, Oasis's Noel Gallagher. Its 1999 music video was directed by Michel Gondry, who reimagined kaleidoscope visuals practically — instead of a digital effect, he filmed real dancers multiplying into repeated, perfectly synchronized formations. The video went on to win a string of major awards.

title: The Boxer
fact: "The Boxer," from 2005's Push the Button, features vocals and a co-write from Charlatans frontman Tim Burgess, marking his second collaboration with the Chemical Brothers after "Life Is Sweet" a decade earlier. The track builds on a sample of the duo's own earlier instrumental, "Orange Wedge."

title: Have You Seen Her
album: Give More Power To The People

title: Career Opportunities
fact: On The Clash's 1977 debut, "Career Opportunities" got its title the same way the band got its name — pulled from a headline guitarist Mick Jones and bassist Paul Simonon spotted in a London newspaper. Jones also wrote one line straight from his own resume: before joining the band, he'd had a government job opening mail to check that letters weren't rigged with bombs.

title: Clash Citry Rockers
fact: "Clash City Rockers," written by Joe Strummer and Mick Jones, was released as a standalone single in February 1978 between The Clash's first two albums. Its middle musical section is built on the old English nursery rhyme "Oranges and Lemons," giving the band's self-mythologizing anthem an unexpectedly playful foundation.

title: Gates of the West
fact: "Gates of the West" grew out of an early, pre-Clash Mick Jones song called "Ooh Baby Ooh," and the band spent well over a year reworking it, first attempting it during the Give 'Em Enough Rope sessions before finishing it in New York and London. Musically it nods to Booker T & the MGs' "Time Is Tight" and Mott the Hoople's "All the Way from Memphis" — fittingly, since the arrangement was apparently tricky enough that The Clash never once played it live.

title: Pressure Drop
fact: The Clash's version of this reggae standard, written by Toots Hibbert and first recorded by Toots & the Maytals in 1969, started life as a staple of their live sets on the 1977 White Riot tour before the band finally nailed a studio take at Marquee Studios in March 1978. It was released as the B-side to their 1979 single "English Civil War."

title: Safe European Home
fact: "Safe European Home" opens The Clash's 1978 album Give 'Em Enough Rope, the band's first record made with an outside producer: American hard-rock veteran Sandy Pearlman, best known for his work with Blue Oyster Cult. Pairing a scrappy UK punk band with a polished American studio pro was controversial among punk purists at the time, but the album gave The Clash their biggest audience yet.

title: Should I Stay or Should I Go
fact: Mick Jones wrote "Should I Stay or Should I Go" (from 1982's Combat Rock) about his on-and-off relationship with singer Ellen Foley, though he later said the song "wasn't about anything specific" and was really just the band's attempt at writing a classic rock song. The Clash had famously racked up hit singles without ever cracking the UK Top Ten — until the song soundtracked a 1991 Levi's commercial and was rereleased, finally giving the band their only UK number-one single.

title: Straight to Hell
fact: This 1982 Combat Rock track got a huge second life in 2007 when Diplo built the beat for M.I.A.'s 'Paper Planes' around its guitar riff, turning Joe Strummer, Mick Jones and the rest of The Clash into credited co-writers on one of the biggest crossover hits of the 2000s. The sample rippled even further when Jay-Z and T.I. sampled 'Paper Planes' itself for 'Swagga Like Us' — meaning a 25-year-old Clash riff ended up on a hip-hop chart hit too.

title: This Is England
fact: This Is England was released September 30, 1985 as the lead and only single from the Clash's sixth and final album. The song leans on a drum machine and synthesizers, and Joe Strummer called it his last great Clash song.

title: Don't Leave Me This Way (with Sarah Jane Morris)
Don't Say Nothin' Bad (About My Baby)
Garbageman
fact: 'Garbageman' helped launch The Cramps' 1980 debut LP, Songs the Lord Taught Us, which the band recorded in Memphis with Big Star's Alex Chilton producing at the old post-Sun Sam Phillips Recording studio. Rolling Stone later named the album one of its 80 greatest records of 1980, cementing its reputation as a founding psychobilly landmark.

title: Dreams
album: Everybody Else Is Doing It, So Why Can’t We?

title: He Hit Me (It Felt Like a Kiss)
A Fragile Thing
fact: "A Fragile Thing" appears on The Cure's 2024 album Songs of a Lost World, the band's first studio record in sixteen years. Robert Smith revealed the song was originally written under the working title "Kill the Sun" and changed considerably before reaching its final form; the band had already debuted it live back in November 2022, where it became a staple of their tour.

title: A Letter to Elise (7" Remix Edit)
Alone
fact: 'Alone' opens The Cure's 2024 album Songs of a Lost World, the band's first new album in 16 years and first new song since 2008's 4:13 Dream. Robert Smith has said the lyrics grew out of rediscovering the Ernest Dowson poem 'Dregs' in an old journal and borrowing its imagery. The album was recorded at Rockfield Studios in Wales, and Smith has said that once 'Alone' was finished, he knew immediately it had to be the opening track because it unlocked the whole record for him.

title: Boys Don't Cry
fact: "Boys Don't Cry" was first released as a standalone UK single in June 1979 and, despite later becoming one of The Cure's most beloved songs, failed to crack the UK top 75 at the time. It became the title track of the American compilation album Boys Don't Cry, issued in February 1980, and was written by founding members Michael Dempsey, Robert Smith, and Lol Tolhurst.

title: Catch
album: Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me
fact: The Cure's “Catch” is a light, whimsical love song about a girl from Robert Smith's past whose name he can barely remember - a deliberate 180-degree turn from the album's more aggressive opening track.

title: Disintegration
fact: "Disintegration," the eight-minute title track of The Cure's 1989 album, was recorded at Hookend Recording Studios with longtime co-producer David M. Allen. Robert Smith has said his emotions were so raw during the vocal sessions that he broke down at times while recording; he wrote much of the album while dreading turning 30, worried he'd aged out of making his best work.

title: Fascination Street
fact: "Fascination Street" wasn't even supposed to be the lead single from Disintegration, that job was meant for "Lullaby," until The Cure's U.S. label pushed for this one instead. It paid off: the song became the first track ever to top Billboard's brand-new Modern Rock Tracks chart in 1989. One more quirk from those sessions: Robert Smith reportedly refused to speak out loud in the studio, passing notes to his bandmates instead.

title: From the Edge of the Deep Green Sea
High
fact: "High" was released in March 1992 as the lead single from The Cure's album Wish, reaching number one on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart and number eight on the UK Singles Chart. It's credited to all five members of the band at the time (Robert Smith, Simon Gallup, Porl Thompson, Boris Williams, and Perry Bamonte) and was produced by Smith with David Allen.

title: In Between Days
fact: "In Between Days" was released July 19, 1985 as the first single from The Cure's album The Head on the Door, becoming the band's first single to chart on the US Billboard Hot 100. Director Tim Pope's music video, filmed in a single day at Fulham Studios, was made as a colorful pastiche of 1960s films like A Hard Day's Night, complete with hand-drawn, doodled-on socks.

title: Just Like Heaven
album: Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me

title: Lullaby
fact: Robert Smith has said "Lullaby" grew out of a recurring childhood nightmare in which he was eaten by a giant spider, combined with memories of bedtime songs his father sang him that had oddly dark, cautionary endings. The Tim Pope-directed music video won Best British Video at the 1990 Brit Awards.

title: It's Funky Enough
album: No One Can Do It Better

title: Neat Neat Neat
fact: "Neat Neat Neat," the Damned's second single, was released on Stiff Records in February 1977 alongside their debut album Damned Damned Damned. Written by guitarist Brian James and produced by Nick Lowe at Pathway Studios in London, its driving bassline was later ranked among Stylus Magazine's Top 50 basslines of all time.

title: New Rose
fact: "New Rose" was released in October 1976 by Stiff Records as the first single ever released by a British punk band, more than a month before the Sex Pistols' debut. Written by guitarist Brian James and produced by Nick Lowe, it was recorded in a single day at Pathway Studios in London, and its spoken intro parodies the Shangri-Las' "Leader of the Pack."

title: Smash It Up, Part I
fact: Smash It Up came out in 1979 from The Damned's third album, Machine Gun Etiquette. The band had been the first UK punk group to release a single, New Rose, back in 1976.

title: Danzig With Myself (feat. Frank Black)
fact: The title started as a studio joke -- guitarist/frontman Courtney Taylor-Taylor said the song's central riff sounded like something out of Misfits or Danzig, and the nickname stuck as a working title until it became permanent. Pixies frontman Frank Black joined almost by chance: Taylor-Taylor was simply checking in with him while he happened to be in Zurich, and the visit turned into a studio session for the track, which appears on the Dandy Warhols' 2024 album Rockmaker.

title: I'd Like To Help You With Your Problem (Feat Slash)
fact: This 2024 single comes from The Dandy Warhols' album Rockmaker and features a guitar solo from Slash. Frontman Courtney Taylor-Taylor described the track's sound as "real Vietnam-era acid rock," and the band has said they "just stared at each other with our mouths open" the first time they heard Slash's contributions played back in the studio.

title: I Believe in a Thing Called Love
Punk Rock Girl
fact: Punk Rock Girl was the first single from The Dead Milkmen's 1988 album Beelzebubba, recorded at Arlyn Studios in Austin, Texas. Its video, directed by Adam Bernstein and filmed partly at Eastern State Penitentiary, got heavy play on MTV and made it the Philadelphia band's best-known song.

title: A Beginning Song
album: What A Terrible World, What A Beautiful World
fact: The Decemberists closed their album What a Terrible World, What a Beautiful World with “A Beginning Song” - a hopeful, cathartic track meant to feel like something new being born out of the album's earlier, heavier songs.

title: Burial Ground
album: As It Ever Was, So It Will Be Again

title: Calamity Song
fact: Colin Meloy wrote 'Calamity Song' shortly after finishing David Foster Wallace's novel Infinite Jest, and even pitched a music video built around a recreation of the book's apocalyptic tennis-court war game 'Eschaton.' Meloy has also said the song grew out of binge-listening to R.E.M.'s second album Reckoning, and the opening guitar riff bears a close resemblance to that record's 'Talk About the Passion.'

title: California One / Youth and Beauty Brigade
Cavalry Captain
album: What A Terrible World, What A Beautiful World

title: Foregone
fact: "Foregone" was recorded during the same early-2010 sessions at Pendarvis Farm outside Portland, Oregon, that produced The Decemberists' twangy, folk-leaning album The King Is Dead. The band held the song back and released it more than a year later as the second track on Long Live the King, a six-song EP collecting outtakes from those sessions, where its pedal-steel-flecked, country-rock feel fit right in.

title: Here I Dreamt I Was an Architect
I Was Meant for the Stage
January Hymn
fact: The Decemberists take their name from the Decembrist revolt, an 1825 uprising in Imperial Russia - frontman Colin Meloy has said the name was also meant to capture the "drama and melancholy" of the month of December.

album: What A Terrible World, What A Beautiful World

album: What A Terrible World, What A Beautiful World

title: Sons & Daughters
fact: Sons & Daughters closes The Decemberists' 2006 album The Crane Wife, which was loosely inspired by a Japanese folktale about a bird who takes human form. Colin Meloy's bouzouki gives the singable, round-style finale its warmth.

title: Sucker's Prayer
fact: The Decemberists' "Sucker's Prayer," from 2018's I'll Be Your Girl, grew out of Colin Meloy just sitting with a single chord for a while - he's said he had a Karen Dalton song in mind while working it out, and the band had already been playing it live for about a year and a half before they finally recorded it.

title: The Crane Wife 3
fact: The Crane Wife trilogy that closes the album is based on Tsuru no Ongaeshi, a centuries-old Japanese folktale about a man who nurses an injured crane back to health, only for a mysterious woman to later arrive and become his wife. Colin Meloy discovered the story in the children's section of a Portland bookstore and built the album's title and closing suite around it. The Crane Wife 3 picks up the man's side of the tale after the woman's secret is revealed.

title: The Sporting Life
fact: Colin Meloy has said "The Sporting Life" is semi-autobiographical, inspired by his own unglamorous youth-sports days growing up in Helena, Montana. Built on jaunty horns and a rhythm the band has likened to Iggy Pop's "Lust for Life," the song turns one embarrassing on-field stumble into a wry look at how seriously people take competitive sports.

title: The Wrong Year
album: What A Terrible World, What A Beautiful World

title: This Is Why We Fight
fact: "This Is Why We Fight" closes out The Decemberists' 2011 album The King Is Dead, which the band recorded in just six weeks in a barn at Pendarvis Farm outside Portland, Oregon. Aiming for a more concise, Americana-leaning sound, the band drew on R.E.M., Neil Young, and the Byrds, and brought in R.E.M.'s Peter Buck as a guest guitarist on several tracks. The stripped-down approach was a deliberate departure from the band's earlier prog-folk epics.

title: We Both Go Down Together
fact: The Decemberists' "We Both Go Down Together" is the second track on 2005's Picaresque - its dramatic string arrangement is carried by violinist Petra Haden, whose playing became one of the album's most talked-about elements.

title: Yankee Bayonet (I Will Be Home Then)
What Do You Want Me to Say?
fact: An early version of "What Do You Want Me to Say?" was first released as a 7-inch single in November 1997, before the song was re-recorded for the Dismemberment Plan's 1999 album Emergency & I. That album was produced by J. Robbins and Chad Clark, primarily at Water Music Studios with additional sessions at Inner Ear Studios.

title: Mirror in the Bathroom
fact: "Mirror in the Bathroom," written by Dave Wakeling, was released in 1980 as a single from The Beat's debut album I Just Can't Stop It. It reached number 4 on the UK singles chart, the band's biggest hit until 1983, and NME ranked it the third-best track of that year. The song's skittering ska-pop sound, built around David Steele's bassline, became one of the defining singles of the 2 Tone era.

title: Ranking Full Stop
fact: "Ranking Full Stop" was the lead single from The English Beat's 1980 debut I Just Can't Stop It. Its title borrows from Jamaican sound-system slang — "ranking" was a boastful term of respect used by toasting MCs, fitting since the band's own toaster performed under the stage name Ranking Roger.

title: Tears of a Clown
fact: The English Beat (known simply as The Beat in the UK) turned Smokey Robinson and the Miracles' "The Tears of a Clown" into a ska song in 1979, and it reached number 6 in the UK. It was the band's first single and helped launch the British ska revival, then appeared on their 1980 debut album I Just Can't Stop It.

title: Eat Y'self Fitter
fact: "Eat Y'self Fitter" opens The Fall's 1983 album Perverted by Language. Mark E. Smith built the song's chant-like chorus around ad slogans lifted from a Kellogg's All-Bran cereal campaign, and DJ John Peel later named it among his all-time favorite tracks.

title: Garden
fact: "Garden" appeared on The Fall's 1983 album Perverted by Language. Around the same time, the band recorded it for a BBC session for DJ John Peel, taped on December 12, 1983 and broadcast the following January alongside session versions of "Smile" and "Eat Y'self Fitter," part of the band's long-running relationship with Peel's show.

title: Let's Go
fact: "Let's Go" is track six on The Feelies' 1986 album The Good Earth, released on Coyote Records. The album was co-produced by R.E.M.'s Peter Buck, who had been a Feelies fan going back to his days working as a record store clerk.

title: Moscow Nights
fact: "Moscow Nights" appears on The Feelies' 1980 debut album Crazy Rhythms, recorded at Vanguard Studios in New York. The band refused to let an outside producer shape their sound, and it reportedly took them weeks of experimentation to land on their tight, jittery guitar tone. They got it in part by plugging their guitars directly into the recorder with no amplifiers in the signal chain at all.

title: The Boy With The Perpetual Nervousness
Red Skies
fact: Red Skies was the fourth and final single from The Fixx's debut album, Shuttered Room (MCA Records, 1982). It came out in the UK in June 1982 and in the US in January 1983, helped along by an MTV video, and reached number 13 on Billboard's Album Rock Tracks chart.

title: The Sign Of Fire
fact: "The Sign of Fire" was released in November 1983 as a single from The Fixx's album Reach the Beach, following the band's breakout hit "One Thing Leads to Another." It peaked at No. 32 in the US and No. 20 on the mainstream rock chart.

title: A Spoonful Weighs a Ton
fact: "A Spoonful Weighs a Ton" is from The Flaming Lips' 1999 album The Soft Bulletin, the record where the band moved toward lush, symphonic arrangements. The song sets a calm, orchestral feel against deep bass blasts.

title: Do You Realize??
fact: "Do You Realize??," from The Flaming Lips' 2002 album Yoshimi Battles the Pink Robots, was named Oklahoma's official state rock song in 2009 by executive order of Governor Brad Henry. The honor followed an online poll in which the Oklahoma City band's song beat out nine other finalists, including "Heartbreak Hotel," co-written by Oklahoman Mae Boren Axton.

title: Ego Tripping at the Gates of Hell
fact: "Ego Tripping at the Gates of Hell" first appeared on The Flaming Lips' 2002 album Yoshimi Battles the Pink Robots, then lent its title to a 2003 EP featuring club remixes of the song plus new original tracks. Several of those extra recordings were later gathered into the band's 2022 20th-anniversary Yoshimi box set.

It's one of the more musically expansive, bluesy numbers on a record where the band stretched beyond their earlier bar-rock sound.

Absolute Beginners
fact: "Absolute Beginners" was a stand-alone single released in October 1981 that reached number 4 in the UK and never appeared on a Jam studio album. Paul Weller named it after Colin MacInnes' novel, one of his favorites, and the B-side was "Tales from the Riverbank."

title: Beat Surrender
fact: Paul Weller wrote 'Beat Surrender' to mark the end of The Jam, and the band went out on top - it became their fourth and final UK number-one single in December 1982. The title plays on the 1979 disco hit 'Sweet Surrender' and the military term 'beating retreat,' and the band's other contender for the single, 'Solid Bond in Your Heart,' later became a hit for Weller's next band, the Style Council.

title: Down in the Tube Station at Midnight
In the City
fact: "In the City" was The Jam's debut single, released in April 1977 when songwriter Paul Weller was just 18 years old. Weller called it the sound of "young Woking, if not London," a song about trying to break out of the suburbs, and it became the band's first UK Top 40 hit, kicking off a run of 18 consecutive Top 40 singles for the group.

title: Start!
fact: The Jam's 1980 UK number-one single "Start!" borrows its bouncing bassline from George Harrison's Beatles song "Taxman." Bassist Bruce Foxton said the band had been listening heavily to the Beatles' Revolver album at the time, and the riff crept into their new song without them fully intending it.

title: The Eton Rifles
fact: Released in October 1979, "The Eton Rifles" became The Jam's first UK top-ten hit, climbing from a chart entry at No. 29 all the way to No. 3 within a month. Written by Paul Weller, it was the only single pulled from the band's album Setting Sons.

title: The Modern World
fact: "The Modern World" was released as a single in October 1977, taken from The Jam's second album, This Is the Modern World. That album's tepid reception, plus a rough North American tour opening for Blue Oyster Cult, left frontman Paul Weller with such severe writer's block that the band scrapped its first batch of follow-up songs, regrouping to record the far more successful All Mod Cons the next year.

title: Never Understand
fact: "Never Understand" was the debut single from The Jesus and Mary Chain, later included on their 1985 album Psychocandy. A demo tape of the song (along with "Upside Down") made its way to Primal Scream's Bobby Gillespie, who passed it to Alan McGee of Creation Records — leading McGee to become the band's manager and launch their career.

title: Something's Wrong
fact: "Something's Wrong" is track B6 on The Jesus and Mary Chain's 1985 debut, Psychocandy. The album is built on layers of guitar feedback and distortion that brothers William and Jim Reid buried beneath Phil Spector-style "wall of sound" melodies. That noisy, lo-fi production approach became hugely influential on later shoegaze and noise-pop bands.

title: Sometimes Always
fact: "Sometimes Always" is a 1994 duet by The Jesus and Mary Chain's Jim Reid with Mazzy Star singer Hope Sandoval, released as the lead single from the album Stoned & Dethroned. In the song the two trade verses playing an ex-couple weighing whether to get back together, and it became a minor UK hit.

Cheap and Cheerful
fact: "Cheap and Cheerful" comes from The Kills' 2008 album Midnight Boom, which the duo recorded with producer Alexander "Armani XXXchange" Epton after relocating from a Los Angeles studio to the quieter Key Club Recording Company in Benton Harbor, Michigan. The band has said they drew inspiration from old TV documentaries about 1960s youth culture, aiming to write "modern playground songs."

title: U R A Fever
fact: "U.R.A. Fever" opens The Kills' 2008 album Midnight Boom, built from clattering, scrapyard-style percussion and metallic clunks rather than conventional drums. The duo recorded the album in Benton Harbor, Michigan, working with producer Alex Epton to push their raw blues-rock sound into grittier, more rhythmic territory.

title: Count The Ways
fact: "Count The Ways" is the second track on The Last Dinner Party's second album, From the Pyre (October 2025), produced by Markus Dravs. The band debuted it live at a fan pop-up event in New York City in September 2025, before the album came out.

title: Nothing Matters
fact: "Nothing Matters" was the debut single from UK band The Last Dinner Party, released in April 2023 ahead of their album Prelude to Ecstasy. Singer Abigail Morris originally wrote it as a slow, sad ballad, but the band reworked it into a maximalist anthem that went viral on TikTok and Instagram Reels, becoming the group's first UK Top 20 single at No. 16.

title: Sinner
fact: "Sinner" was the second single from The Last Dinner Party's debut album Prelude to Ecstasy, written by guitarist Lizzie Mayland and produced by James Ford. The album went on to debut at Number One on the UK Albums Chart, the biggest first-week showing for a debut band album in nine years.

title: I Just Can't Get Over Losing You
fact: True to form for the D'Addario brothers, Brian and Michael wrote and produced "I Just Can't Get Over Losing You" themselves — it's the lead single off their 2026 album "Look for Your Mind!," fleshed out with touring members including Eva Chambers of Tchotchke.

title: Look For Your Mind
fact: Look for Your Mind! is the sixth album by The Lemon Twigs (May 8, 2026), produced by brothers Brian and Michael D'Addario. They recorded it mainly at their Brooklyn studio to 16-track tape, and bassist Eva Chambers of Tchotchke also designed the cover art.

title: Burning Out
fact: "Burning Out" was The Linda Lindas' first single after signing to Reprise/Warner Records, written just weeks after guitarist-singer Lucia de la Garza graduated high school. The still-teenage band turned that strange, in-between feeling — watching the world move on while you figure out what's next — into an anthem that rides the line between feeling lost and feeling free.

title: No Obligation
fact: "No Obligation" is the title track of The Linda Lindas' 2024 sophomore album. Bassist Eloise Wong wrote the song as the band's statement of purpose, opening with the line "I don't got no obligation" to declare that they make music for themselves rather than to meet anyone else's expectations.

title: Yo Me Estreso
fact: "Yo Me Estreso" is a Spanish-language song from The Linda Lindas' 2024 album No Obligation about the everyday experience of feeling stressed and anxious. Musically it was inspired by corridos tumbados, banda, and Duranguense styles filtered through the band's own punk sound, and its video features a guest appearance by "Weird Al" Yankovic on accordion.

fact: The Magnetic Fields is largely the vision of songwriter Stephin Merritt, who started the project as essentially a one-man show before childhood friend Claudia Gonson joined as drummer and manager. Their best-known work, 69 Love Songs, is a three-disc, 69-track concept album spanning genres from country to synth-pop.

title: 100,000 Fireflies
fact: "100,000 Fireflies" was the first single by The Magnetic Fields, taken from their 1991 debut album Distant Plastic Trees. It features the sparse, soprano vocals of Susan Anway, who sang on the band's early records but never performed live with them, and the song went on to become a cult favorite of 1990s mixtape culture, even earning a rocked-up cover from Superchunk.

title: Absolutely Cuckoo
fact: This jaunty, ukulele-strummed opener was meant to kick off an even bigger project — Stephin Merritt first planned 69 Love Songs as a 100-song set before runtime reality set in. The whole album traces back to a songwriting dare Merritt set for himself, inspired by composer Charles Ives's 114 Songs, and 'Absolutely Cuckoo' still carries a trace of an even earlier plan to make the record alphabetical from A to Z.

title: California Girls
fact: "California Girls," from The Magnetic Fields' 2008 album Distortion, is Stephin Merritt's tongue-in-cheek answer song to the Beach Boys' classic of the same name. For the whole record, Merritt aimed to sound "more Jesus and Mary Chain than Jesus and Mary Chain," running nearly every instrument, including guitars, piano, accordion, and strings, through tiny Smokey Amplifiers to build a deliberately overloaded wall-of-noise production.

title: Everything Is One Big Christmas Tree
fact: "Everything Is One Big Christmas Tree" appears on The Magnetic Fields' 2010 album Realism, a deliberately "back to basics," all-acoustic follow-up to their electronic record Distortion. The charmingly ramshackle holiday tune has been praised for sounding like the soundtrack to a half-remembered vintage animated Christmas special.

album: The Charm of the Highway Strip

title: I Don't Believe You
fact: 'I Don't Believe You' appears on The Magnetic Fields' 2004 album i, a concept record where all 14 songs - sung entirely by Stephin Merritt and sequenced alphabetically - begin with the letter 'I.' Unlike much of Merritt's other work, i was recorded using only hand-played instruments, with no synthesizers at all.

title: I Don't Want to Get Over You
fact: "I Don't Want to Get Over You" appears on The Magnetic Fields' sprawling 1999 triple album 69 Love Songs, 69 tracks about love written and sung by frontman Stephin Merritt for Merge Records. Its deadpan baritone vocal and bittersweet melody made it one of the collection's most enduring cuts, later covered by artists including Ben Gibbard and Superchunk.

title: I Think I Need a New Heart
I Thought You Were My Boyfriend
The Book of Love
fact: 'The Book of Love' is track 12 on disc one of The Magnetic Fields' sprawling 1999 concept album 69 Love Songs, written by Stephin Merritt. On the surface it's a dry, deadpan send-up of love-song cliches - opening with the line 'The book of love is long and boring' - but many listeners read it as a sincere marriage proposal hidden inside a joke, which is part of why it has become one of the most popular wedding songs of the 2000s and has been covered by numerous artists since.

title: Wi' Nae Wee Bairn Ye'll Me Beget
You and Me and the Moon
fact: "You and Me and the Moon" is track five on The Magnetic Fields' 1995 album Get Lost, written by the band's Stephin Merritt. In 2018, singer-songwriter Owen Ashworth covered it under his Advance Base project for the album Animal Companionship, part of a long line of artists who've cited Merritt's songwriting as a major influence.

title: Roulette Dares (The Haunt Of)
fact: Roulette Dares (The Haunt Of) comes from The Mars Volta's 2003 debut album, De-Loused in the Comatorium, made after the breakup of El Paso band At the Drive-In. Written by Omar Rodriguez-Lopez and Cedric Bixler-Zavala, the track stretches into extended, Pink Floyd-style instrumental passages that became a hallmark of the band's prog-influenced sound. The album eventually went Gold in the US.

title: My Roots Are Strong and Deep
fact: "My Roots Are Strong and Deep" is track B2 on The Microphones' 2001 album The Glow Pt. 2, the project's third studio release. The song has a hymn-like quality, built around a clanging, unsteady piano sound and washes of distorted toy piano.

Astral Plane
fact: The Modern Lovers' "Astral Plane" was produced by John Cale of the Velvet Underground during their mid-1970s demo sessions - Jonathan Richman's lyrics turn a rejected pickup line into a promise to meet someone on a higher plane of existence instead.

title: Andrew Eldritch Is Moving Back to Leeds
Candlebox
fact: "Candlebox" is from The Mountain Goats' 24th album, Days (August 2026), which John Darnielle originally planned to call Grunges as a spiritual sequel to 2017's Goths. The song follows a fictional bar band that lands a tour opening for '90s rockers Candlebox, and the real Mountain Goats then announced a tour with Candlebox.

title: Charlie Sheen Reaches Out to the Feds
fact: This one kicks off Days, the Mountain Goats' 24th studio album, which John Darnielle wrote in a single two-week burst while his wife was away — a writing situation he's compared to how he banged out All Hail West Texas back in 2002. The record was cut at Sear Sound in Manhattan with producer John Congleton, with guests including harpist Mikaela Davis and backing vocals from Janis Siegel of the Manhattan Transfer.

title: Cold at Night
album: Through This Fire Across From Peter Balkan
fact: "Cold at Night" comes from the Mountain Goats' 2025 concept album Through This Fire Across From Peter Balkan, about a group of shipwreck survivors stranded on a desert island, dedicated to longtime bassist Peter Hughes. The track brings in a stacked list of guest players: bass from Tommy Stinson (the Replacements, Guns N' Roses), guitar from Josh Kaufman (Bonny Light Horseman, the National), harp from Mikaela Davis, and harmony vocals from Lin-Manuel Miranda.

title: Fall of the Star High School Running Back
Get Famous
fact: "Get Famous" is the horn-backed second track on The Mountain Goats' 2020 album Getting into Knives, recorded in a single week at Sam Phillips Recording in Memphis with producer Matt Ross-Spang and a crew of local session musicians. Its 2020 music video portrays the band members as bobblehead dolls.

title: Make You Suffer
fact: "Make You Suffer" is from The Mountain Goats' 2022 album "Bleed Out," produced entirely by Bully's Alicia Bognanno and tracked in about a week at Sylvan Esso's Betty's studio near Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Frontman John Darnielle drew lyrical inspiration from vintage action movies of the 1960s through '80s.

title: Mobile
fact: "Mobile," from The Mountain Goats' 2021 album Dark in Here, recasts the Biblical story of Jonah with a Southern setting on the Gulf Coast in Mobile, Alabama. The track features veteran Muscle Shoals session players Spooner Oldham on electric piano and Will McFarlane on lead guitar.

title: Sicilian Crest
fact: 'Sicilian Crest,' from The Mountain Goats' 2019 album In League with Dragons, reportedly started as just a strange phrase John Darnielle had jotted in a notebook before he built the song around it while messing around at the piano with his son. Musically, it's one of the album's grandest, lushest moments, driven by florid piano and explosive drumming from Jon Wurster, with a dance-rock feel critics compared to New Order.

title: This Year
fact: "This Year" appears on the Mountain Goats' acclaimed 2005 album The Sunset Tree and has become the band's single most-performed song in concert. Setlist.fm logs it at more than 600 live performances, typically with the whole room singing the chorus back as one.

title: Training Montage
fact: "Training Montage" is the lead single from The Mountain Goats' 2022 album Bleed Out, which John Darnielle wrote by pausing favorite action movies from the '60s, '70s and '80s to jot lyrics on a boombox before hitting play again. The album was produced by Alicia Bognanno, frontwoman of the band Bully.

title: Wage Wars Get Rich Die Handsome
Bittersweet Demons
fact: The Murlocs were formed in 2010 by Ambrose Kenny-Smith, who also sings and plays harmonica in King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard - he'd known Murlocs drummer Matt Blach since primary school, though the two didn't start playing together until Kenny-Smith met guitarist Cal Shortal at a house party. "Bittersweet Demons," the title track from their 2021 album, gave the band their first top-ten entry on Australia's ARIA charts.

title: Alphabet City
fact: "Alphabet City" was released in August 2023 as one of two surprise new singles alongside "Space Invader," both arriving with visualizer videos directed by Pauline de Lassus (who records under the name Mina Tindle). "Space Invader" later resurfaced on the band's surprise second album that year, Laugh Track.

title: Apartment Story
fact: The National's "Apartment Story," from 2007's Boxer, was written by Matt Berninger and Aaron Dessner and produced by longtime collaborator Peter Katis - it became the album's second single after the band debuted it that same year on The Late Late Show with Craig Ferguson.

title: Day I Die
fact: "Day I Die" was released August 29, 2017 as the fourth single from The National's seventh album, Sleep Well Beast, following "The System Only Dreams in Total Darkness," "Guilty Party," and "Carin at the Liquor Store."

title: Demons
fact: Demons was the first single from The National's 2013 album Trouble Will Find Me. The album was recorded across several studios, from upstate New York to Los Angeles and the Michelberger Hotel in Berlin.

title: Don't Swallow The Cap
fact: The National formed in Brooklyn in 1999 after Cincinnati natives Aaron and Bryce Dessner - childhood friends of drummer Bryan Devendorf - were invited to join his band. They later started their own label, Brassland, to release their debut album.

title: Eucalyptus
fact: Guitarist Bryce Dessner sent an early demo of "Eucalyptus" to Matt Berninger so long before the song was finished that Berninger had nearly forgotten about it. Berninger eventually wrote lyrics for it and asked to debut it at soundcheck hours before a show at New York's Capitol Theatre; the band had never even rehearsed it with a full demo, and part of what ended up on the First Two Pages of Frankenstein (2023) album was captured live that night.

title: Hey Rosey
fact: "Hey Rosey" grew out of a collaboration between The National and filmmaker Mike Mills that became the band's 2019 album I Am Easy to Find, released alongside a short film starring Alicia Vikander. Its lyrics were written by Carin Besser, wife of frontman Matt Berninger, and keyboardist Aaron Dessner has said Mills' suggestion to let the pianist improvise the song's opening reshaped its final arrangement.

title: I Need My Girl
fact: 'I Need My Girl' is a single from The National's 2013 album Trouble Will Find Me. It's one of the band's more plaintive, piano-driven songs, with Matt Berninger's lyrics capturing the quiet relief of having one steady person to come home to - a hallmark of the band's knack for turning everyday adult unease into vivid, specific imagery.

title: Light Years
fact: The National's "Light Years" closes out 2019's I Am Easy to Find, an album recorded at their Long Pond studio in the Hudson Valley with sessions also in Paris, Berlin, Cincinnati, Austin, Dublin, and Brooklyn - it features guest vocals across the record from Sharon Van Etten, Lisa Hannigan, Mina Tindle, and the Brooklyn Youth Chorus.

title: Lit Up
fact: "Lit Up" appears on The National's 2005 album Alligator, but it had already been a staple of the band's live shows for a while before they recorded it. The album itself was tracked almost entirely in band members' home studios around Brooklyn, with composer Padma Newsome of the group Clogs guesting on piano, violin, and viola throughout.

title: Rylan
fact: "Rylan" dates back to the sessions for The National's 2010 album High Violet, and the band first played it live in December 2011. It then mostly vanished from their sets for years, and wasn't put on an album until I Am Easy to Find in 2019, when it was released as a single.

title: The Alcott (feat. Taylor Swift)
album: The First Two Pages of Frankenstein

title: The System Only Dreams In Total Darkness
fact: This lead single from The National's 2017 album Sleep Well Beast features something rare for the band: an honest-to-goodness guitar solo from Aaron Dessner. The National usually spreads the spotlight evenly across its members instead of letting one player take over, which makes the fuzzed-out solo here stand out. The album was recorded at Dessner's converted barn studio in New York's Hudson Valley and went on to win the Grammy for Best Alternative Music Album.

title: Tropic Morning News
fact: The title phrase was coined by Matt Berninger's wife and longtime co-writer Carin Besser, who used "tropic morning news" as a name for the overwhelming daily flood of news people scroll through. As the lead single from 2023's First Two Pages of Frankenstein, the album version blends a live performance recorded in Hamburg with parts played by the London Symphony Orchestra.

title: Weird Goodbyes (feat. Bon Iver)
fact: "Weird Goodbyes" grew out of National guitarist Aaron Dessner's ongoing side project Big Red Machine with Bon Iver's Justin Vernon, and that creative partnership is what brought Vernon onto the track. First released as a standalone single in 2022, the song later found a home on The National's surprise 2023 album Laugh Track.

title: You Had You Soul With You
Your Mind Is Not Your Friend (feat. Phoebe Bridgers)

The video was directed by Bridgers' brother, Jackson.

title: Another Girl, Another Planet
fact: Written by Peter Perrett, "Another Girl, Another Planet" is the second track on The Only Ones' 1978 debut album and was recorded at Escape Studios in Kent, England. It didn't chart on release, but after appearing on the 1991 compilation The Sound of the Suburbs it was reissued and reached number 57 in the UK, and it's now the band's best-known song.

title: I'm in Love With a German Film Star
fact: Despite the title, The Passions' "I'm in Love with a German Film Star" isn't really about a German film star - singer Barbara Gogan wrote it about Steve "Roadent" Connelly, a British former roadie for the Clash and Sex Pistols who happened to land a few minor German TV and film roles.

Turn Around
fact: Turn Around was left off The Postal Service's 2003 album Give Up and only surfaced on the Deluxe 10th Anniversary Edition in 2013. The band's name came from how they made the record: Jimmy Tamborello mailed CDs of electronic tracks from Los Angeles to Ben Gibbard in Seattle, who added vocals and melodies.

Message of Love
fact: Written by Chrissie Hynde and produced by Chris Thomas, "Message of Love" was recorded at Pathé Marconi Studios in Paris in 1980. Drummer Martin Chambers recalled that the song came together quickly from a rough sketch — the band set up, rehearsed, and had it on tape in about two hours — and it went on to reach No. 11 on the UK singles chart.

title: Fairytale in the Supermarket
fact: "Fairytale in the Supermarket" was the debut single by London post-punk band The Raincoats, recorded in March 1979 and released that April on Rough Trade. The all-female group performed it along with two other songs for BBC Radio 1 DJ John Peel around the same time. The song found a second life decades later after Kurt Cobain publicly praised the band, and it was later featured on the soundtrack to Mike Mills' 2016 film "20th Century Women."

title: Psychobilly Freakout
fact: "Psychobilly Freakout" began as a 7-inch single released in December 1990 on Sub Pop's Singles Club, pressed in a limited run of 1,000 copies (250 on blue vinyl, the rest black) before landing on the band's 1992 debut album. The song later turned up in a Buell Motorcycles commercial and in the video games Guitar Hero II and Guitar Hero Smash Hits.

title: (I'M) Stranded
fact: "(I'm) Stranded" was recorded in Brisbane in June 1976 and released that September on the band's own Fatal Records label, making The Saints the first punk band outside the US to put out a record, ahead of the Sex Pistols and The Clash. It was written by guitarist Ed Kuepper and singer Chris Bailey, and rave reviews in Britain got them signed to EMI.

title: Give Him A Great Big Kiss
Know Your Onion!
fact: "Know Your Onion!" opens The Shins' 2001 debut, Oh, Inverted World. Frontman James Mercer has said the song is about a young person who feels overwhelmed and misunderstood, finding escape in music and books; he name-checks "lucked out and found my favorite record lying in wait at the Birmingham mall." The title itself borrows the old idiom "know your onions," meaning to really know your stuff.

title: Name For You
fact: The Shins' "Name For You," from their 2017 album Heartworms, was inspired by frontman James Mercer's three daughters - a song of encouragement for young women.

title: Sleeping Lessons
fact: James Mercer has said 'Sleeping Lessons' was 'loosely based on a number of jobs I've had,' inspired by watching coworkers stay stuck in lives of drudgery they didn't have to accept. Musically, he built the song's guitar line as a twist on a blues run inspired by 1960s singer Gary 'U.S.' Bonds. It opens the Shins' 2007 album Wincing the Night Away, a title that nods to Mercer's long bout of insomnia.

title: Sometimes II
fact: The Shivas formed in Portland, Oregon in 2006 as high-school best friends - brothers Jared and Colby Molyneux plus Eric Shanafelt - and have since toured over 25 countries together.

title: Bending Hectic
fact: "Bending Hectic," from The Smile's 2024 album Wall of Eyes, was recorded at Abbey Road Studios with string arrangements by the London Contemporary Orchestra. The eight-minute track, written by Thom Yorke, Jonny Greenwood, and Tom Skinner, was performed live nearly two years before its release, debuting at Switzerland's Montreux Jazz Festival in July 2022. It builds slowly from a single detuned guitar into a heavy, crashing crescendo.

title: Bodies Laughing
fact: 'Bodies Laughing' appears on The Smile's 2024 album Cutouts, which was recorded during the very same sessions as its predecessor, Wall of Eyes. Thom Yorke and the band actually debuted the song live at a concert in Berlin back in 2022, two years before fans ever heard the studio version, which features Jonny Greenwood's ondes Martenot weaving through the mix. The Smile played that earlier live arrangement dozens of times before retooling it for the album.

title: Don't Get Me Started
fact: "Don't Get Me Started" was recorded by The Smile — Radiohead's Thom Yorke and Jonny Greenwood with drummer Tom Skinner — across sessions in Oxford and at Abbey Road Studios, produced and mixed by Sam Petts-Davies, who also helmed the band's Wall of Eyes. It arrived on vinyl paired with a sister track, "The Slip," and its music video was directed by Weirdcore, the longtime visual collaborator of Aphex Twin.

title: Foreign Spies
fact: The Smile is the side project of Radiohead's Thom Yorke and Jonny Greenwood together with drummer Tom Skinner, who first worked with Greenwood scoring the 2012 film The Master. Greenwood invited Skinner to jam in 2018, and the pair brought in Yorke a few months later to complete the trio. "Foreign Spies" comes from their 2024 album Cutouts, recorded during the same sessions as its predecessor Wall of Eyes, partly at Abbey Road Studios.

title: The Opposite
fact: 'The Opposite' is the second track on The Smile's 2022 debut album A Light for Attracting Attention, the trio project formed by Radiohead's Thom Yorke and Jonny Greenwood with drummer Tom Skinner. It's cheekily sequenced right after the album's opening track, 'The Same' - two songs with deliberately contrasting titles. Musically it locks into a tight, math-rock-style groove built from Greenwood's interlocking, finger-tapped guitar lines under Yorke's vocal.

title: Wall Of Eyes
fact: "Wall of Eyes" opens and titles the second album by The Smile, the trio of Thom Yorke, Jonny Greenwood, and drummer Tom Skinner. The track builds slowly from a single strummed acoustic guitar and muted floor-tom hits into a fuller arrangement, produced by Sam Petts-Davies, who has also worked on several of Yorke's solo projects.

title: You Will Never Work in Television Again
Zero Sum
fact: "Zero Sum" was recorded during the same sessions that produced The Smile's 2024 album Wall of Eyes, but ended up instead on their follow-up record, Cutouts, released that October. The band had been playing the rhythmically busy, punk-funk track live for months before the studio version surfaced alongside a Weirdcore-directed video.

title: A Rush and a Push and the Land Is Ours
Barbarism Begins at Home
fact: On "Barbarism Begins at Home," from 1985's Meat Is Murder, drummer Mike Joyce cued his part off Andy Rourke's repetitive, funk-inspired bass line rather than Johnny Marr's guitar — a rare arrangement choice in the Smiths' catalog. Marr later praised Rourke's bass work on the track as a highlight of the record.

title: Frankly, Mr. Shankly
fact: Johnny Marr wrote the music for Frankly, Mr. Shankly in late summer 1985, around the same time as There Is a Light That Never Goes Out. It is a comic letter to a boss on The Queen Is Dead, and is widely reputed to be aimed at Rough Trade Records head Geoff Travis.

title: Hand in Glove
fact: "Hand in Glove" was The Smiths' debut single, released in May 1983 on Rough Trade Records and recorded for just L250 at Strawberry Studios in Stockport. Johnny Marr wrote the music and Morrissey the lyrics, with Marr adding a harmonica overdub. A year later, 1960s pop star Sandie Shaw recorded her own version backed by the Smiths, giving her first UK hit in a decade, and the band performed barefoot alongside her on Top of the Pops as a nod to her famous bare feet performances in the 1960s.

title: I Know It's Over
fact: "I Know It's Over" was recorded in 1985 at Jacobs Studios for The Smiths' 1986 album The Queen Is Dead. The band originally considered adding trumpet over the song's closing refrain, even joking about a Shirley Bassey-style horn flourish, before scrapping the idea. Johnny Marr has called Morrissey's vocal take on the song one of the best performances of his career, saying simply, "It was that good, that strong."

title: Please, Please, Please Let Me Get What I Want
album: Please, Please, Please Let Me Get What I Want

title: Some Girls Are Bigger Than Others
Still Ill
fact: The Smiths' Still Ill got its title from a real conversation - Morrissey's friend, artist Linder Sterling, greeted him at a weekly rooftop-restaurant meetup by asking, "Are you still ill?"

title: Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before
The Boy With the Thorn in His Side
There Is a Light That Never Goes Out
This Night Has Opened My Eyes
fact: The Smiths' "This Night Has Opened My Eyes" was inspired by the play A Taste of Honey - Morrissey has said the play accounts for at least half of his reason for writing in the first place. The version released on 1984's Hatful of Hollow actually comes from a BBC Radio 1 John Peel session, not a proper studio single.

title: Well I Wonder
fact: "Well I Wonder" was the first song written for The Smiths' 1985 album Meat Is Murder. Guitarist Johnny Marr deliberately moved back to Manchester during pre-production to capture the right rainy atmosphere for the band's more instrumental, textured songs, and the finished track closes with the actual sound of rain and one of Morrissey's rare falsetto vocal turns.

title: Big Boy
fact: The Snails are a tongue-in-cheek side project born in Baltimore in 2008, featuring members of the band Future Islands performing under cartoonish snail aliases like Sandy Snailbelow and Snailliam. "Big Boy" appears on their 2013 release Worth the Wait.

title: SWEAT
fact: SWEAT is from GOLDSTAR (March 13, 2026), the album from The Sophs, who signed to Rough Trade after their demos impressed label founders Geoff Travis and Jeannette Lee.

title: SWEETIEPIE
fact: The Sophs are a six-piece from Los Angeles who signed to Rough Trade after cold-emailing demos to label heads Geoff Travis and Jeannette Lee before ever playing a show. SWEETIEPIE, from their debut album GOLDSTAR (2026), pairs a deadpan, Weezer-like vocal with country twang and a jaw harp.

title: That's What Girls Are Made For
The Rubberband Man

title: I Am The Resurrection
fact: "I Am the Resurrection" grew out of a joke in rehearsal: bassist Mani liked playing the riff from the Beatles' "Taxman" backwards while guitarist John Squire and drummer Reni fooled around on top of it. The eight-minute track closes the Stone Roses' 1989 debut album, and the band nailed its extended instrumental outro in a single take. It became the traditional set-closer at nearly every Stone Roses concert from then on.

title: Made of Stone
fact: "Made of Stone" was released in March 1989 and recorded across three studios -- Battery, Konk (owned by Kinks frontman Ray Davies), and Rockfield in Wales -- with the Stone Roses working through the night rather than during the day to nail the track. Produced by John Leckie, the song later re-entered the UK singles chart on six separate occasions between 1989 and 2022, and it also marked the band's national television debut on BBC's The Late Show that September.

title: She Bangs the Drums
fact: "She Bangs the Drums" was the second single from the Stone Roses' self-titled 1989 debut album and became the Manchester band's first UK Top 40 hit, peaking at No. 36. Ian Brown wrote the verse lyrics and John Squire the chorus, with the song generally described as being about the euphoria of falling in love.

title: Fuzz Bass Queen
fact: 'Fuzz Bass Queen' is a 2025 single from The Stone Souls, a desert-rock band out of Newcastle upon Tyne founded by Theodor Versteegen. Built around a heavily distorted, fuzzed-out bass line, the track mixes punk energy reminiscent of Green Day and Blink-182 with stoner-rock swagger, and its lyrics serve as a tribute to powerful women. One reviewer called it a contender for the best pop-punk anthem of the year.

title: Dry Your Eyes
album: A Grand Don't Come for Free

title: Fit but You Know It
album: A Grand Don't Come for Free

title: Brooklyn Bridge to Chorus
fact: "Brooklyn Bridge to Chorus" was released April 6, 2020 as the third single from The Strokes' The New Abnormal, the band's first album produced by Rick Rubin. Its synth-driven, new-wave sound drew comparisons to Julian Casablancas's solo work with The Voidz.

title: Eternal Summer
fact: "Eternal Summer" is a sprawling, six-minute-plus track from The Strokes' 2020 album "The New Abnormal," the band's first album in seven years. Julian Casablancas stretches his voice over a wash of psychedelic synths and guitars, building to a dramatic crescendo before the song loops back into a circular closing coda.

title: Falling Out of Love
fact: Falling Out of Love is the second single from The Strokes' seventh album, Reality Awaits (2026), produced by Rick Rubin. Recording began in 2022 in Costa Rica and continued at Rubin's Shangri-La and The Mansion studios in California.

title: Going Shopping
fact: To tease "Going Shopping," The Strokes mailed out 100 numbered cassette tapes to fans on their text list the morning before the song's official release. The track, lead single from their 2026 album Reality Awaits, went on to spend two weeks at number one on Billboard's Adult Alternative Airplay chart.

title: Happy Ending
fact: "Happy Ending" closes out The Strokes' 2013 album Comedown Machine. Guitarists Nick Valensi and Albert Hammond Jr. ran their guitars through effects to make them sound like vintage synthesizers, an '80s-leaning production trick that gives the track its funky, electro-tinged groove.

title: Lonely in the Future
fact: Lonely in the Future is track 3 on Reality Awaits, The Strokes' first album in six years and the follow-up to 2020's The New Abnormal. The band played the song in full live for the first time in Tokyo.

title: Oblivius
fact: 'Oblivius' was one of three songs on The Strokes' 2016 EP Future Present Past, alongside 'Drag Queen' and 'Threat of Joy,' each meant to represent a different timeframe for the band; 'Oblivius' stood in for the present. It was recorded with producer Gus Oberg in sessions split between New York City and Austin, Texas, blending the lo-fi feel of Room on Fire with the moodier touches of First Impressions of Earth.

title: Selfless
fact: Selfless, from The Strokes' 2020 album The New Abnormal, is built around a delicate string arrangement that gives the track an unusually dreamy, atmospheric quality for the band. It's introduced by a short snippet of studio chatter and a brief preview of the song bleeding in at the end of the preceding track. Singer Julian Casablancas leans into a softer falsetto for the song, a departure from the band's usual rougher vocal style.

title: Take It or Leave It
fact: "Take It or Leave It" closes The Strokes' 2001 debut album "Is This It," written by Julian Casablancas and produced by Gordon Raphael. The entire album was tracked in only about six weeks at Raphael's small Transporterraum studio in New York City, with Casablancas pushing the band to keep performances raw, often recording songs in just a take or two.

title: The Adults Are Talking
fact: "The Adults Are Talking" opens The Strokes' 2020 album "The New Abnormal," their first LP produced by Rick Rubin, recorded at his Shangri-La studio in Malibu. The band actually debuted the song live at the Wiltern Theatre in Los Angeles in May 2019, almost a full year before its studio version was released. Its music video, directed by Roman Coppola, imagines a future where the band competes against android ballplayers.

title: Birthday
fact: "Birthday" was The Sugarcubes' first international single, and it came together almost by accident: after a festival promoter couldn't pay the band for a gig, he offered them free studio time instead, and this song is what they wrote with it. Released in 1987, it introduced a young Bjork to audiences outside Iceland and topped John Peel's Festive Fifty list that year.

title: Regina
fact: "Regina" was the lead single from The Sugarcubes' second album, Here Today, Tomorrow, Next Week! (1989), and became the Icelandic band's biggest U.S. hit, reaching No. 2 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart.

title: Here's Where the Story Ends
fact: "Here's Where the Story Ends" was written by Sundays members David Gavurin and Harriet Wheeler for the band's 1990 debut album "Reading, Writing and Arithmetic," produced by the band with Ray Shulman. It became the group's biggest international hit, topping the US Modern Rock Tracks chart even though it was never issued as a UK single. In 1998, dance duo Tin Tin Out reworked the song into a UK top-10 hit that went on to win the 1999 Ivor Novello Award for Best Contemporary Song.

title: Life Goes On
fact: The Sundays' “Life Goes On” opens with “Build me up don't get me down, weather the storm, well, life goes on” - a simple, steady message of resilience from their final album, Static & Silence.

title: You're Not the Only One I Know
fact: "You're Not the Only One I Know" appears on the Sundays' 1990 debut album Reading, Writing and Arithmetic, one of the era-defining releases of the British jangle-pop scene. Thirty-five years after its release, the song found a whole new audience when it went viral on social media alongside the band's other classic tracks.

Stoop To Me
fact: Stoop to Me is a single from Hard Life, the new album from London band The Tubs on Merge Records. Fiddle player Chris Haigh adds jangly licks, and the band calls it their most power-pop song, with nods to Bob Mould.

title: Who s Gonna Love You Now?
fact: "Who's Gonna Love You Now?" is the lead single from Hard Life (2026, Merge Records), the third album by London band The Tubs, following 2025's Cotton Crown. Singer Owen Williams describes it as a Northern Soul-inspired pop song with organs, influenced by the Australian band Royal Headache.

title: Dying for It
fact: "Dying for It" is the title track of the Scottish duo The Vaselines' 1988 EP, recorded at Pierhouse Studios in Edinburgh and released on 53rd & 3rd Records. Kurt Cobain named the EP one of his all-time favorite releases, and Nirvana went on to cover two of its other songs, "Molly's Lips" and "Jesus Wants Me for a Sunbeam."

title: Jesus Wants Me for a Sunbeam
Molly's Lips
fact: "Molly's Lips" was written and first recorded by Scottish duo Eugene Kelly and Frances McKee of The Vaselines, appearing on their 1988 "Dying for It" EP. Kurt Cobain was a huge fan and had Nirvana cover the song for a 1990 BBC Radio 1 John Peel session (drummer Dave Grohl's first with the band), later included on 1992's "Incesticide." Cobain's championing of the duo helped reunite The Vaselines, and Kelly even joined Nirvana on stage to perform the song at the 1991 Reading Festival.

title: An Ocean in Between the Waves
Best Night
fact: "Best Night" appears on The War on Drugs' 2011 album Slave Ambient and was later issued as its own single in 2012. Adam Granduciel wrote and co-produced the track with Jeff Zeigler, with onetime member Kurt Vile — who'd left the band a few years earlier to focus on his solo career — guesting on guitar.

title: Eyes To The Wind
fact: 'Eyes to the Wind' appears on The War on Drugs' 2014 breakthrough album Lost in the Dream, and frontman Adam Granduciel has called it his favorite song on the record. It's a reflective, anthemic track about returning home and realizing how much you've changed while you were away. The album took about 18 months to record and was shaped partly by Granduciel's love of Raymond Carver's spare short stories.

title: Harmonia's Dream
fact: "Harmonia's Dream," from The War on Drugs' 2021 album "I Don't Live Here Anymore," takes its title from the German krautrock supergroup Harmonia, formed by Cluster's Hans-Joachim Roedelius and Dieter Moebius with Neu! guitarist Michael Rother. Frontman Adam Granduciel has described being a longtime devotee of that scene's records. The track, co-produced by Shawn Everett and co-written with keyboardist Robbie Bennett, earned a Grammy nomination for Best Rock Song.

title: Holding On
fact: The War on Drugs' "Holding On" led off 2017's A Deeper Understanding, which won the Grammy for Best Rock Album - Adam Granduciel recorded it with engineer Shawn Everett, who's also worked with Alabama Shakes and Weezer, and the song later turned up on the official soundtrack of EA Sports' FIFA 18.

title: I Don't Live Here Anymore
fact: The War on Drugs' Adam Granduciel has said the title I Don't Live Here Anymore describes a feeling more than a place - "you know exactly what you're not, but that doesn't mean you know where you're going." The record was written as he was becoming a father.

title: Living Proof
fact: This opening track from 2021's I Don't Live Here Anymore marked a change in process for frontman Adam Granduciel, who typically builds songs from layers of overdubs; instead, "Living Proof" was recorded live in real time with the full band at Electro-Vox Studios in Los Angeles. Its music video was shot on 16mm film by director Emmett Malloy at Panoramic Studio in Stinson Beach, California.

title: Red Eyes
fact: "Red Eyes" was released as the lead single from The War on Drugs' Lost in the Dream on December 4, 2013, roughly three months ahead of the full album. Frontman Adam Granduciel spent about 15 months writing, demoing, and recording the record across five different studios in several states, an unusually drawn-out process for the band.

title: Suffering
fact: 'Suffering' is a six-minute slow-burner off The War on Drugs' breakthrough Lost in the Dream (2014), an album that took eight months to make as the band bounced between a half-dozen studios, from the mountains of North Carolina all the way to the boroughs of New York City. That restless, drawn-out process became part of the record's legend, helping turn it into one of the most acclaimed rock albums of the 2010s.

title: Under The Pressure
fact: "Under the Pressure" opens The War on Drugs' 2014 album Lost in the Dream with nearly nine minutes of slow-building krautrock groove, starting with ticking electronics and closing out with over two minutes of swirling, synchronized feedback. The track sets the tone for an album steeped in '80s heartland rock and motorik rhythm. At that length, it's one of the longest tracks the Philadelphia band has ever used to open an album.

title: Who's That
fact: The War on Drugs' "Who's That" was the band's first new recording since 2021's I Don't Live Here Anymore - recorded at Adam Granduciel's own warehouse studio in Burbank, with contributions from Spoon's Alex Fischel alongside the full War on Drugs lineup.

title: Fisherman's Blues
fact: The title track of The Waterboys' 1988 album was recorded on the very first day of sessions that stretched from early 1986 to 1988, producing around 100 songs. Mike Scott moved to Ireland during the recording, and the album's folk and country blend was a big shift from the band's earlier grand rock sound; it became their best-selling record.

title: Neon Signs
fact: "Neon Signs" is the first single from The Weather Station's 2025 album Humanhood on Fat Possum Records. Tamara Lindeman co-produced the record with Marcus Paquin, recording it in fall 2023 with a live band featuring drummer Kieran Adams, keyboardist Ben Boye, percussionist Philippe Melanson, reed player Karen Ng, and bassist Ben Whiteley. Lindeman also co-directed the song's music video.

title: Window
fact: Window is the second single from The Weather Station's 2025 album Humanhood (Fat Possum). Tamara Lindeman co-produced the 13-track album with Marcus Paquin and recorded it in fall 2023 at Canterbury Music Company, mixing 1960s psychedelic pop, jazz and spoken-word collage.

title: Brassneck
fact: Brassneck opens The Wedding Present's 1989 album Bizarro and takes its title from a British slang term for shameless cheek or nerve. It became the Leeds band's highest-charting UK single to date, reaching number 24. The band also changed a key closing lyric for the single edit, swapping the album version's "I don't trust you anymore" for "I don't love you anymore" on the 7-inch release.

title: I Feel It Coming (feat. Daft Punk)
Ball and Biscuit
fact: At 7:17, "Ball and Biscuit" is the longest studio track The White Stripes ever recorded, and Jack White wrote it on the spot while making 2003's Elephant. It was recorded live to an 8-track reel-to-reel machine at Toe Rag Studios in London, a strictly analog session where the band famously used no computers at any stage of recording, mixing, or mastering. The song's heavily distorted guitar solos, run through an octave pedal, were improvised.

title: Dead Leaves and the Dirty Ground
Fell in Love With a Girl
Hello Operator
fact: "Hello Operator" was the only single from The White Stripes' second album, De Stijl (2000), released with a cover of Dolly Parton's "Jolene" on the B-side. The album was recorded in a living room on an 8-track tape machine, and UK DJ John Peel picked the single as his "single of the week" even though it wasn't released in the UK.

title: Hotel Yorba
fact: The Hotel Yorba is a real, slightly run-down building in southwest Detroit that Jack White heard rumors about growing up, and the single version of this song was recorded live, on the sly, right inside room 206 of the actual hotel. The duo later shot the music video outside the building but were refused permission to film inside — legend has it they're banned from the place for life.

title: I Just Don't Know What to Do With Myself
The Big Three Killed My Baby
fact: "The Big Three Killed My Baby," from The White Stripes' self-titled 1999 debut album, takes aim at Detroit's "Big Three" automakers — Ford, GM, and Chrysler — criticizing the industry's practice of planned obsolescence and its resistance to innovations like electric engines. Jack White wrote the track, which was also released as a 7-inch single.

title: There's No Home for You Here
You Don't Know What Love Is (You Do As Your Told)
You're Pretty Good Looking For A Girl
fact: This one started life on 2000's De Stijl, but it got a second life two decades later: a live version recorded at a 2001 Louisville show was dug up for the 20th-anniversary White Blood Cells companion release. Fittingly, it's often singled out as maybe the gentlest, tamest song in the entire White Stripes catalog.

title: Angels
fact: "Angels" was the lead single from The xx's 2012 album Coexist, written and originally demoed solo by Romy Madley Croft before the rest of the band spent nearly the entire recording process figuring out how to arrange it together. Croft has said the song is simply about being in love and is "very positive lyrically."

title: I Dare You
fact: "I Dare You" is widely considered the most upbeat, hopeful song on the xx's 2017 album I See You, with Romy Madley Croft and Oliver Sim trading vulnerable lines about taking a chance on new love. Its music video was shot as a tribute to Los Angeles, where the band wrote and recorded much of the record.

title: Intro
fact: "Intro," the instrumental opening track of The xx's 2009 debut album xx, was composed by the band and produced by Jamie xx. It went on to soundtrack numerous TV commercials, served as the BBC's theme for the UK's 2010 general election coverage, and was later sampled by Rihanna on her 2011 album Talk That Talk.

title: Islands
fact: "Islands," the third single from The xx's self-titled 2009 debut, was co-written by all four original members: Romy Madley Croft, Oliver Sim, Jamie xx, and then-member Baria Qureshi. Its spare, house-influenced production and interlocking male-female vocals helped define the London band's minimalist early sound.

title: Say Something Loving
fact: Two members of The xx, Romy Madley Croft and Oliver Sim, actually met in preschool at age three, growing up in the same London suburb. They reconnected years later at secondary school to start the band.

title: Crushed Grass
fact: John Dwyer of Thee Oh Sees is remarkably prolific, releasing music under the band's various names at a rate of roughly an album a year for two decades. He also co-runs Castle Face Records, a label with nearly 200 releases that's also home to Ty Segall.

title: Don't Let's Start
album: They Might Be Giants (The Pink Album)

title: I Should Be Allowed to Think
Particle Man
fact: "Particle Man" was never released as a single, yet it became one of They Might Be Giants' most recognized songs after Warner Bros. turned it into an animated music video for the 1991 series Tiny Toon Adventures. That TV exposure introduced a lot of young viewers to the band's 1990 album Flood for the first time.

title: They'll Need a Crane
fact: "They'll Need a Crane," from 1988's Lincoln, was the first song They Might Be Giants ever performed on network television, appearing on Late Night with David Letterman in 1989. Songwriter John Linnell said the tune started, as many TMBG songs do, from an old Gerry & the Pacemakers guitar riff paired with a title the band liked, with the song built around it afterward.

title: The Boys Are Back In Town
Billy Came Back
fact: "Billy Came Back" is the lead single from This Is Lorelei's Matador Records debut, The Singer in My Band, released in September 2026. Songwriter Nate Amos (also of Water From Your Eyes) based it on a real local karaoke singer he knew but lost touch with in 2022. The album's cast of characters, including Billy, took shape slowly while Amos was on tour, developing in his head as what he called an "intangible thing" while looking out the van window.

title: Holo Boy
fact: "Holo Boy" is the closing title track of This Is Lorelei's December 2025 album, which collects re-recorded versions of songs Nate Amos originally released across nine different Bandcamp projects between 2014 and 2021. Amos says the roughly 90-second lo-fi track was written in Chicago around 2014-2015, making it the oldest song on the record and one of his personal favorites.

title: Oh No Now My
fact: 'Oh No Now My,' from Nate Amos's 2026 album The Singer in My Band, went through three entirely different versions before landing on its final form. The finished track stacks vocal harmonies up to Beach Boys-level heights over heavier, low-tuned guitars than much of the rest of the record.

title: The Kid With the Crown
fact: This Is Lorelei is a solo alias for Nate Amos, also known as half of the duo Water From Your Eyes. He has released dozens of albums under the name on Bandcamp since 2013.

album: Box for Buddy, Box for Star
fact: "Where's Your Love Now" is a 2024 single by This Is Lorelei, the solo project of Water From Your Eyes' Nate Amos, from his album "Box for Buddy, Box for Star." The song drew wider attention after Waxahatchee's Katie Crutchfield covered it with Brad Cook at a Newport Folk Festival afterparty, calling it one of the best songs she'd ever heard, and later performed it in-studio for KEXP.
